cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which US plan gave massive financial help for reviving Europe’s economy after 1945?
cards.back: America extended massive financial help for reviving Europe’s economy under what was called the ‘Marshall Plan’.
cards.quote: America extended massive financial help for reviving Europe’s economy under what was called the ‘Marshall Plan’.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which collective security structure did the US create in Europe after the Second World War?
cards.back: The US also created a new collective security structure under NATO.
cards.quote: The US also created a new collective security structure under NATO.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which organisation was established in 1948 under the Marshall Plan to channel aid to west European states?
cards.back: Under the Marshall Plan, the Organisation for European Economic Cooperation (OEEC) was established in 1948 to channel aid to the west European states.
cards.quote: Under the Marshall Plan, the Organisation for European Economic Cooperation (OEEC) was established in 1948 to channel aid to the west European states.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The Council of Europe, established in ____, was another step forward in political cooperation.
cards.back: The Council of Europe, established in 1949, was another step forward in political cooperation.
cards.quote: The Council of Europe, established in 1949, was another step forward in political cooperation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When was the European Economic Community formed?
cards.back: leading to the formation of the European Economic Community in 1957.
cards.quote: leading to the formation of the European Economic Community in 1957.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the collapse of the Soviet bloc lead to in Europe?
cards.back: The collapse of the Soviet bloc put Europe on a fast track and resulted in the establishment of the European Union in 1992.
cards.quote: The collapse of the Soviet bloc put Europe on a fast track and resulted in the establishment of the European Union in 1992.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How has the European Union evolved over time?
cards.back: The European Union has evolved over time from an economic union to an increasingly political one.
cards.quote: The European Union has evolved over time from an economic union to an increasingly political one.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the four things the EU has, like a nation state.
cards.back:
flag
anthem
founding date
currency
cards.quote: it has its own flag, anthem, founding date, and currency.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How many stars does the EU flag have, and why that number?
cards.back: It has twelve stars, as the number twelve is traditionally the symbol of perfection, completeness and unity.
cards.quote: It has twelve stars, as the number twelve is traditionally the symbol of perfection, completeness and unity.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What does a Schengen visa allow?
cards.back: Under the Schengen agreement, you have to get a visa from just one of the EU countries and that allows you entry in most of the other European Union countries.
cards.quote: Under the Schengen agreement, you have to get a visa from just one of the EU countries and that allows you entry in most of the other European Union countries.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which EU currency can pose a threat to the dominance of the US dollar?
cards.back: Its currency, the euro, can pose a threat to the dominance of the US dollar.
cards.quote: Its currency, the euro, can pose a threat to the dominance of the US dollar.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why is the EU more assertive in trade disputes with the US and China?
cards.back: Its share of world trade is much larger than that of the United States allowing it to be more assertive in trade disputes with the US and China.
cards.quote: Its share of world trade is much larger than that of the United States allowing it to be more assertive in trade disputes with the US and China.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which EU member holds a permanent seat on the UN Security Council?
cards.back: of the EU, France, holds permanent seat on the UN Security Council.
cards.quote: of the EU, France, holds permanent seat on the UN Security Council.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How do the EU’s combined armed forces rank in the world?
cards.back: Militarily, the EU’s combined armed forces are the second largest in the world.
cards.quote: Militarily, the EU’s combined armed forces are the second largest in the world.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the EU’s rank as a source of space and communications technology?
cards.back: It is also the world’s second most important source of space and communications technology.
cards.quote: It is also the world’s second most important source of space and communications technology.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: As what kind of organisation is the EU able to intervene in economic, political and social areas?
cards.back: As a supranational organisation, the EU is able to intervene in economic, political and social areas.
cards.quote: As a supranational organisation, the EU is able to intervene in economic, political and social areas.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which two EU countries resisted the Maastricht Treaty and the euro?
cards.back: Denmark and Sweden have resisted the Maastricht Treaty and the adoption of the euro, the common European currency.
cards.quote: Denmark and Sweden have resisted the Maastricht Treaty and the adoption of the euro, the common European currency.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was signed in April 1951 and by which six countries?
cards.back: 1951 April: Six west European countries, France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg sign the Treaty of Paris establishing the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC).
cards.quote: 1951 April: Six west European countries, France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg sign the Treaty of Paris establishing the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which treaties of 1957 set up the EEC and Euratom?
cards.back: 1957 March 25: These six countries sign the Treaties of Rome establishing the European Economic Community (EEC) and the European Atomic Energy Community (Euratom).
cards.quote: 1957 March 25: These six countries sign the Treaties of Rome establishing the European Economic Community (EEC) and the European Atomic Energy Community (Euratom).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which countries joined the EEC in January 1973?
cards.back: 1973 January: Denmark, Ireland and the United Kingdom join the European Economic Community (EEC).
cards.quote: 1973 January: Denmark, Ireland and the United Kingdom join the European Economic Community (EEC).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What happened in June 1979 in European integration?
cards.back: 1979 June: First direct elections to the European Parliament
cards.quote: 1979 June: First direct elections to the European Parliament

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which 1985 agreement abolished border controls among EEC members?
cards.back: 1985 June: The Schengen Agreement abolishes border controls among the EEC members.
cards.quote: 1985 June: The Schengen Agreement abolishes border controls among the EEC members.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The Treaty of ____ was signed establishing the European Union (EU).
cards.back: The Treaty of Maastricht was signed establishing the European Union (EU).
cards.quote: The Treaty of Maastricht was signed establishing the European Union (EU).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What happened to the EEC’s name in January 1993?
cards.back: 1993 January: European Economic Community (EEC) was renamed the European Community (EC).
cards.quote: 1993 January: European Economic Community (EEC) was renamed the European Community (EC).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which countries joined the EU in January 1995?
cards.back: 1995 January: Austria, Finland and Sweden join the EU.
cards.quote: 1995 January: Austria, Finland and Sweden join the EU.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When was the euro introduced, and in how many EU members?
cards.back: 2002 January: Euro, the new currency, was introduced in the 12 EU members.
cards.quote: 2002 January: Euro, the new currency, was introduced in the 12 EU members.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which ten new members joined the EU in May 2004?
cards.back: 2004 May: Ten new members, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia join the EU.
cards.quote: 2004 May: Ten new members, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia join the EU.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which countries joined the EU in January 2007?
cards.back: 2007 January: Bulgaria and Romania join the EU.
cards.quote: 2007 January: Bulgaria and Romania join the EU.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which treaty came into force in December 2009?
cards.back: 2009 December: The Lisbon Treaty came into force.
cards.quote: 2009 December: The Lisbon Treaty came into force.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which prize was the EU awarded in 2012?
cards.back: 2012 : The EU is awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
cards.quote: 2012 : The EU is awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which country became the 28th member of the EU in 2013?
cards.back: 2013: Croatia becomes the 28th member of the EU.
cards.quote: 2013: Croatia becomes the 28th member of the EU.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the 2016 referendum in Britain decide?
cards.back: 2016: Referendum in Britain, 51.9 per cent voters decide that Britain exit (Brexit) from the EU.
cards.quote: 2016: Referendum in Britain, 51.9 per cent voters decide that Britain exit (Brexit) from the EU.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When and how was ASEAN established, and by which five countries?
cards.back: ASEAN was established in 1967 by five countries of this region — Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand — by signing the Bangkok Declaration.
cards.quote: ASEAN was established in 1967 by five countries of this region — Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand — by signing the Bangkok Declaration.

source.section: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the five founding members of ASEAN.
cards.back:
Indonesia
Malaysia
the Philippines
Singapore
Thailand
cards.quote: Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand

source.section: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How many members did ASEAN have after Cambodia joined?
cards.back: Cambodia joined ASEAN taking its strength to ten.
cards.quote: Cambodia joined ASEAN taking its strength to ten.

source.section: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the ‘ASEAN Way’?
cards.back: what has become known as the ‘ASEAN Way’, a form of interaction that is informal, non-confrontationist and cooperative.
cards.quote: what has become known as the ‘ASEAN Way’, a form of interaction that is informal, non-confrontationist and cooperative.

source.section: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How does ASEAN differ from the EU on supranational structures?
cards.back: Unlike the EU there is little desire in ASEAN for supranational structures and institutions.
cards.quote: Unlike the EU there is little desire in ASEAN for supranational structures and institutions.

source.section: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is critical to the functioning of ASEAN?
cards.back: The respect for national sovereignty is critical to the functioning of ASEAN.
cards.quote: The respect for national sovereignty is critical to the functioning of ASEAN.

source.section: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the three pillars of the ASEAN Community (agreed in 2003).
cards.back:
ASEAN Security Community
ASEAN Economic Community
ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community
cards.quote: comprising three pillars, namely, the ASEAN Security Community, the ASEAN Economic Community and the ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community.

source.section: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF), which was established in ____,
cards.back: The ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF), which was established in 1994,
cards.quote: The ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF), which was established in 1994,

source.section: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What are the objectives of the ASEAN Economic Community?
cards.back: The objectives of the ASEAN Economic Community are to create a common market and production base within ASEAN states and to aid social and economic development in the region.
cards.quote: The objectives of the ASEAN Economic Community are to create a common market and production base within ASEAN states and to aid social and economic development in the region.

source.section: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: For what has ASEAN focused on creating a Free Trade Area?
cards.back: ASEAN has focused on creating a Free Trade Area (FTA) for investment, labour, and services.
cards.quote: ASEAN has focused on creating a Free Trade Area (FTA) for investment, labour, and services.

source.section: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What has ASEAN’s Vision 2020 defined?
cards.back: Its Vision 2020 has defined an outward-looking role for ASEAN in the international community.
cards.quote: Its Vision 2020 has defined an outward-looking role for ASEAN in the international community.

source.section: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which conflicts has ASEAN mediated the end of?
cards.back: ASEAN has mediated the end of the Cambodian conflict, the East Timor crisis, and meets annually to discuss East Asian cooperation.
cards.quote: ASEAN has mediated the end of the Cambodian conflict, the East Timor crisis, and meets annually to discuss East Asian cooperation.

source.section: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: India’s ‘____’ Policy since the early 1990s and ‘____’ Policy since 2014
cards.back: India’s ‘Look East’ Policy since the early 1990s and ‘Act East’ Policy since 2014
cards.quote: India’s ‘Look East’ Policy since the early 1990s and ‘Act East’ Policy since 2014

source.section: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The ASEAN-India FTA came into effect in ____.
cards.back: The ASEAN-India FTA came into effect in 2010.
cards.quote: The ASEAN-India FTA came into effect in 2010.

source.section: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why is ASEAN unique among regional associations in Asia?
cards.back: It is the only regional association in Asia that provides a political forum where Asian countries and the major powers can discuss political and security concerns.
cards.quote: It is the only regional association in Asia that provides a political forum where Asian countries and the major powers can discuss political and security concerns.

source.section: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: On which model was China’s economy based after 1949?
cards.back: After the inception of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, following the communist revolution under the leadership of Mao, its economy was based on the Soviet model.
cards.quote: After the inception of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, following the communist revolution under the leadership of Mao, its economy was based on the Soviet model.

source.section: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the Soviet-style model China followed after 1949?
cards.back: The model was to create a state-owned heavy industries sector from the capital accumulated from agriculture.
cards.quote: The model was to create a state-owned heavy industries sector from the capital accumulated from agriculture.

source.section: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did China do about imports for want of foreign exchange?
cards.back: China decided to substitute imports by domestic goods.
cards.quote: China decided to substitute imports by domestic goods.

source.section: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: China ended its political and economic isolation with the establishment of relations with the United States in ____.
cards.back: China ended its political and economic isolation with the establishment of relations with the United States in 1972.
cards.quote: China ended its political and economic isolation with the establishment of relations with the United States in 1972.

source.section: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the four modernisations proposed by Zhou Enlai in 1973.
cards.back:
agriculture
industry
science and technology
military
cards.quote: Premier Zhou Enlai proposed the ‘four modernisations’ (agriculture, industry, science and technology and military) in 1973.

source.section: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who announced the ‘open door’ policy in China, and by when?
cards.back: By 1978, the then leader Deng Xiaoping announced the ‘open door’ policy and economic reforms in China.
cards.quote: By 1978, the then leader Deng Xiaoping announced the ‘open door’ policy and economic reforms in China.

source.section: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the aim of China’s ‘open door’ policy?
cards.back: The policy was to generate higher productivity by investments of capital and technology from abroad.
cards.quote: The policy was to generate higher productivity by investments of capital and technology from abroad.

source.section: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did China introduce a market economy, unlike shock therapy?
cards.back: The Chinese did not go for ‘shock therapy’ but opened their economy step by step.
cards.quote: The Chinese did not go for ‘shock therapy’ but opened their economy step by step.

source.section: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When were agriculture and industry privatised in China?
cards.back: The privatisation of agriculture in 1982 was followed by the privatisation of industry in 1998.
cards.quote: The privatisation of agriculture in 1982 was followed by the privatisation of industry in 1998.

source.section: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In China, where were trade barriers eliminated and foreign investors allowed to set up enterprises?
cards.back: Trade barriers were eliminated only in Special Economic Zones (SEZs) where foreign investors could set up enterprises.
cards.quote: Trade barriers were eliminated only in Special Economic Zones (SEZs) where foreign investors could set up enterprises.

source.section: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What role did the state play in China’s market economy?
cards.back: In China, the state played and continues to play a central role in setting up a market economy.
cards.quote: In China, the state played and continues to play a central role in setting up a market economy.

source.section: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In which year did China accede to the WTO?
cards.back: WTO in 2001 has been a further step in its opening to the outside world.
cards.quote: WTO in 2001 has been a further step in its opening to the outside world.

source.section: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which problems accompanied the benefits of China’s reforms?
cards.back: Environmental degradation and corruption have increased besides a rise in economic inequality between rural and urban residents and coastal and inland provinces.
cards.quote: Environmental degradation and corruption have increased besides a rise in economic inequality between rural and urban residents and coastal and inland provinces.

source.section: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How does China hope to resolve its differences with Taiwan?
cards.back: It hopes to resolve its differences with Taiwan, which it regards as a renegade province, by integrating it closely into its economy.
cards.quote: It hopes to resolve its differences with Taiwan, which it regards as a renegade province, by integrating it closely into its economy.

source.section: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did China ease fears of its rise in ASEAN?
cards.back: Fears of China’s rise have also been mitigated by its contributions to the stability of the ASEAN economies after the 1997 financial crisis.
cards.quote: Fears of China’s rise have also been mitigated by its contributions to the stability of the ASEAN economies after the 1997 financial crisis.

source.section: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: On what system was China’s influence on its periphery based?
cards.back: China had considerable influence and control on the periphery of its borders based on its unique tributary system.
cards.quote: China had considerable influence and control on the periphery of its borders based on its unique tributary system.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which slogan was briefly popular in India–China relations?
cards.back: For a brief while, the slogan of ‘Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai’
cards.quote: For a brief while, the slogan of ‘Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai’

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What differences arose between India and China soon after independence?
cards.back: Soon after independence, both states were involved in differences arising from the Chinese takeover of Tibet in 1950 and the final settlement of the Sino-Indian border.
cards.quote: Soon after independence, both states were involved in differences arising from the Chinese takeover of Tibet in 1950 and the final settlement of the Sino-Indian border.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Over which regions was the 1962 India–China border conflict fought?
cards.back: China and India were involved in a border conflict in 1962 over competing territorial claims principally in Arunachal Pradesh and in the Aksai Chin region of Ladakh.
cards.quote: China and India were involved in a border conflict in 1962 over competing territorial claims principally in Arunachal Pradesh and in the Aksai Chin region of Ladakh.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Until which year were diplomatic relations between India and China downgraded after the 1962 conflict?
cards.back: Diplomatic relations between the two countries were downgraded until 1976.
cards.quote: Diplomatic relations between the two countries were downgraded until 1976.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did China’s policy change after the mid to late 1970s?
cards.back: After the change in China’s political leadership from the mid to late 1970s, China’s policy became more pragmatic and less ideological.
cards.quote: After the change in China’s political leadership from the mid to late 1970s, China’s policy became more pragmatic and less ideological.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In which year were talks to resolve the India-China border issue initiated?
cards.back: A series of talks to resolve the border issue were also initiated in 1981.
cards.quote: A series of talks to resolve the border issue were also initiated in 1981.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Whose visit in December 1988 improved India–China relations?
cards.back: Rajiv Gandhi’s visit to China in December 1988 provided the impetus for an improvement in India–China relations.
cards.quote: Rajiv Gandhi’s visit to China in December 1988 provided the impetus for an improvement in India–China relations.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which agreements did India and China sign after 1988?
cards.back: They have also signed agreements on cultural exchanges and cooperation in science and technology, and opened four border posts for trade.
cards.quote: They have also signed agreements on cultural exchanges and cooperation in science and technology, and opened four border posts for trade.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In which international economic institutions do India and China adopt similar policies?
cards.back: At the global level, India and China have adopted similar policies in international economic institutions like the World Trade Organisation.
cards.quote: At the global level, India and China have adopted similar policies in international economic institutions like the World Trade Organisation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the two Indian concerns about China's role in South Asia (Pakistan; Bangladesh and Myanmar).
cards.back:
China was seen as contributing to the build up of Pakistan’s nuclear programme
China’s military relations with Bangladesh and Myanmar were viewed as hostile to Indian interests in South Asia
cards.quote: China was seen as contributing to the build up of Pakistan’s nuclear programme. China’s military relations with Bangladesh and Myanmar were viewed as hostile to Indian interests in South Asia.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the factors for the recent downslide in India–China relations.
cards.back:
Border disputes
China-Pakistan economic corridor
China’s support to Pakistan in UN against India’s move to counter terrorism
cards.quote: Border disputes, China-Pakistan economic corridor and China’s support to Pakistan in UN against India’s move to counter terrorism are some of the factors for it.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Japan became a member of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) in ____.
cards.back: Japan became a member of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) in 1964.
cards.quote: Japan became a member of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) in 1964.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Japan: what is its position in the G-7?
cards.back: It is the only Asian member of the G-7.
cards.quote: It is the only Asian member of the G-7.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What distinction does Japan hold regarding nuclear bombs?
cards.back: Japan is the only nation that suffered the destruction caused by nuclear bombs.
cards.quote: Japan is the only nation that suffered the destruction caused by nuclear bombs.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Japan has a security alliance with the US since ____.
cards.back: Japan has a security alliance with the US since 1951.
cards.quote: Japan has a security alliance with the US since 1951.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which provision of the Japanese Constitution renounces war as a sovereign right?
cards.back: As per Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution, “the Japanese people forever renounce war as a sovereign right of the nation and the threat or use of force as means of settling international disputes.”
cards.quote: As per Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution, “the Japanese people forever renounce war as a sovereign right of the nation and the threat or use of force as means of settling international disputes.”

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Along which line was the Korean peninsula divided at the end of the Second World War?
cards.back: The Korean peninsula was divided into South Korea (Republic of Korea) and North Korea (Democratic People’s Republic of Korea) at the end of the Second World War along the 38th Parallel.
cards.quote: The Korean peninsula was divided into South Korea (Republic of Korea) and North Korea (Democratic People’s Republic of Korea) at the end of the Second World War along the 38th Parallel.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did both the Koreas become Members of the UN?
cards.back: Both the Koreas finally became Members of the UN on 17 September 1991.
cards.quote: Both the Koreas finally became Members of the UN on 17 September 1991.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is South Korea’s rapid growth in the 1960s–1980s termed?
cards.back: Between the 1960s and the 1980s, it rapidly developed into an economic power, which is termed as “Miracle on the Han River”.
cards.quote: Between the 1960s and the 1980s, it rapidly developed into an economic power, which is termed as “Miracle on the Han River”.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Signalling its all-round development, South Korea became a Member of the OECD in ____.
cards.back: Signalling its all-round development, South Korea became a Member of the OECD in 1996.
cards.quote: Signalling its all-round development, South Korea became a Member of the OECD in 1996.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the factors behind South Korea’s high human development.
cards.back:
successful land reforms
rural development
extensive human resources development
rapid equitable economic growth
cards.quote: high human development include “successful land reforms, rural development, extensive human resources development and rapid equitable economic growth.”

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the three challenges of nation-building negotiated in the first decade after 1947.
cards.back:
Freedom came with partition, which resulted in large scale violence and displacement and challenged the very idea of a secular India.
The integration of the princely states into the Indian union needed urgent resolution.
The internal boundaries of the country needed to be drawn afresh to meet the aspirations of the people who spoke different languages.
cards.quote: Freedom came with partition, which resulted in large scale violence and displacement and challenged the very idea of a secular India. The integration of the princely states into the Indian union needed urgent resolution. The internal boundaries of the country needed to be drawn afresh to meet the aspirations of the people who spoke different languages.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did India attain independence?
cards.back: At the hour of midnight on 14-15 August 1947, India attained independence.
cards.quote: At the hour of midnight on 14-15 August 1947, India attained independence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who delivered the famous ‘tryst with destiny’ speech to the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: Jawaharlal Nehru, the first prime minister of free India, addressed a special session of the Constituent Assembly that night. This was the famous tryst with destiny speech that you are familiar with.
cards.quote: Jawaharlal Nehru, the first prime minister of free India, addressed a special session of the Constituent Assembly that night. This was the famous tryst with destiny speech that you are familiar with.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the two goals almost everyone in the national movement agreed upon.
cards.back:
that after independence, we shall run our country through democratic government
that the government will be run for the good of all, particularly the poor and the socially disadvantaged groups
cards.quote: there were two goals almost everyone agreed upon: one, that after independence, we shall run our country through democratic government; and two, that the government will be run for the good of all, particularly the poor and the socially disadvantaged groups.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who said: “Tomorrow we shall be free from the slavery of the British domination. But at midnight India will be partitioned.”?
cards.back: Mahatma Gandhi 14 August 1947, Kolkata.
cards.quote: Tomorrow we shall be free from the slavery of the British domination. But at midnight India will be partitioned. Tomorrow will thus be a day of rejoicing as well as of mourning. Mahatma Gandhi 14 August 1947, Kolkata.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the first and immediate challenge faced by independent India?
cards.back: The first and the immediate challenge was to shape a nation that was united, yet accommodative of the diversity in our society.
cards.quote: The first and the immediate challenge was to shape a nation that was united, yet accommodative of the diversity in our society.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the second challenge faced by independent India?
cards.back: The second challenge was to establish democracy.
cards.quote: The second challenge was to establish democracy.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: India adopted representative democracy based on the ____ form of government.
cards.back: India adopted representative democracy based on the parliamentary form of government.
cards.quote: India adopted representative democracy based on the parliamentary form of government.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why was a democratic constitution alone not enough to establish democracy?
cards.back: A democratic constitution is necessary but not sufficient for establishing a democracy. The challenge was to develop democratic practices in accordance with the Constitution.
cards.quote: A democratic constitution is necessary but not sufficient for establishing a democracy. The challenge was to develop democratic practices in accordance with the Constitution.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the third challenge faced by independent India?
cards.back: The third challenge was to ensure the development and wellbeing of the entire society and not only of some sections.
cards.quote: The third challenge was to ensure the development and wellbeing of the entire society and not only of some sections.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The Constitution also set out in the ____ the welfare goals that democratic politics must achieve.
cards.back: The Constitution also set out in the Directive Principles of State Policy the welfare goals that democratic politics must achieve.
cards.quote: The Constitution also set out in the Directive Principles of State Policy the welfare goals that democratic politics must achieve.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who said: “You may belong to any religion or caste or creed — that has nothing to do with the business of the State.”?
cards.back: Mohammad Ali Jinnah, Presidential Address to the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan at Karachi, 11 August 1947.
cards.quote: You may belong to any religion or caste or creed — that has nothing to do with the business of the State. Mohammad Ali Jinnah, Presidential Address to the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan at Karachi, 11 August 1947.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who wrote: “If we fail to do so, we shall have a festering sore which will eventually poison the whole body politic”?
cards.back: Jawaharlal Nehru, Letter to Chief Ministers, 15 October 1947.
cards.quote: If we fail to do so, we shall have a festering sore which will eventually poison the whole body politic and probably destroy it. Jawaharlal Nehru, Letter to Chief Ministers, 15 October 1947.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is ‘partition’?
cards.back: This was a result of ‘partition’, the division of British India into India and Pakistan.
cards.quote: This was a result of ‘partition’, the division of British India into India and Pakistan.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the ‘two-nation theory’?
cards.back: According to the ‘two-nation theory’ advanced by the Muslim League, India consisted of not one but two ‘people’, Hindus and Muslims.
cards.quote: According to the ‘two-nation theory’ advanced by the Muslim League, India consisted of not one but two ‘people’, Hindus and Muslims.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Muslim League demand on the basis of the two-nation theory?
cards.back: That is why it demanded Pakistan, a separate country for the Muslims.
cards.quote: That is why it demanded Pakistan, a separate country for the Muslims.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which party opposed the two-nation theory and the demand for Pakistan?
cards.back: The Congress opposed this theory and the demand for Pakistan.
cards.quote: The Congress opposed this theory and the demand for Pakistan.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: On what principle was British India partitioned?
cards.back: It was decided to follow the principle of religious majorities. This basically means that areas where the Muslims were in majority would make up the territory of Pakistan. The rest was to stay with India.
cards.quote: It was decided to follow the principle of religious majorities. This basically means that areas where the Muslims were in majority would make up the territory of Pakistan. The rest was to stay with India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why did Pakistan comprise two territories, West and East Pakistan?
cards.back: There were two areas of concentration, one in the west and one in the east. There was no way these two parts could be joined. So it was decided that the new country, Pakistan, will comprise two territories, West and East Pakistan separated by a long expanse of Indian territory.
cards.quote: There were two areas of concentration, one in the west and one in the east. There was no way these two parts could be joined. So it was decided that the new country, Pakistan, will comprise two territories, West and East Pakistan separated by a long expanse of Indian territory.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who was known as ‘Frontier Gandhi’ and opposed the two-nation theory?
cards.back: Khan Abdul Gaffar Khan, the undisputed leader of the North Western Frontier Province and known as ‘Frontier Gandhi’, was staunchly opposed to the two-nation theory.
cards.quote: Khan Abdul Gaffar Khan, the undisputed leader of the North Western Frontier Province and known as ‘Frontier Gandhi’, was staunchly opposed to the two-nation theory.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What happened to the NWFP despite Khan Abdul Gaffar Khan’s opposition?
cards.back: Eventually, his voice was simply ignored and the NWFP was made to merge with Pakistan.
cards.quote: Eventually, his voice was simply ignored and the NWFP was made to merge with Pakistan.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which two provinces were bifurcated according to the religious majority at the district level?
cards.back: The third problem was that two of the Muslim majority provinces of British India, Punjab and Bengal, had very large areas where the non-Muslims were in majority. Eventually it was decided that these two provinces would be bifurcated according to the religious majority at the district or even lower level.
cards.quote: The third problem was that two of the Muslim majority provinces of British India, Punjab and Bengal, had very large areas where the non-Muslims were in majority. Eventually it was decided that these two provinces would be bifurcated according to the religious majority at the district or even lower level.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the fourth and most intractable problem of partition?
cards.back: This was related to the fourth and the most intractable of all the problems of partition. This was the problem of ‘minorities’ on both sides of the border.
cards.quote: This was related to the fourth and the most intractable of all the problems of partition. This was the problem of ‘minorities’ on both sides of the border.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What phrase did survivors use to describe partition?
cards.back: While recounting the trauma of Partition, they have often used the phrase that the survivors themselves used to describe partition — as a ‘division of hearts’.
cards.quote: While recounting the trauma of Partition, they have often used the phrase that the survivors themselves used to describe partition — as a ‘division of hearts’.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How many people migrated, and how many were killed, because of Partition?
cards.back: It is estimated that the Partition forced about 80 lakh people to migrate across the new border. Between five to ten lakh people were killed in partition related violence.
cards.quote: It is estimated that the Partition forced about 80 lakh people to migrate across the new border. Between five to ten lakh people were killed in partition related violence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The ____ was formed to protect the interests of the Muslims in colonial India.
cards.back: The Muslim League was formed to protect the interests of the Muslims in colonial India.
cards.quote: The Muslim League was formed to protect the interests of the Muslims in colonial India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Where was Mahatma Gandhi on 15 August 1947?
cards.back: On the 15th August 1947 Mahatma Gandhi did not participate in any of the independence day celebrations. He was in Kolkata in the areas which were torn by gruesome riots between Hindus and Muslims.
cards.quote: On the 15th August 1947 Mahatma Gandhi did not participate in any of the independence day celebrations. He was in Kolkata in the areas which were torn by gruesome riots between Hindus and Muslims.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did Mahatma Gandhi undertake his last fast?
cards.back: With all this in mind he undertook what turned out to be his last fast in January 1948.
cards.quote: With all this in mind he undertook what turned out to be his last fast in January 1948.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who assassinated Mahatma Gandhi, and when?
cards.back: Finally, on 30 January 1948, one such extremist, Nathuram Vinayak Godse, walked up to Gandhiji during his evening prayer in Delhi and fired three bullets at him, killing him instantly.
cards.quote: Finally, on 30 January 1948, one such extremist, Nathuram Vinayak Godse, walked up to Gandhiji during his evening prayer in Delhi and fired three bullets at him, killing him instantly.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What ideal did most national leaders cherish, and where was it enshrined?
cards.back: They cherished therefore the ideal of a secular nation. This ideal was enshrined in the Indian Constitution.
cards.quote: They cherished therefore the ideal of a secular nation. This ideal was enshrined in the Indian Constitution.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What kind of country did most leaders of the national movement say India should not be?
cards.back: India should not be a country that gave superior status to adherents of one faith and inferior to those who practiced another religion. All citizens would be equal irrespective of their religious affiliation. Being religious or a believer would not be a test of citizenship.
cards.quote: India should not be a country that gave superior status to adherents of one faith and inferior to those who practiced another religion. All citizens would be equal irrespective of their religious affiliation. Being religious or a believer would not be a test of citizenship.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What were the Princely States?
cards.back: On the other hand, several large and small states ruled by princes, called the Princely States, enjoyed some form of control over their internal affairs as long as they accepted British supremacy. This was called paramountcy or suzerainty of the British crown.
cards.quote: On the other hand, several large and small states ruled by princes, called the Princely States, enjoyed some form of control over their internal affairs as long as they accepted British supremacy. This was called paramountcy or suzerainty of the British crown.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What share of the land area of the British Indian Empire did the Princely States cover?
cards.back: Princely States covered one-third of the land area of the British Indian Empire and one out of four Indians lived under princely rule.
cards.quote: Princely States covered one-third of the land area of the British Indian Empire and one out of four Indians lived under princely rule.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the British announce about paramountcy just before Independence?
cards.back: Just before Independence it was announced by the British that with the end of their rule over India, paramountcy of the British crown over Princely States would also lapse. This meant that all these states, as many as 565 in all, would become legally independent.
cards.quote: Just before Independence it was announced by the British that with the end of their rule over India, paramountcy of the British crown over Princely States would also lapse. This meant that all these states, as many as 565 in all, would become legally independent.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who decided whether a princely state joined India, joined Pakistan or stayed independent?
cards.back: The British government took the view that all these states were free to join either India or Pakistan or remain independent if they so wished. This decision was left not to the people but to the princely rulers of these states.
cards.quote: The British government took the view that all these states were free to join either India or Pakistan or remain independent if they so wished. This decision was left not to the people but to the princely rulers of these states.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which princely ruler first announced that his state had decided on Independence?
cards.back: First of all, the ruler of Travancore announced that the state had decided on Independence.
cards.quote: First of all, the ruler of Travancore announced that the state had decided on Independence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who wrote to the princely rulers in 1947: “We are at a momentous stage in the history of India…”?
cards.back: Sardar Patel Letter to Princely rulers, 1947.
cards.quote: We are at a momentous stage in the history of India. By common endeavour, we can raise the country to new greatness, while lack of unity will expose us to unexpected calamities. I hope the Indian States will realise fully that if we do not cooperate and work together in the general interest, anarchy and chaos will overwhelm us all, great and small, and lead us to total ruin... Sardar Patel Letter to Princely rulers, 1947.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What role did Sardar Patel play in integrating the princely states?
cards.back: Sardar Patel was India's Deputy Prime Minister and the Home Minister during the crucial period immediately following Independence. He played a historic role in negotiating with the rulers of princely states firmly but diplomatically and bringing most of them into the Indian Union.
cards.quote: Sardar Patel was India's Deputy Prime Minister and the Home Minister during the crucial period immediately following Independence. He played a historic role in negotiating with the rulers of princely states firmly but diplomatically and bringing most of them into the Indian Union.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the three considerations that guided the government's approach to the Princely States.
cards.back:
the people of most of the princely states clearly wanted to become part of the Indian union
the government was prepared to be flexible in giving autonomy to some regions
the integration and consolidation of the territorial boundaries of the nation had assumed supreme importance
cards.quote: The government's approach was guided by three considerations. Firstly, the people of most of the princely states clearly wanted to become part of the Indian union. Secondly, the government was prepared to be flexible in giving autonomy to some regions. The idea was to accommodate plurality and adopt a flexible approach in dealing with the demands of the regions. Thirdly, in the backdrop of partition which brought into focus the contest over demarcation of territory, the integration and consolidation of the territorial boundaries of the nation had assumed supreme importance.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the ‘Instrument of Accession’?
cards.back: The rulers of most of the states signed a document called the ‘Instrument of Accession’ which meant that their state agreed to become a part of the Union of India.
cards.quote: The rulers of most of the states signed a document called the ‘Instrument of Accession’ which meant that their state agreed to become a part of the Union of India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which four Princely States proved more difficult to accede to India?
cards.back: Accession of the Princely States of Junagadh, Hyderabad, Kashmir and Manipur proved more difficult than the rest.
cards.quote: Accession of the Princely States of Junagadh, Hyderabad, Kashmir and Manipur proved more difficult than the rest.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How was the issue of Junagadh resolved?
cards.back: The issue of Junagarh was resolved after a plebiscite confirmed people's desire to join India.
cards.quote: The issue of Junagarh was resolved after a plebiscite confirmed people's desire to join India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which was the largest Princely State, and what title did its ruler carry?
cards.back: Hyderabad, the largest of the Princely States was surrounded entirely by Indian territory. Some parts of the old Hyderabad state are today parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. Its ruler carried the title, ‘Nizam’, and he was one of the world's richest men.
cards.quote: Hyderabad, the largest of the Princely States was surrounded entirely by Indian territory. Some parts of the old Hyderabad state are today parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. Its ruler carried the title, ‘Nizam’, and he was one of the world's richest men.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What agreement did the Nizam of Hyderabad enter into with India in November 1947?
cards.back: The Nizam wanted an independent status for Hyderabad. He entered into what was called the Standstill Agreement with India in November 1947 for a year while negotiations with the Indian government were going on.
cards.quote: The Nizam wanted an independent status for Hyderabad. He entered into what was called the Standstill Agreement with India in November 1947 for a year while negotiations with the Indian government were going on.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which region's peasantry rose against the Nizam's oppressive rule?
cards.back: The peasantry in the Telangana region in particular, was the victim of Nizam's oppressive rule and rose against him.
cards.quote: The peasantry in the Telangana region in particular, was the victim of Nizam's oppressive rule and rose against him.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who was in the forefront of the movement against the Nizam's rule?
cards.back: The Communists and the Hyderabad Congress were in the forefront of the movement.
cards.quote: The Communists and the Hyderabad Congress were in the forefront of the movement.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The Nizam responded by unleashing a para-military force known as the ____ on the people.
cards.back: The Nizam responded by unleashing a para-military force known as the Razakars on the people.
cards.quote: The Nizam responded by unleashing a para-military force known as the Razakars on the people.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did Hyderabad accede to India?
cards.back: In September 1948, Indian army moved in to control the Nizam's forces. After a few days of intermittent fighting, the Nizam surrendered. This led to Hyderabad's accession to India.
cards.quote: In September 1948, Indian army moved in to control the Nizam's forces. After a few days of intermittent fighting, the Nizam surrendered. This led to Hyderabad's accession to India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who was the Maharaja of Manipur who signed the Instrument of Accession?
cards.back: A few days before Independence, the Maharaja of Manipur, Bodhachandra Singh, signed the Instrument of Accession with the Indian government on the assurance that the internal autonomy of Manipur would be maintained.
cards.quote: A few days before Independence, the Maharaja of Manipur, Bodhachandra Singh, signed the Instrument of Accession with the Indian government on the assurance that the internal autonomy of Manipur would be maintained.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which was the first part of India to hold an election based on universal adult franchise?
cards.back: Under the pressure of public opinion, the Maharaja held elections in Manipur in June 1948 and the state became a constitutional monarchy. Thus Manipur was the first part of India to hold an election based on universal adult franchise.
cards.quote: Under the pressure of public opinion, the Maharaja held elections in Manipur in June 1948 and the state became a constitutional monarchy. Thus Manipur was the first part of India to hold an election based on universal adult franchise.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did the Maharaja of Manipur sign the Merger Agreement?
cards.back: The Government of India succeeded in persuading the Maharaja into signing a Merger Agreement in September 1949.
cards.quote: The Government of India succeeded in persuading the Maharaja into signing a Merger Agreement in September 1949.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What challenge followed partition and the integration of the Princely States?
cards.back: The process of nation-building did not come to an end with partition and integration of Princely States. Now the challenge was to draw the internal boundaries of the Indian states.
cards.quote: The process of nation-building did not come to an end with partition and integration of Princely States. Now the challenge was to draw the internal boundaries of the Indian states.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: On what basis were state boundaries drawn during colonial rule?
cards.back: During colonial rule, the state boundaries were drawn either on administrative convenience or simply coincided with the territories annexed by the British government or the territories ruled by the princely powers.
cards.quote: During colonial rule, the state boundaries were drawn either on administrative convenience or simply coincided with the territories annexed by the British government or the territories ruled by the princely powers.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What basis for the formation of states had the national movement promised?
cards.back: Our national movement had rejected these divisions as artificial and had promised the linguistic principle as the basis of formation of states.
cards.quote: Our national movement had rejected these divisions as artificial and had promised the linguistic principle as the basis of formation of states.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Nagpur session of Congress in 1920 recognise as the basis of reorganising the party?
cards.back: In fact after the Nagpur session of Congress in 1920 the principle was recognised as the basis of the reorganisation of the Indian National Congress party itself.
cards.quote: In fact after the Nagpur session of Congress in 1920 the principle was recognised as the basis of the reorganisation of the Indian National Congress party itself.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why did the central leadership postpone the formation of linguistic states after Independence?
cards.back: Things changed after Independence and partition. Our leaders felt that carving out states on the basis of language might lead to disruption and disintegration. It was also felt that this would draw attention away from other social and economic challenges that the country faced. The central leadership decided to postpone matters.
cards.quote: Things changed after Independence and partition. Our leaders felt that carving out states on the basis of language might lead to disruption and disintegration. It was also felt that this would draw attention away from other social and economic challenges that the country faced. The central leadership decided to postpone matters.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Where did protests against postponing linguistic states begin?
cards.back: This decision of the national leadership was challenged by the local leaders and the people. Protests began in the Telugu speaking areas of the old Madras province, which included present day Tamil Nadu, parts of Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Karnataka.
cards.quote: This decision of the national leadership was challenged by the local leaders and the people. Protests began in the Telugu speaking areas of the old Madras province, which included present day Tamil Nadu, parts of Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Karnataka.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who died after a 56-day fast demanding a separate Andhra state?
cards.back: Potti Sriramulu, a Congress leader and a veteran Gandhian, went on an indefinite fast that led to his death after 56 days.
cards.quote: Potti Sriramulu, a Congress leader and a veteran Gandhian, went on an indefinite fast that led to his death after 56 days.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When was the formation of a separate Andhra state announced?
cards.back: Finally, the Prime Minister announced the formation of a separate Andhra state in December 1952.
cards.quote: Finally, the Prime Minister announced the formation of a separate Andhra state in December 1952.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did Potti Sriramulu begin his fast unto death, and when did he die?
cards.back: undertook a fast unto death from 19 October 1952 demanding separate state of Andhra; died during the fast on 15 December 1952.
cards.quote: undertook a fast unto death from 19 October 1952 demanding separate state of Andhra; died during the fast on 15 December 1952.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the effect of the formation of Andhra on other parts of the country?
cards.back: The formation of Andhra spurred the struggle for making of other states on linguistic lines in other parts of the country.
cards.quote: The formation of Andhra spurred the struggle for making of other states on linguistic lines in other parts of the country.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When was the States Reorganisation Commission appointed, and why?
cards.back: These struggles forced the Central Government into appointing a States Reorganisation Commission in 1953 to look into the question of redrawing of the boundaries of states.
cards.quote: These struggles forced the Central Government into appointing a States Reorganisation Commission in 1953 to look into the question of redrawing of the boundaries of states.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the main recommendation of the States Reorganisation Commission?
cards.back: The Commission in its report accepted that the boundaries of the state should reflect the boundaries of different languages.
cards.quote: The Commission in its report accepted that the boundaries of the state should reflect the boundaries of different languages.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 lead to?
cards.back: On the basis of its report the States Reorganisation Act was passed in 1956. This led to the creation of 14 states and six union territories.
cards.quote: On the basis of its report the States Reorganisation Act was passed in 1956. This led to the creation of 14 states and six union territories.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why did the leadership finally choose linguistic states?
cards.back: But the leadership, under popular pressure, finally made a choice in favour of linguistic states. It was hoped that if we accept the regional and linguistic claims of all regions, the threat of division and separatism would be reduced.
cards.quote: But the leadership, under popular pressure, finally made a choice in favour of linguistic states. It was hoped that if we accept the regional and linguistic claims of all regions, the threat of division and separatism would be reduced.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did linguistic states change who could enter politics and power?
cards.back: The path to politics and power was now open to people other than the small English speaking elite.
cards.quote: The path to politics and power was now open to people other than the small English speaking elite.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the effect of linguistic reorganisation on national unity?
cards.back: Linguistic reorganisation also gave some uniform basis to the drawing of state boundaries. It did not lead to disintegration of the country as many had feared earlier. On the contrary it strengthened national unity.
cards.quote: Linguistic reorganisation also gave some uniform basis to the drawing of state boundaries. It did not lead to disintegration of the country as many had feared earlier. On the contrary it strengthened national unity.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Above all, the linguistic states underlined the acceptance of the principle of ____.
cards.back: Above all, the linguistic states underlined the acceptance of the principle of diversity.
cards.quote: Above all, the linguistic states underlined the acceptance of the principle of diversity.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When were Maharashtra and Gujarat created out of bilingual Bombay state?
cards.back: There was an experiment of ‘bilingual’ Bombay state, consisting of Gujarati- and Marathi-speaking people. After a popular agitation, the states of Maharashtra and Gujarat were created in 1960.
cards.quote: There was an experiment of ‘bilingual’ Bombay state, consisting of Gujarati- and Marathi-speaking people. After a popular agitation, the states of Maharashtra and Gujarat were created in 1960.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When was Punjab constituted as a state, and which territories were separated from it?
cards.back: Statehood for Punjab came ten years later, in 1966, when the territories of today's Haryana and Himachal Pradesh were separated from the larger Punjab state.
cards.quote: Statehood for Punjab came ten years later, in 1966, when the territories of today's Haryana and Himachal Pradesh were separated from the larger Punjab state.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which states emerged in the north-east in 1972?
cards.back: Meghalaya was carved out of Assam in 1972. Manipur and Tripura too emerged as separate states in the same year.
cards.quote: Meghalaya was carved out of Assam in 1972. Manipur and Tripura too emerged as separate states in the same year.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland become states?
cards.back: The states of Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh came into being in 1987. Nagaland had become a state much earlier in 1963.
cards.quote: The states of Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh came into being in 1987. Nagaland had become a state much earlier in 1963.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which three states were created in 2000?
cards.back: Three such states, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand, were created in 2000.
cards.quote: Three such states, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand, were created in 2000.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did Telangana emerge as a new state?
cards.back: Telangana has emerged as a new state on 2 June, 2014.
cards.quote: Telangana has emerged as a new state on 2 June, 2014.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: When did Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru pass away?
cards.back: Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru passed away in May 1964.
cards.quote: Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru passed away in May 1964.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: Who consulted party leaders after Nehru died, and whom did the consensus favour?
cards.back: K. Kamraj, the president of the Congress party consulted party leaders and Congress members of Parliament and found that there was a consensus in favour of Lal Bahadur Shastri.
cards.quote: K. Kamraj, the president of the Congress party consulted party leaders and Congress members of Parliament and found that there was a consensus in favour of Lal Bahadur Shastri.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: Shastri was the country's Prime Minister from 1964 to ____.
cards.back: Shastri was the country's Prime Minister from 1964 to 1966.
cards.quote: Shastri was the country's Prime Minister from 1964 to 1966.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: Which slogan of Shastri symbolised the country's resolve to face the food crisis and the war with Pakistan?
cards.back: Shastri's famous slogan Jai Jawan Jai Kisan, symbolised the country's resolve to face both these challenges.
cards.quote: Shastri's famous slogan Jai Jawan Jai Kisan, symbolised the country's resolve to face both these challenges.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: Where and when did Shastri's Prime Ministership come to an abrupt end?
cards.back: Shastri's Prime Ministership came to an abrupt end on 11 January 1966, when he suddenly expired in Tashkent
cards.quote: Shastri's Prime Ministership came to an abrupt end on 11 January 1966, when he suddenly expired in Tashkent

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: Why was Shastri in Tashkent in January 1966, and with whom?
cards.back: He was there to discuss and sign an agreement with Muhammad Ayub Khan, the then President of Pakistan, to end the war.
cards.quote: He was there to discuss and sign an agreement with Muhammad Ayub Khan, the then President of Pakistan, to end the war.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: How was the 1966 contest between Indira Gandhi and Morarji Desai resolved?
cards.back: The contest was resolved through a secret ballot among Congress MPs. Indira Gandhi defeated Morarji Desai by securing the support of more than two-thirds of the party's MPs.
cards.quote: The contest was resolved through a secret ballot among Congress MPs. Indira Gandhi defeated Morarji Desai by securing the support of more than two-thirds of the party's MPs.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: How was the peaceful transition of power in 1966 seen?
cards.back: A peaceful transition of power, despite intense competition for leadership, was seen as a sign of maturity of India's democracy.
cards.quote: A peaceful transition of power, despite intense competition for leadership, was seen as a sign of maturity of India's democracy.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: During which years was Indira Gandhi Prime Minister of India?
cards.back: Prime Minister of India from 1966 to 1977 and 1980 to 1984
cards.quote: Prime Minister of India from 1966 to 1977 and 1980 to 1984

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: In which general elections did Indira Gandhi lead the Congress party to victory?
cards.back: led the Congress party to victory in 1967, 1971 and 1980 general elections
cards.quote: led the Congress party to victory in 1967, 1971 and 1980 general elections

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: When was Indira Gandhi assassinated?
cards.back: assassinated on 31 October 1984
cards.quote: assassinated on 31 October 1984

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: The year ____ is considered a landmark year in India's political and electoral history.
cards.back: The year 1967 is considered a landmark year in India's political and electoral history.
cards.quote: The year 1967 is considered a landmark year in India's political and electoral history.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: What was one of the first decisions of the Indira Gandhi government, seen as taken under US pressure?
cards.back: One of the first decisions of the Indira Gandhi government was to devaluate the Indian rupee, under what was seen to be pressure from the US.
cards.quote: One of the first decisions of the Indira Gandhi government was to devaluate the Indian rupee, under what was seen to be pressure from the US.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: Who gave the strategy of opposition unity against the Congress the name "non-Congressism"?
cards.back: The socialist leader Ram Manohar Lohia gave this strategy the name of non-Congressism.
cards.quote: The socialist leader Ram Manohar Lohia gave this strategy the name of non-Congressism.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: As the Congress changed its character, what strategy did other opposition parties rely on more and more?
cards.back: With the change in the nature of the Congress party, other opposition parties relied more and more on what is known in Indian politics as ‘non-Congressism’.
cards.quote: With the change in the nature of the Congress party, other opposition parties relied more and more on what is known in Indian politics as ‘non-Congressism’.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: Why did parties opposed to the Congress come together before the 1967 elections?
cards.back: Parties opposed to the Congress realised that the division of their votes kept the Congress in power. Thus parties that were entirely different and disparate in their programmes and ideology got together to form anti-Congress fronts in some states and entered into electoral adjustments of sharing seats in others.
cards.quote: Parties opposed to the Congress realised that the division of their votes kept the Congress in power. Thus parties that were entirely different and disparate in their programmes and ideology got together to form anti-Congress fronts in some states and entered into electoral adjustments of sharing seats in others.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: What was Lohia's theoretical argument in defence of non-Congressism?
cards.back: Congress rule was undemocratic and opposed to the interests of ordinary poor people; therefore, the coming together of the non-Congress parties was necessary for reclaiming democracy for the people.
cards.quote: Congress rule was undemocratic and opposed to the interests of ordinary poor people; therefore, the coming together of the non-Congress parties was necessary for reclaiming democracy for the people.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: The fourth general elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies were held in ____.
cards.back: The fourth general elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies were held in February 1967.
cards.quote: The fourth general elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies were held in February 1967.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: What was new for the Congress in the fourth general elections of 1967?
cards.back: The Congress was facing the electorate for the first time without Nehru.
cards.quote: The Congress was facing the electorate for the first time without Nehru.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: Many contemporary political observers described the election results as a ____.
cards.back: Many contemporary political observers described the election results as a political earthquake.
cards.quote: Many contemporary political observers described the election results as a political earthquake.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: What was the Congress performance in the Lok Sabha in 1967?
cards.back: The Congress did manage to get a majority in the Lok Sabha, but with its lowest tally of seats and share of votes since 1952.
cards.quote: The Congress did manage to get a majority in the Lok Sabha, but with its lowest tally of seats and share of votes since 1952.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: Name the Congress stalwarts who lost their constituencies in 1967, with their States.
cards.back:
Kamaraj in Tamil Nadu
S.K. Patil in Maharashtra
Atulya Ghosh in West Bengal
K. B. Sahay in Bihar
cards.quote: Half the ministers in Indira Gandhi's cabinet were defeated. The political stalwarts who lost in their constituencies included Kamaraj in Tamil Nadu, S.K. Patil in Maharashtra, Atulya Ghosh in West Bengal and K. B. Sahay in Bihar.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: In how many States did the Congress lose majority in 1967, and in how many more did defections stop it forming a government?
cards.back: The Congress lost majority in as many as seven States. In two other States defections prevented it from forming a government.
cards.quote: The Congress lost majority in as many as seven States. In two other States defections prevented it from forming a government.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: Name the nine States where the Congress lost power in 1967.
cards.back:
Punjab
Haryana
Uttar Pradesh
Madhya Pradesh
Bihar
West Bengal
Orissa
Madras
Kerala
cards.quote: These nine States where the Congress lost power were spread across the country – Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Orissa, Madras and Kerala.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: Which regional party won a clear majority in Madras State in 1967?
cards.back: In Madras State (now called Tamil Nadu), a regional party – the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) – came to power by securing a clear majority.
cards.quote: In Madras State (now called Tamil Nadu), a regional party – the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) – came to power by securing a clear majority.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: On what issue had the DMK led a massive student agitation before winning power in Madras?
cards.back: The DMK won power after having led a massive anti-Hindi agitation by students against the centre on the issue of imposition of Hindi as the official language.
cards.quote: The DMK won power after having led a massive anti-Hindi agitation by students against the centre on the issue of imposition of Hindi as the official language.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: What was the significance of the DMK victory in Madras in 1967?
cards.back: This was the first time any non-Congress party had secured a majority of its own in any State.
cards.quote: This was the first time any non-Congress party had secured a majority of its own in any State.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: What popular saying captured the Congress losses of 1967?
cards.back: A popular saying was that one could take a train from Delhi to Howrah and not pass through a single Congress ruled State.
cards.quote: A popular saying was that one could take a train from Delhi to Howrah and not pass through a single Congress ruled State.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: What was a Samyukt Vidhayak Dal (SVD)?
cards.back: Since no single party had got majority, various non-Congress parties came together to form joint legislative parties (called Samyukt Vidhayak Dal in Hindi) that supported non-Congress governments.
cards.quote: Since no single party had got majority, various non-Congress parties came together to form joint legislative parties (called Samyukt Vidhayak Dal in Hindi) that supported non-Congress governments.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: Which parties formed the SVD government in Bihar after 1967?
cards.back: The SVD government in Bihar, for instance, included the two socialist parties – SSP and the PSP – along with the CPI on the left and Jana Sangh on the right.
cards.quote: The SVD government in Bihar, for instance, included the two socialist parties – SSP and the PSP – along with the CPI on the left and Jana Sangh on the right.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: What is defection?
cards.back: Defection means an elected representative leaves the party on whose symbol he/she was elected and joins another party.
cards.quote: Defection means an elected representative leaves the party on whose symbol he/she was elected and joins another party.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.chapter: Challenges to & Restoration of the Congress System
cards.front: In which three States did breakaway Congress legislators install non-Congress governments after 1967?
