cards.back: Privatisation of state assets and corporate ownership patterns were to be immediately brought in. Collective farms were to be replaced by private farming and capitalism in agriculture.
cards.quote: Privatisation of state assets and corporate ownership patterns were to be immediately brought in. Collective farms were to be replaced by private farming and capitalism in agriculture.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the shock therapy transition rule out?
cards.back: This transition ruled out any alternate or 'third way', other than state-controlled socialism or capitalism.
cards.quote: This transition ruled out any alternate or 'third way', other than state-controlled socialism or capitalism.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How was development envisaged under shock therapy, and what switch was considered essential?
cards.back: Development was now envisaged through more trade, and thus a sudden and complete switch to free trade was considered essential.
cards.quote: Development was now envisaged through more trade, and thus a sudden and complete switch to free trade was considered essential.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The free trade regime and ____ were to be the main engines of change.
cards.back: The free trade regime and foreign direct investment (FDI) were to be the main engines of change.
cards.quote: The free trade regime and foreign direct investment (FDI) were to be the main engines of change.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What three things did shock therapy's external orientation involve alongside free trade and FDI?
cards.back:
openness to foreign investment
financial opening up or deregulation
currency convertibility
cards.quote: This also involved openness to foreign investment, financial opening up or deregulation, and currency convertibility.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What happened to trade alliances among the Soviet bloc countries under shock therapy?
cards.back: the transition also involved a break up of the existing trade alliances among the countries of the Soviet bloc.
cards.quote: the transition also involved a break up of the existing trade alliances among the countries of the Soviet bloc.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the general outcome of shock therapy in the 1990s?
cards.back: The shock therapy administered in the 1990s did not lead the people into the promised utopia of mass consumption. Generally, it brought ruin to the economies and disaster upon the people of the entire region.
cards.quote: The shock therapy administered in the 1990s did not lead the people into the promised utopia of mass consumption. Generally, it brought ruin to the economies and disaster upon the people of the entire region.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the sale of Russian industries under shock therapy called?
cards.back: This was called 'the largest garage sale in history', as valuable industries were undervalued and sold at throwaway prices.
cards.quote: This was called 'the largest garage sale in history', as valuable industries were undervalued and sold at throwaway prices.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What happened to the old system of social welfare after shock therapy?
cards.back: The old system of social welfare was systematically destroyed.
cards.quote: The old system of social welfare was systematically destroyed.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What kind of executive did most post-communist constitutions, including Russia's, establish?
cards.back: The constitutions of all these countries were drafted in a hurry and most, including Russia, had a strong executive president with the widest possible powers that rendered elected parliaments relatively weak.
cards.quote: The constitutions of all these countries were drafted in a hurry and most, including Russia, had a strong executive president with the widest possible powers that rendered elected parliaments relatively weak.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why did most post-communist economies, especially Russia, start reviving in 2000?
cards.back: The reason for the revival for most of their economies was the export of natural resources like oil, natural gas and minerals.
cards.quote: The reason for the revival for most of their economies was the export of natural resources like oil, natural gas and minerals.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the major oil and gas producers among the former Soviet republics.
cards.back:
Azerbaijan
Kazakhstan
Russia
Turkmenistan
Uzbekistan
cards.quote: Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Russia, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan are major oil and gas producers.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which two republics in Russia have had violent secessionist movements?
cards.back: In Russia, two republics, Chechnya and Dagestan, have had violent secessionist movements.
cards.quote: In Russia, two republics, Chechnya and Dagestan, have had violent secessionist movements.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Central Asian country witnessed a civil war that went on for ten years till 2001?
cards.back: In Central Asia, Tajikistan witnessed a civil war that went on for ten years till 2001.
cards.quote: In Central Asia, Tajikistan witnessed a civil war that went on for ten years till 2001.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In which province of Azerbaijan do local Armenians want to secede and join Armenia?
cards.back: In Azerbaijan's province of Nagorno-Karabakh, some local Armenians want to secede and join Armenia.
cards.quote: In Azerbaijan's province of Nagorno-Karabakh, some local Armenians want to secede and join Armenia.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the US want in Central Asia after 11 September 2001?
cards.back: After 11 September 2001, the US wanted military bases in the region and paid the governments of all Central Asian states to hire bases and to allow airplanes to fly over their territory during the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.
cards.quote: After 11 September 2001, the US wanted military bases in the region and paid the governments of all Central Asian states to hire bases and to allow airplanes to fly over their territory during the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What does Russia call the Central Asian states, and what does it believe about them?
cards.back: Russia perceives these states as its 'Near Abroad' and believes that they should be under Russian influence.
cards.quote: Russia perceives these states as its 'Near Abroad' and believes that they should be under Russian influence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did Czechoslovakia split into two countries?
cards.back: Czechoslovakia split peacefully into two, with the Czechs and the Slovaks forming independent countries.
cards.quote: Czechoslovakia split peacefully into two, with the Czechs and the Slovaks forming independent countries.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Where in eastern Europe did the most severe conflict take place after 1991?
cards.back: Balkan republics of Yugoslavia
cards.quote: But the most severe conflict took place in the Balkan republics of Yugoslavia.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which provinces of Yugoslavia declared independence after 1991?
cards.back: After 1991, it broke apart with several provinces like Croatia, Slovenia and Bosnia and Herzegovina declaring independence.
cards.quote: After 1991, it broke apart with several provinces like Croatia, Slovenia and Bosnia and Herzegovina declaring independence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What followed the inter-ethnic civil war in Yugoslavia?
cards.back: The NATO intervention and the bombing of Yugoslavia followed the inter-ethnic civil war.
cards.quote: The NATO intervention and the bombing of Yugoslavia followed the inter-ethnic civil war.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: With which post-communist country does India have the strongest relations?
cards.back: India has maintained good relations with all the postcommunist countries. But the strongest relations are still those between Russia and India.
cards.quote: India has maintained good relations with all the postcommunist countries. But the strongest relations are still those between Russia and India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What world order do Russia and India share a vision of?
cards.back: a multipolar world order
cards.quote: Russia and India share a vision of a multipolar world order.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What does a multipolar world order mean for India and Russia? Name its features.
cards.back:
co-existence of several powers in the international system
collective security
greater regionalism
negotiated settlements of international conflicts
an independent foreign policy for all countries
decision making through bodies like the UN that should be strengthened, democratised, and empowered
cards.quote: the co-existence of several powers in the international system, collective security (in which an attack on any country is regarded as a threat to all countries and requires a collective response), greater regionalism, negotiated settlements of international conflicts, an independent foreign policy for all countries, and decision making through bodies like the UN that should be strengthened, democratised, and empowered

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is collective security?
cards.back: an attack on any country is regarded as a threat to all countries and requires a collective response
cards.quote: an attack on any country is regarded as a threat to all countries and requires a collective response

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How many bilateral agreements were signed under the Indo-Russian Strategic Agreement of 2001?
cards.back: More than 80 bilateral agreements have been signed between India and Russia as part of the Indo-Russian Strategic Agreement of 2001.
cards.quote: More than 80 bilateral agreements have been signed between India and Russia as part of the Indo-Russian Strategic Agreement of 2001.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the four dimensions of the India-USSR relationship in the Cold War era, with NCERT's first line on each.
cards.back:
Economic: The Soviet Union assisted India's public sector companies at a time when such assistance was difficult to get.
Political: The Soviet Union supported India's positions on the Kashmir issue in the UN.
Military: India received most of its military hardware from the Soviet Union at a time when few other countries were willing to part with military technologies.
Culture: Hindi films and Indian culture were popular in the Soviet Union.
cards.quote: Economic: The Soviet Union assisted India's public sector companies at a time when such assistance was difficult to get. It gave aid and technical assistance for steel plants like Bhilai, Bokaro, Visakhapatnam, and machinery plants like Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd., etc. The Soviet Union accepted Indian currency for trade when India was short of foreign exchange. Political: The Soviet Union supported India's positions on the Kashmir issue in the UN. It also supported India during its major conflicts, especially during the war with Pakistan in 1971. India too supported Soviet foreign policy in some crucial but indirect ways. Military: India received most of its military hardware from the Soviet Union at a time when few other countries were willing to part with military technologies. The Soviet Union entered into various agreements allowing India to jointly produce military equipment. Culture: Hindi films and Indian culture were popular in the Soviet Union.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: For which steel plants did the USSR give India aid and technical assistance?
cards.back: It gave aid and technical assistance for steel plants like Bhilai, Bokaro, Visakhapatnam, and machinery plants like Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd., etc.
cards.quote: It gave aid and technical assistance for steel plants like Bhilai, Bokaro, Visakhapatnam, and machinery plants like Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd., etc.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did the USSR support India on Kashmir and in the 1971 war with Pakistan?
cards.back: The Soviet Union supported India's positions on the Kashmir issue in the UN. It also supported India during its major conflicts, especially during the war with Pakistan in 1971.
cards.quote: The Soviet Union supported India's positions on the Kashmir issue in the UN. It also supported India during its major conflicts, especially during the war with Pakistan in 1971.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why does Russia benefit from its relationship with India as far as arms are concerned?
cards.back: Russia stands to benefit from this relationship because India is the second largest arms market for Russia.
cards.quote: Russia stands to benefit from this relationship because India is the second largest arms market for Russia.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why is Russia important to India as an oil-importing nation?
cards.back: Since India is an oil-importing nation, Russia is important to India and has repeatedly come to the assistance of India during its oil crises.
cards.quote: Since India is an oil-importing nation, Russia is important to India and has repeatedly come to the assistance of India during its oil crises.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: From which republics besides Russia is India seeking to increase energy imports?
cards.back: India is seeking to increase its energy imports from Russia and the republics of Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.
cards.quote: India is seeking to increase its energy imports from Russia and the republics of Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did Russia help India's nuclear energy plans and space industry?
cards.back: Russia is important for India's nuclear energy plans and assisted India's space industry by giving, for example, the cryogenic rocket when India needed it.
cards.quote: Russia is important for India's nuclear energy plans and assisted India's space industry by giving, for example, the cryogenic rocket when India needed it.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why must environmental issues become part of world politics?
cards.back: Most of them are such that no single government can address them fully. Therefore they have to become part of 'world politics'.
cards.quote: Most of them are such that no single government can address them fully. Therefore they have to become part of 'world politics'.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which global think tank published Limits to Growth in 1972?
cards.back: The Club of Rome, a global think tank, published a book in 1972 entitled Limits to Growth
cards.quote: The Club of Rome, a global think tank, published a book in 1972 entitled Limits to Growth

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: From which decade did awareness of the environmental consequences of economic growth become increasingly political?
cards.back: awareness of the environmental consequences of economic growth acquired an increasingly political character from the 1960s onwards
cards.quote: awareness of the environmental consequences of economic growth acquired an increasingly political character from the 1960s onwards

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which UN agency began holding international conferences and promoting studies on environmental problems?
cards.back: International agencies, including the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), began holding international conferences and promoting detailed studies
cards.quote: International agencies, including the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), began holding international conferences and promoting detailed studies

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which 1992 conference consolidated the focus on environmental issues in global politics?
cards.back: The growing focus on environmental issues within the arena of global politics was firmly consolidated at the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in June 1992. This was also called the Earth Summit.
cards.quote: The growing focus on environmental issues within the arena of global politics was firmly consolidated at the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in June 1992. This was also called the Earth Summit.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which 1987 report warned that traditional patterns of economic growth were not sustainable in the long term?
cards.back: the 1987 Brundtland Report, Our Common Future, had warned that traditional patterns of economic growth were not sustainable in the long term
cards.quote: the 1987 Brundtland Report, Our Common Future, had warned that traditional patterns of economic growth were not sustainable in the long term

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is meant by the 'global North'?
cards.back: the rich and developed countries of the First World, generally referred to as the `global North'
cards.quote: the rich and developed countries of the First World, generally referred to as the `global North'

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is meant by the 'global South'?
cards.back: the poor and developing countries of the Third World, called the `global South'
cards.quote: the poor and developing countries of the Third World, called the `global South'

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did the environmental concerns of the global North and South differ at Rio?
cards.back: Whereas the Northern states were concerned with ozone depletion and global warming, the Southern states were anxious to address the relationship between economic development and environmental management.
cards.quote: Whereas the Northern states were concerned with ozone depletion and global warming, the Southern states were anxious to address the relationship between economic development and environmental management.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the outcomes of the Rio Summit.
cards.back:
conventions dealing with climate change, biodiversity, forestry
a list of development practices called `Agenda 21'
cards.quote: The Rio Summit produced conventions dealing with climate change, biodiversity, forestry, and recommended a list of development practices called `Agenda 21'.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is 'sustainable development'?
cards.back: There was a consensus on combining economic growth with ecological responsibility. This approach to development is commonly known as `sustainable development'.
cards.quote: There was a consensus on combining economic growth with ecological responsibility. This approach to development is commonly known as `sustainable development'.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Some critics have pointed out that ____ was biased in favour of economic growth rather than ensuring ecological conservation.
cards.back: Some critics have pointed out that Agenda 21 was biased in favour of economic growth rather than ensuring ecological conservation.
cards.quote: Some critics have pointed out that Agenda 21 was biased in favour of economic growth rather than ensuring ecological conservation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What are 'commons'?
cards.back: `Commons' are those resources which are not owned by anyone but rather shared by a community.
cards.quote: `Commons' are those resources which are not owned by anyone but rather shared by a community.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What are the global commons (res communis humanitatis)?
cards.back: areas or regions of the world which are located outside the sovereign jurisdiction of any one state, and therefore require common governance by the international community. These are known as res communis humanitatis or global commons.
cards.quote: areas or regions of the world which are located outside the sovereign jurisdiction of any one state, and therefore require common governance by the international community. These are known as res communis humanitatis or global commons.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the global commons.
cards.back:
the earth's atmosphere
Antarctica
the ocean floor
outer space
cards.quote: They include the earth's atmosphere, Antarctica (see Box), the ocean floor, and outer space.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the path-breaking agreements on the global commons.
cards.back:
the 1959 Antarctic Treaty
the 1987 Montreal Protocol
the 1991 Antarctic Environmental Protocol
cards.quote: There have been many path-breaking agreements such as the 1959 Antarctic Treaty, the 1987 Montreal Protocol, and the 1991 Antarctic Environmental Protocol.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is a major problem underlying all ecological issues?
cards.back: A major problem underlying all ecological issues relates to the difficulty of achieving consensus on common environmental agendas
cards.quote: A major problem underlying all ecological issues relates to the difficulty of achieving consensus on common environmental agendas

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which countries have made legal claims to sovereign rights over Antarctic territory?
cards.back:
the UK
Argentina
Chile
Norway
France
Australia
New Zealand
cards.quote: Some countries like the UK, Argentina, Chile, Norway, France, Australia and New Zealand have made legal claims to sovereign rights over Antarctic territory.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What view do most other states take on the Antarctic's status?
cards.back: Most other states have taken the opposite view that the Antarctic is a part of the global commons and not subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of any state.
cards.quote: Most other states have taken the opposite view that the Antarctic is a part of the global commons and not subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of any state.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Since 1959, which activities have been allowed in the Antarctic region?
cards.back: Since 1959, activities in the area have been limited to scientific research, fishing and tourism.
cards.quote: Since 1959, activities in the area have been limited to scientific research, fishing and tourism.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which term came into popular vocabulary after the 1970s drought in Africa?
cards.back: a drought turned the best cropland in five countries into cracked and barren earth. In fact, the term environmental refugees came into popular vocabulary after this.
cards.quote: a drought turned the best cropland in five countries into cracked and barren earth. In fact, the term environmental refugees came into popular vocabulary after this.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What does the global North want regarding responsibility for ecological conservation?
cards.back: The developed countries of the North want to discuss the environmental issue as it stands now and want everyone to be equally responsible for ecological conservation.
cards.quote: The developed countries of the North want to discuss the environmental issue as it stands now and want everyone to be equally responsible for ecological conservation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the South's argument about the cause of ecological degradation?
cards.back: The developing countries of the South feel that much of the ecological degradation in the world is the product of industrial development undertaken by the developed countries.
cards.quote: The developing countries of the South feel that much of the ecological degradation in the world is the product of industrial development undertaken by the developed countries.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In which 1992 document was the principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities' accepted?
cards.back: This argument was accepted in the Rio Declaration at the Earth Summit in 1992 and is called the principle of `common but differentiated responsibilities'.
cards.quote: This argument was accepted in the Rio Declaration at the Earth Summit in 1992 and is called the principle of `common but differentiated responsibilities'.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which declaration says states shall cooperate in global partnership to conserve and restore the Earth's ecosystem?
cards.back: The relevant part of the Rio Declaration says that "States shall cooperate in the spirit of global partnership to conserve, protect and restore the health and integrity of the Earth's ecosystem.
cards.quote: The relevant part of the Rio Declaration says that "States shall cooperate in the spirit of global partnership to conserve, protect and restore the health and integrity of the Earth's ecosystem.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: On what basis does the 1992 UNFCCC say parties should act to protect the climate system?
cards.back: on the basis of equity and in accordance with their common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities
cards.quote: on the basis of equity and in accordance with their common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: According to the UNFCCC parties, where did the largest share of historical and current greenhouse gas emissions originate?
cards.back: The parties to the Convention agreed that the largest share of historical and current global emissions of greenhouse gases has originated in developed countries.
cards.quote: The parties to the Convention agreed that the largest share of historical and current global emissions of greenhouse gases has originated in developed countries.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which countries were exempted from the requirements of the Kyoto Protocol?
cards.back: China, India, and other developing countries were, therefore, exempted from the requirements of the Kyoto Protocol.
cards.quote: China, India, and other developing countries were, therefore, exempted from the requirements of the Kyoto Protocol.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the Kyoto Protocol?
cards.back: The Kyoto Protocol is an international agreement setting targets for industrialised countries to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.
cards.quote: The Kyoto Protocol is an international agreement setting targets for industrialised countries to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which gases are considered at least partly responsible for global warming?
cards.back: Certain gases like Carbon dioxide, Methane, Hydrofluoro carbons etc. are considered at least partly responsible for global warming
cards.quote: Certain gases like Carbon dioxide, Methane, Hydrofluoro carbons etc. are considered at least partly responsible for global warming

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When and where was the Kyoto Protocol agreed?
cards.back: The protocol was agreed to in 1997 in Kyoto in Japan, based on principles set out in UNFCCC.
cards.quote: The protocol was agreed to in 1997 in Kyoto in Japan, based on principles set out in UNFCCC.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the underlying norm of common property resources?
cards.back: The underlying norm here is that members of the group have both rights and duties with respect to the nature, levels of use, and the maintenance of a given resource.
cards.quote: The underlying norm here is that members of the group have both rights and duties with respect to the nature, levels of use, and the maintenance of a given resource.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the factors that have caused common property to dwindle.
cards.back:
privatisation
agricultural intensification
population growth
ecosystem degradation
cards.quote: A combination of factors, including privatisation, agricultural intensification, population growth and ecosystem degradation have caused common property to dwindle

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What are sacred groves in India?
cards.back: parcels of uncut forest vegetation in the name of certain deities or natural or ancestral spirits
cards.quote: parcels of uncut forest vegetation in the name of certain deities or natural or ancestral spirits

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: By whom have sacred groves along the forest belt of South India traditionally been managed?
cards.back: Along the forest belt of South India, sacred groves have been traditionally managed by village communities.
cards.quote: Along the forest belt of South India, sacred groves have been traditionally managed by village communities.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did India sign and ratify the Kyoto Protocol?
cards.back: India signed and ratified the 1997 Kyoto Protocol in August 2002.
cards.quote: India signed and ratified the 1997 Kyoto Protocol in August 2002.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did India point out at the G-8 meeting in June 2005?
cards.back: At the G-8 meeting in June 2005, India pointed out that the per capita emission rates of the developing countries are a tiny fraction of those in the developed world.
cards.quote: At the G-8 meeting in June 2005, India pointed out that the per capita emission rates of the developing countries are a tiny fraction of those in the developed world.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Where does India say the major responsibility of curbing emission rests?
cards.back: India is of the view that the major responsibility of curbing emission rests with the developed countries, which have accumulated emissions over a long period of time.
cards.quote: India is of the view that the major responsibility of curbing emission rests with the developed countries, which have accumulated emissions over a long period of time.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: On which principle does India's international negotiating position rely heavily?
cards.back: India's international negotiating position relies heavily on principles of historical responsibility, as enshrined in UNFCCC.
cards.quote: India's international negotiating position relies heavily on principles of historical responsibility, as enshrined in UNFCCC.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: According to UNFCCC, what are the first and overriding priorities of developing country parties?
cards.back: economic and social development are the first and overriding priorities of the developing country parties
cards.quote: economic and social development are the first and overriding priorities of the developing country parties

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What discussions within UNFCCC is India wary of?
cards.back: India is wary of recent discussions within UNFCCC about introducing binding commitments on rapidly industrialising countries (such as Brazil, China and India) to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.
cards.quote: India is wary of recent discussions within UNFCCC about introducing binding commitments on rapidly industrialising countries (such as Brazil, China and India) to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name India's policies and laws for global environmental efforts.
cards.back:
National Auto-fuel Policy mandates cleaner fuels for vehicles
The Energy Conservation Act, passed in 2001, outlines initiatives to improve energy efficiency
the Electricity Act of 2003 encourages the use of renewable energy
cards.quote: India's National Auto-fuel Policy mandates cleaner fuels for vehicles. The Energy Conservation Act, passed in 2001, outlines initiatives to improve energy efficiency. Similarly, the Electricity Act of 2003 encourages the use of renewable energy.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was a key conclusion of India's 1997 review of the Rio agreements?
cards.back: One of the key conclusions was that there had been no meaningful progress with respect to transfer of new and additional financial resources and environmentally-sound technology on concessional terms to developing nations.
cards.quote: One of the key conclusions was that there had been no meaningful progress with respect to transfer of new and additional financial resources and environmentally-sound technology on concessional terms to developing nations.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Forest movements of the South vs the North: the difference on the forests.
cards.back: What distinguishes the forest movements of the South from those of the North is that the forests of the former are still peopled, whilst the forests of the latter are more or less devoid of human habitat or, at least, are perceived as thus.
cards.quote: What distinguishes the forest movements of the South from those of the North is that the forests of the former are still peopled, whilst the forests of the latter are more or less devoid of human habitat or, at least, are perceived as thus.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which NGO has initiated and funded many wilderness campaigns with local people?
cards.back: Many of these campaigns have been initiated and funded by NGOs such as the Worldwide Wildlife Fund (WWF), in association with local people.
cards.quote: Many of these campaigns have been initiated and funded by NGOs such as the Worldwide Wildlife Fund (WWF), in association with local people.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why have many wilderness issues been renamed biodiversity issues?
cards.back: Many of the wilderness issues have been renamed biodiversity issues in recent times, as the concept of wilderness has been proved difficult to sell in the South.
cards.quote: Many of the wilderness issues have been renamed biodiversity issues in recent times, as the concept of wilderness has been proved difficult to sell in the South.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What are antidam movements increasingly becoming?
cards.back: Increasingly antidam movements are pro-river movements for more sustainable and equitable management of river systems and valleys.
cards.quote: Increasingly antidam movements are pro-river movements for more sustainable and equitable management of river systems and valleys.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which was the first anti-dam movement launched in the North, in the early 1980s?
cards.back: The early 1980s saw the first anti-dam movement launched in the North, namely, the campaign to save the Franklin River and its surrounding forests in Australia.
cards.quote: The early 1980s saw the first anti-dam movement launched in the North, namely, the campaign to save the Franklin River and its surrounding forests in Australia.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: India has had some of the leading anti-dam, pro-river movements. ____ is one of the best known of these movements.
cards.back: India has had some of the leading anti-dam, pro-river movements. Narmada Bachao Andolan is one of the best known of these movements.
cards.quote: India has had some of the leading anti-dam, pro-river movements. Narmada Bachao Andolan is one of the best known of these movements.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the most important shared idea in anti-dam and other environmental movements in India?
cards.back: It is significant to note that, in anti-dam and other environmental movements in India, the most important shared idea is non-violence.
cards.quote: It is significant to note that, in anti-dam and other environmental movements in India, the most important shared idea is non-violence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is resource geopolitics?
cards.back: Resource geopolitics is all about who gets what, when, where and how.
cards.quote: Resource geopolitics is all about who gets what, when, where and how.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the methods the industrialised North used during the Cold War to ensure a steady flow of resources.
cards.back:
deployment of military forces near exploitation sites and along sea-lanes of communication
the stockpiling of strategic resources
efforts to prop up friendly governments in producing countries
support to multinational companies and favourable international agreements
cards.quote: deployment of military forces near exploitation sites and along sea-lanes of communication, the stockpiling of strategic resources, efforts to prop up friendly governments in producing countries, as well as support to multinational companies and favourable international agreements.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which resource continues to be the most important in global strategy?
cards.back: oil continues to be the most important resource in global strategy
cards.quote: oil continues to be the most important resource in global strategy

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What have some commentators called the possibility of violent conflict over freshwater?
cards.back: Some commentators on world politics have referred to `water wars' to describe the possibility of violent conflict over this life-sustaining resource.
cards.quote: Some commentators on world politics have referred to `water wars' to describe the possibility of violent conflict over this life-sustaining resource.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is a typical disagreement between lower and upper riparian states?
cards.back: a typical disagreement is a downstream (lower riparian) state's objection to pollution, excessive irrigation, or the construction of dams by an upstream (upper riparian) state, which might decrease or degrade the quality of water available to the downstream state
cards.quote: a typical disagreement is a downstream (lower riparian) state's objection to pollution, excessive irrigation, or the construction of dams by an upstream (upper riparian) state, which might decrease or degrade the quality of water available to the downstream state

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How does the UN define indigenous populations?
cards.back: The UN defines indigenous populations as comprising the descendants of peoples who inhabited the present territory of a country at the time when persons of a different culture or ethnic origin arrived there from other parts of the world and overcame them.
cards.quote: The UN defines indigenous populations as comprising the descendants of peoples who inhabited the present territory of a country at the time when persons of a different culture or ethnic origin arrived there from other parts of the world and overcame them.

source.section: The Indigenous Peoples and Their Rights

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What do indigenous voices in world politics call for?
cards.back: The indigenous voices in world politics call for the admission of indigenous people to the world community as equals.
cards.quote: The indigenous voices in world politics call for the admission of indigenous people to the world community as equals.

source.section: The Indigenous Peoples and Their Rights

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which phrase do indigenous people use for their continued occupancy of their lands?
cards.back: `Since times immemorial' is the phrase used by indigenous people all over the world to refer to their continued occupancy of the lands from which they originate.
cards.quote: `Since times immemorial' is the phrase used by indigenous people all over the world to refer to their continued occupancy of the lands from which they originate.

source.section: The Indigenous Peoples and Their Rights

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In India, to whom is the description 'indigenous people' usually applied?
cards.back: In India, the description `indigenous people' is usually applied to the Scheduled Tribes who constitute nearly eight per cent of the population of the country.
cards.quote: In India, the description `indigenous people' is usually applied to the Scheduled Tribes who constitute nearly eight per cent of the population of the country.

source.section: The Indigenous Peoples and Their Rights

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which group is the single largest among people displaced by developmental projects since independence?
cards.back: they are the single largest group among the people displaced by various developmental projects since independence
cards.quote: they are the single largest group among the people displaced by various developmental projects since independence

source.section: The Indigenous Peoples and Their Rights

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When was the World Council of Indigenous Peoples formed?
cards.back: The World Council of Indigenous Peoples was formed in 1975.
cards.quote: The World Council of Indigenous Peoples was formed in 1975.

source.section: The Indigenous Peoples and Their Rights

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When was the Constitution adopted, signed and brought into effect?
cards.back: the Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and signed on 24 January 1950 and it came into effect on 26 January 1950
cards.quote: the Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and signed on 24 January 1950 and it came into effect on 26 January 1950

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When was the Election Commission of India set up and who became the first Chief Election Commissioner?
cards.back: The Election Commission of India was set up in January 1950. Sukumar Sen became the first Chief Election Commissioner.
cards.quote: The Election Commission of India was set up in January 1950. Sukumar Sen became the first Chief Election Commissioner.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Types of non-democratic rule in countries that gained freedom from colonialism.
cards.back:
nominal democracy but effective control by one leader
one party rule
direct army rule
cards.quote: Therefore many of the countries that gained freedom from colonialism experienced non-democratic rule. It took various forms: nominal democracy but effective control by one leader, one party rule or direct army rule.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is delimitation?
cards.back: Holding an election required delimitation or drawing the boundaries of the electoral constituencies.
cards.quote: Holding an election required delimitation or drawing the boundaries of the electoral constituencies.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What are electoral rolls?
cards.back: preparing the electoral rolls, or the list of all the citizens eligible to vote.
cards.quote: It also required preparing the electoral rolls, or the list of all the citizens eligible to vote.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How many Members of Lok Sabha were elected in the first general election?
cards.back: At that time there were 17 crore eligible voters, who had to elect about 3,200 MLAs and 489 Members of Lok Sabha.
cards.quote: At that time there were 17 crore eligible voters, who had to elect about 3,200 MLAs and 489 Members of Lok Sabha.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did voters cast their vote in the first general election?
cards.back: In the first general election, it was decided to place inside each polling booth a box for each candidate with the election symbol of that candidate.
cards.quote: In the first general election, it was decided to place inside each polling booth a box for each candidate with the election symbol of that candidate.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How was the voting method changed after the first two general elections?
cards.back: After the first two elections, this method was changed. Now the ballot paper carried the names and symbols of all the candidates and the voter was required to put a stamp on the name of the candidate they wanted to vote for.
cards.quote: After the first two elections, this method was changed. Now the ballot paper carried the names and symbols of all the candidates and the voter was required to put a stamp on the name of the candidate they wanted to vote for.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Towards the end of 1990s the Election Commission started using the EVM. By ____ the entire country had shifted to the EVM.
cards.back: Towards the end of 1990s the Election Commission started using the EVM. By 2004 the entire country had shifted to the EVM.
cards.quote: Towards the end of 1990s the Election Commission started using the EVM. By 2004 the entire country had shifted to the EVM.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did an Indian editor call India's experiment with universal adult franchise in the first election?
cards.back: An Indian editor called it “the biggest gamble in history”.
cards.quote: An Indian editor called it “the biggest gamble in history”.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When was the first general election held, and why is it called the 1952 election?
cards.back: The elections had to be postponed twice and finally held from October 1951 to February 1952. But this election is referred to as the 1952 election since most parts of the country voted in January 1952.
cards.quote: The elections had to be postponed twice and finally held from October 1951 to February 1952. But this election is referred to as the 1952 election since most parts of the country voted in January 1952.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did India's general election of 1952 prove about democracy?
cards.back: It was no longer possible to argue that democratic elections could not be held in conditions of poverty or lack of education. It proved that democracy could be practiced anywhere in the world.
cards.quote: It was no longer possible to argue that democratic elections could not be held in conditions of poverty or lack of education. It proved that democracy could be practiced anywhere in the world.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why was the Congress expected to win the first general election?
cards.back:
had inherited the legacy of the national movement
It was the only party then to have an organisation spread all over the country
in Jawaharlal Nehru, the party had the most popular and charismatic leader in Indian politics
cards.quote: The Congress party, as it was popularly known, had inherited the legacy of the national movement. It was the only party then to have an organisation spread all over the country. And finally, in Jawaharlal Nehru, the party had the most popular and charismatic leader in Indian politics.

source.section: Congress dominance in the first three general elections

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How many of the 489 seats did the Congress win in the first Lok Sabha?
cards.back: The party won 364 of the 489 seats in the first Lok Sabha and finished way ahead of any other challenger.
cards.quote: The party won 364 of the 489 seats in the first Lok Sabha and finished way ahead of any other challenger.

source.section: Congress dominance in the first three general elections

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which party came next to the Congress in the first general election, and with how many seats?
cards.back: The Communist Party of India that came next in terms of seats won only 16 seats.
cards.quote: The Communist Party of India that came next in terms of seats won only 16 seats.

source.section: Congress dominance in the first three general elections

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In which states did the Congress fail to win a majority in the first state elections?
cards.back: The Congress scored big victory in those elections as well. It won a majority of seats in all the states except Travancore-Cochin (part of today’s Kerala), Madras and Orissa.
cards.quote: The Congress scored big victory in those elections as well. It won a majority of seats in all the states except Travancore-Cochin (part of today’s Kerala), Madras and Orissa.

source.section: Congress dominance in the first three general elections

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the Congress performance in the second and third general elections?
cards.back: In the second and the third general elections, held in 1957 and 1962 respectively, the Congress maintained the same position in the Lok Sabha by winning three-fourth of the seats.
cards.quote: In the second and the third general elections, held in 1957 and 1962 respectively, the Congress maintained the same position in the Lok Sabha by winning three-fourth of the seats.

source.section: Congress dominance in the first three general elections

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did the opposition parties fare against the Congress in 1957 and 1962?
cards.back: None of the opposition parties could win even one-tenth of the number of seats won by the Congress.
cards.quote: None of the opposition parties could win even one-tenth of the number of seats won by the Congress.

source.section: Congress dominance in the first three general elections

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which was the most significant state where the Congress did not get a majority in the state assembly elections?
cards.back: The most significant of these cases was in Kerala in 1957 when a coalition led by the CPI formed the government.
cards.quote: The most significant of these cases was in Kerala in 1957 when a coalition led by the CPI formed the government.

source.section: Congress dominance in the first three general elections

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In 1952, for example, the Congress obtained ____ of the total votes. But it managed to win ____ of the seats.
cards.back: In 1952, for example, the Congress obtained 45 per cent of the total votes. But it managed to win 74 per cent of the seats.
cards.quote: In 1952, for example, the Congress obtained 45 per cent of the total votes. But it managed to win 74 per cent of the seats.

source.section: Congress dominance in the first three general elections

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did the Socialist Party fare in votes and seats in 1952?
cards.back: The Socialist Party, the second largest party in terms of votes, secured more than 10 per cent of the votes all over the country. But it could not even win three per cent of the seats.
cards.quote: The Socialist Party, the second largest party in terms of votes, secured more than 10 per cent of the votes all over the country. But it could not even win three per cent of the seats.

source.section: Congress dominance in the first three general elections

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did the first-past-the-post system work in favour of the Congress?
cards.back: In this system of election, that has been adopted in our country, the party that gets more votes than others tends to get much more than its proportional share.
cards.quote: In this system of election, that has been adopted in our country, the party that gets more votes than others tends to get much more than its proportional share.

source.section: Congress dominance in the first three general elections

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why did the Congress win even though non-Congress votes added up to more?
cards.back: If we add up the votes of all the non-Congress candidates it was more than the votes of the Congress. But the non-Congress votes were divided between different rival parties and candidates.
cards.quote: If we add up the votes of all the non-Congress candidates it was more than the votes of the Congress. But the non-Congress votes were divided between different rival parties and candidates.

source.section: Congress dominance in the first three general elections

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How many of the 126 seats in the Kerala legislature did the Communist Party win in March 1957?
cards.back: The party won 60 of the 126 seats and had the support of five independents.
cards.quote: The party won 60 of the 126 seats and had the support of five independents.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who formed the Communist ministry in Kerala in 1957, and what was unique about it?
cards.back: The governor invited E. M. S. Namboodiripad, the leader of the Communist legislature party, to form the ministry. For the first time in the world, a Communist party government had come to power through democratic elections.
cards.quote: The governor invited E. M. S. Namboodiripad, the leader of the Communist legislature party, to form the ministry. For the first time in the world, a Communist party government had come to power through democratic elections.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Congress begin on losing power in Kerala in 1957?
cards.back: On losing power in the State, the Congress party began a ‘liberation struggle’ against the elected government.
cards.quote: On losing power in the State, the Congress party began a ‘liberation struggle’ against the elected government.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In 1959 the Congress government at the Centre dismissed the Communist government in Kerala under Article ____ of the Constitution.
cards.back: In 1959 the Congress government at the Centre dismissed the Communist government in Kerala under Article 356 of the Constitution.
cards.quote: In 1959 the Congress government at the Centre dismissed the Communist government in Kerala under Article 356 of the Constitution.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why was the 1959 dismissal of the Communist government in Kerala controversial?
cards.back: This decision proved very controversial and was widely cited as one of the prominent instances of the misuse of constitutional emergency powers.
cards.quote: This decision proved very controversial and was widely cited as one of the prominent instances of the misuse of constitutional emergency powers.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The Congress Socialist party (CSP) was formed within the Congress in ____ by a group of young leaders.
cards.back: The Congress Socialist party (CSP) was formed within the Congress in 1934 by a group of young leaders.
cards.quote: The Congress Socialist party (CSP) was formed within the Congress in 1934 by a group of young leaders.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why did the Socialists form a separate Socialist Party in 1948?
cards.back: In 1948, the Congress amended its constitution to prevent its members from having a dual party membership. This forced the Socialists to form a separate Socialist Party in 1948.
cards.quote: In 1948, the Congress amended its constitution to prevent its members from having a dual party membership. This forced the Socialists to form a separate Socialist Party in 1948.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The socialists believed in the ideology of ____ which distinguished them both from the Congress as well as from the Communists.
cards.back: The socialists believed in the ideology of democratic socialism which distinguished them both from the Congress as well as from the Communists.
cards.quote: The socialists believed in the ideology of democratic socialism which distinguished them both from the Congress as well as from the Communists.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the socialists criticise the Congress for?
cards.back: They criticised the Congress for favouring capitalists and landlords and for ignoring the workers and the peasants.
cards.quote: They criticised the Congress for favouring capitalists and landlords and for ignoring the workers and the peasants.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What dilemma did the socialists face in 1955?
cards.back: But the socialists faced a dilemma when in 1955 the Congress declared its goal to be the socialist pattern of society.
cards.quote: But the socialists faced a dilemma when in 1955 the Congress declared its goal to be the socialist pattern of society.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did Rammanohar Lohia and Asoka Mehta differ in their approach to the Congress?
cards.back: Some of them, led by Rammanohar Lohia, increased their distance from and criticism of the Congress party. Some others like Asoka Mehta advocated a limited cooperation with the Congress.
cards.quote: Some of them, led by Rammanohar Lohia, increased their distance from and criticism of the Congress party. Some others like Asoka Mehta advocated a limited cooperation with the Congress.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the three socialist parties NCERT says formed after the Socialist Party's splits and reunions.
cards.back:
Kisan Mazdoor Praja Party
Praja Socialist Party
Samyukta Socialist Party
cards.quote: The Socialist Party went through many splits and reunions leading to the formation of many socialist parties. These included the Kisan Mazdoor Praja Party, the Praja Socialist Party and Samyukta Socialist Party.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the four contemporary parties NCERT names as tracing their origins to the Socialist Party.
cards.back:
Samajwadi Party
Rashtriya Janata Dal
Janata Dal (United)
Janata Dal (Secular)
cards.quote: Many parties in contemporary India, like the Samajwadi Party, the Rashtriya Janata Dal, Janata Dal (United) and the Janata Dal (Secular) trace their origins to the Socialist Party.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What distinguished Congress dominance in India from one-party dominance in other countries?
cards.back: What distinguished the dominance of the Congress party in India from all these cases was it happened under democratic conditions. Many parties contested elections in conditions of free and fair elections and yet the Congress managed to win election after election.
cards.quote: What distinguished the dominance of the Congress party in India from all these cases was it happened under democratic conditions. Many parties contested elections in conditions of free and fair elections and yet the Congress managed to win election after election.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The dominance of the Congress in India was similar to the dominance of which party in South Africa?
cards.back: This was similar to the dominance the African National Congress has enjoyed in South Africa after the end of apartheid.
cards.quote: This was similar to the dominance the African National Congress has enjoyed in South Africa after the end of apartheid.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Where do the roots of the Congress party's extraordinary success go back to?
cards.back: The roots of this extraordinary success of the Congress party go back to the legacy of the freedom struggle.
cards.quote: The roots of this extraordinary success of the Congress party go back to the legacy of the freedom struggle.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Many parties formed only around independence or later; what advantage did that give the Congress?
cards.back: In fact, many parties were formed only around independence or after that. Thus, the Congress had the ‘first off the blocks’ advantage.
cards.quote: In fact, many parties were formed only around independence or after that. Thus, the Congress had the ‘first off the blocks’ advantage.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What organisational strength did the Congress have by the time of independence?
cards.back: By the time of independence the party had not only spread across the length and breadth of the country as we had seen in the maps but also had an organisational network down to the local level.
cards.quote: By the time of independence the party had not only spread across the length and breadth of the country as we had seen in the maps but also had an organisational network down to the local level.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why was the Congress all-inclusive in nature?
cards.back: Most importantly, as the Congress was till recently a national movement, its nature was all-inclusive.
cards.quote: Most importantly, as the Congress was till recently a national movement, its nature was all-inclusive.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Congress evolved from its origins in ____ as a pressure group for the newly educated, professional and commercial classes
cards.back: Congress evolved from its origins in 1885 as a pressure group for the newly educated, professional and commercial classes
cards.quote: Congress evolved from its origins in 1885 as a pressure group for the newly educated, professional and commercial classes

source.section: Congress as social and ideological coalition

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which sections dominated the Congress when it began, and what widened its social base?
cards.back: Thus the Congress began as a party dominated by the English speaking, upper caste, upper middle-class and urban elite. But with every civil disobedience movement it launched, its social base widened.
cards.quote: Thus the Congress began as a party dominated by the English speaking, upper caste, upper middle-class and urban elite. But with every civil disobedience movement it launched, its social base widened.

source.section: Congress as social and ideological coalition

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which groups found space in the Congress?
cards.back: Peasants and industrialists, urban dwellers and villagers, workers and owners, middle, lower and upper classes and castes, all found space in the Congress.
cards.quote: Peasants and industrialists, urban dwellers and villagers, workers and owners, middle, lower and upper classes and castes, all found space in the Congress.

source.section: Congress as social and ideological coalition

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What had the Congress been transformed into by the time of independence?
cards.back: By the time of independence, the Congress was transformed into a rainbow-like social coalition broadly representing India’s diversity in terms of classes and castes, religions and languages and various interests.
cards.quote: By the time of independence, the Congress was transformed into a rainbow-like social coalition broadly representing India’s diversity in terms of classes and castes, religions and languages and various interests.

source.section: Congress as social and ideological coalition

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What role did the Congress play for groups, interests and parties in the national movement?
cards.back: The Congress was a ‘platform’ for numerous groups, interests and even political parties to take part in the national movement.
cards.quote: The Congress was a ‘platform’ for numerous groups, interests and even political parties to take part in the national movement.

source.section: Congress as social and ideological coalition

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was allowed in pre-independence days within the Congress?
cards.back: In pre-independence days, many organisations and parties with their own constitution and organisational structure were allowed to exist within the Congress.
cards.quote: In pre-independence days, many organisations and parties with their own constitution and organisational structure were allowed to exist within the Congress.

source.section: Congress as social and ideological coalition

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What inspired the emergence of communist groups in India in the early 1920s?
cards.back: In the early 1920s communist groups emerged in different parts of India taking inspiration from the Bolshevik revolution in Russia and advocating socialism as the solution to problems affecting the country.
cards.quote: In the early 1920s communist groups emerged in different parts of India taking inspiration from the Bolshevik revolution in Russia and advocating socialism as the solution to problems affecting the country.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why did the Communists part ways with the Congress in December 1941?
cards.back: A parting of ways took place in December 1941, when the Communists decided to support the British in their war against Nazi Germany.
cards.quote: A parting of ways took place in December 1941, when the Communists decided to support the British in their war against Nazi Germany.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What strength did the CPI have at the time of independence?
cards.back: Unlike other non-Congress parties the CPI had a well-oiled party machinery and dedicated cadre at the time of independence.
cards.quote: Unlike other non-Congress parties the CPI had a well-oiled party machinery and dedicated cadre at the time of independence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Where did the Communists encourage violent uprisings soon after independence?
cards.back: Soon after independence, the party thought that the transfer of power in 1947 was not true independence and encouraged violent uprisings in Telangana.
cards.quote: Soon after independence, the party thought that the transfer of power in 1947 was not true independence and encouraged violent uprisings in Telangana.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In ____ the Communist Party abandoned the path of violent revolution and decided to participate in the approaching general elections.
cards.back: In 1951 the Communist Party abandoned the path of violent revolution and decided to participate in the approaching general elections.
cards.quote: In 1951 the Communist Party abandoned the path of violent revolution and decided to participate in the approaching general elections.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did the CPI fare in the first general election and where was its support concentrated?
cards.back: In the first general election, CPI won 16 seats and emerged as the largest opposition party. The party’s support was more concentrated in Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, Bihar and Kerala.
cards.quote: In the first general election, CPI won 16 seats and emerged as the largest opposition party. The party’s support was more concentrated in Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, Bihar and Kerala.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What led to the 1964 split in the Communist Party?
cards.back: The Party went through a major split in 1964 following the ideological rift between Soviet Union and China. The pro-Soviet faction remained as the CPI, while the opponents formed the CPI(M).
cards.quote: The Party went through a major split in 1964 following the ideological rift between Soviet Union and China. The pro-Soviet faction remained as the CPI, while the opponents formed the CPI(M).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What are the hallmarks of a coalition?
cards.back: Compromise and inclusiveness are the hallmarks of a coalition.
cards.quote: Compromise and inclusiveness are the hallmarks of a coalition.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why was the Congress strategy of a coalition a difficulty for the opposition?
cards.back: This strategy put the opposition in a difficulty. Anything that the opposition wanted to say, would also find a place in the programme and ideology of the Congress.
cards.quote: This strategy put the opposition in a difficulty. Anything that the opposition wanted to say, would also find a place in the programme and ideology of the Congress.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What are factions within a party?
cards.back: That is why, even if a group was not happy with the position of the party or with its share of power, it would remain inside the party and fight the other groups rather than leaving the party and becoming an ‘opposition’. These groups inside the party are called factions.
cards.quote: That is why, even if a group was not happy with the position of the party or with its share of power, it would remain inside the party and fight the other groups rather than leaving the party and becoming an ‘opposition’. These groups inside the party are called factions.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: On what were the factions within the Congress based?
cards.back: Some of these factions were based on ideological considerations but very often these factions were rooted in personal ambitions and rivalries.
cards.quote: Some of these factions were based on ideological considerations but very often these factions were rooted in personal ambitions and rivalries.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh was formed in ____ with ____ as its founder-President.
cards.back: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh was formed in 1951 with Shyama Prasad Mukherjee as its founder-President.
cards.quote: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh was formed in 1951 with Shyama Prasad Mukherjee as its founder-President.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: From which organisations can the lineage of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh be traced?
cards.back: Its lineage however can be traced back to the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and the Hindu Mahasabha before independence.
cards.quote: Its lineage however can be traced back to the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and the Hindu Mahasabha before independence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What idea did the Jana Sangh emphasise?
cards.back: The Jana Sangh was different from other parties in terms of ideology and programmes. It emphasised the idea of one country, one culture and one nation
cards.quote: The Jana Sangh was different from other parties in terms of ideology and programmes. It emphasised the idea of one country, one culture and one nation

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Jana Sangh call for in relation to India and Pakistan?
cards.back: The party called for a reunion of India and Pakistan in Akhand Bharat.
cards.quote: The party called for a reunion of India and Pakistan in Akhand Bharat.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the Jana Sangh's position on language and on concessions to minorities?
cards.back: The party was in forefront of the agitation to replace English with Hindi as the official language of India and was also opposed to the granting of concessions to religious and cultural minorities.
cards.quote: The party was in forefront of the agitation to replace English with Hindi as the official language of India and was also opposed to the granting of concessions to religious and cultural minorities.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which party advocated that India develop nuclear weapons, especially after China's atomic tests in 1964?
cards.back: The party was a consistent advocate of India developing nuclear weapons especially after China carried out its atomic tests in 1964.
cards.quote: The party was a consistent advocate of India developing nuclear weapons especially after China carried out its atomic tests in 1964.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How many Lok Sabha seats did the Jana Sangh win in 1952 and 1957?
cards.back: In the 1950s Jana Sangh remained on the margins of the electoral politics and was able to secure only 3 Lok Sabha seats in 1952 elections and 4 seats in 1957 general elections to Lok Sabha.
cards.quote: In the 1950s Jana Sangh remained on the margins of the electoral politics and was able to secure only 3 Lok Sabha seats in 1952 elections and 4 seats in 1957 general elections to Lok Sabha.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Where did the Jana Sangh's support come from in the early years?
cards.back: In the early years its support came mainly from the urban areas in the Hindi speaking states like Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh.
cards.quote: In the early years its support came mainly from the urban areas in the Hindi speaking states like Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which earlier party does the Bharatiya Janata Party trace its roots to?
cards.back: The Bharatiya Janata Party traces its roots to the Bharatiya Jana Sangh.
cards.quote: The Bharatiya Janata Party traces its roots to the Bharatiya Jana Sangh.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why did leaders of different interests and ideologies stay within the Congress?
cards.back: Since there was room within the party for various factions to fight with each other, it meant that leaders representing different interests and ideologies remained within the Congress rather than go out and form a new party.
cards.quote: Since there was room within the party for various factions to fight with each other, it meant that leaders representing different interests and ideologies remained within the Congress rather than go out and form a new party.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What function did the system of factions serve within the ruling party?
cards.back: The system of factions functioned as balancing mechanism within the ruling party. Political competition therefore took place within the Congress.
cards.quote: The system of factions functioned as balancing mechanism within the ruling party. Political competition therefore took place within the Congress.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did the other parties influence policy during Congress dominance?
cards.back: The other parties primarily attempted to influence these factions and thereby indirectly influenced policy and decision making from the “margins”.
cards.quote: The other parties primarily attempted to influence these factions and thereby indirectly influenced policy and decision making from the “margins”.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the ‘Congress system’?
cards.back: In that sense, in the first decade of electoral competition the Congress acted both as the ruling party as well as the opposition. That is why this period of Indian politics has been described as the ‘Congress system’.
cards.quote: In that sense, in the first decade of electoral competition the Congress acted both as the ruling party as well as the opposition. That is why this period of Indian politics has been described as the ‘Congress system’.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The roots of almost all the non-Congress parties of today can be traced to one or the other of the opposition parties of the ____.
cards.back: The roots of almost all the non-Congress parties of today can be traced to one or the other of the opposition parties of the 1950s.
cards.quote: The roots of almost all the non-Congress parties of today can be traced to one or the other of the opposition parties of the 1950s.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What role did the opposition parties play despite their token representation?
cards.back: Yet their presence played a crucial role in maintaining the democratic character of the system.
cards.quote: Yet their presence played a crucial role in maintaining the democratic character of the system.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did the opposition parties keep the ruling Congress under check?
cards.back: These parties offered a sustained and often principled criticism of the policies and practices of the Congress party. This kept the ruling party under check and often changed the balance of power within the Congress.
cards.quote: These parties offered a sustained and often principled criticism of the policies and practices of the Congress party. This kept the ruling party under check and often changed the balance of power within the Congress.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the opposition parties prevent by keeping a democratic political alternative alive?
cards.back: these parties prevented the resentment with the system from turning anti-democratic.
cards.quote: these parties prevented the resentment with the system from turning anti-democratic.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which opposition leaders were in the interim government cabinet?
cards.back: The interim government that ruled the country after the declaration of Independence and the first general election included opposition leaders like Dr. Ambedkar and Shyama Prasad Mukherjee in the cabinet.
cards.quote: The interim government that ruled the country after the declaration of Independence and the first general election included opposition leaders like Dr. Ambedkar and Shyama Prasad Mukherjee in the cabinet.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which socialist leader does NCERT name as one Nehru invited to join his government?
cards.back: Jawaharlal Nehru often referred to his fondness for the Socialist Party and invited socialist leaders like Jayaprakash Narayan to join his government.
cards.quote: Jawaharlal Nehru often referred to his fondness for the Socialist Party and invited socialist leaders like Jayaprakash Narayan to join his government.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What led other political parties to gain greater significance?
cards.back: As the ability of the Congress to accommodate all interests and all aspirants for political power steadily declined, other political parties started gaining greater significance.
cards.quote: As the ability of the Congress to accommodate all interests and all aspirants for political power steadily declined, other political parties started gaining greater significance.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What does globalisation as a concept fundamentally deal with?
cards.back: Globalisation as a concept fundamentally deals with flows.
cards.quote: Globalisation as a concept fundamentally deals with flows.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the four kinds of flows with which globalisation deals.
cards.back:
ideas moving from one part of the world to another
capital shunted between two or more places
commodities being traded across borders
people moving in search of better livelihoods to different parts of the world
cards.quote: These flows could be of various kinds -- ideas moving from one part of the world to another, capital shunted between two or more places, commodities being traded across borders, and people moving in search of better livelihoods to different parts of the world.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The crucial element is the `____' that is created and sustained as a consequence of these constant flows.
cards.back: The crucial element is the `worldwide interconnectedness' that is created and sustained as a consequence of these constant flows.
cards.quote: The crucial element is the `worldwide interconnectedness' that is created and sustained as a consequence of these constant flows.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Is globalisation only about economic issues, and does influence always flow from rich to poor countries?
cards.back: These examples also show us that globalisation need not be only about the economic issues, nor is the direction of influence always from the rich to the poor countries.
cards.quote: These examples also show us that globalisation need not be only about the economic issues, nor is the direction of influence always from the rich to the poor countries.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Globalisation is a ____ concept. It has political, economic and cultural manifestations, and these must be adequately distinguished.
