cards.back: Globalisation is a multidimensional concept. It has political, economic and cultural manifestations, and these must be adequately distinguished.
cards.quote: Globalisation is a multidimensional concept. It has political, economic and cultural manifestations, and these must be adequately distinguished.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the manifestations (dimensions) of globalisation.
cards.back:
political
economic
cultural
cards.quote: It has political, economic and cultural manifestations, and these must be adequately distinguished.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How is the impact of globalisation described in NCERT?
cards.back: The impact of globalisation is vastly uneven -- it affects some societies more than others and some parts of some societies more than others
cards.quote: The impact of globalisation is vastly uneven -- it affects some societies more than others and some parts of some societies more than others

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Has globalisation in terms of the four flows taken place in earlier history?
cards.back: Globalisation in terms of these four flows has taken place through much of human history.
cards.quote: Globalisation in terms of these four flows has taken place through much of human history.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What makes contemporary globalisation unique, according to those who see it as distinct?
cards.back: those who argue that there is something distinct about contemporary globalisation point out that it is the scale and speed of these flows that account for the uniqueness of globalisation in the contemporary era.
cards.quote: those who argue that there is something distinct about contemporary globalisation point out that it is the scale and speed of these flows that account for the uniqueness of globalisation in the contemporary era.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: While globalisation is not caused by any single factor, ____ remains a critical element.
cards.back: While globalisation is not caused by any single factor, technology remains a critical element.
cards.quote: While globalisation is not caused by any single factor, technology remains a critical element.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which inventions have revolutionised communication between different parts of the world?
cards.back:
the telegraph
the telephone
the microchip
cards.quote: the invention of the telegraph, the telephone, and the microchip in more recent times has revolutionised communication between different parts of the world.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When printing initially came into being it laid the basis for the creation of ____.
cards.back: When printing initially came into being it laid the basis for the creation of nationalism.
cards.quote: When printing initially came into being it laid the basis for the creation of nationalism.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which flows are quicker and wider: capital and commodities, or the movement of peoples?
cards.back: The pace of these flows may vary. For instance, the movement of capital and commodities will most likely be quicker and wider than the movement of peoples across different parts of the world.
cards.quote: The pace of these flows may vary. For instance, the movement of capital and commodities will most likely be quicker and wider than the movement of peoples across different parts of the world.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Besides improved communications, what is important for globalisation to emerge?
cards.back: Globalisation, however, does not emerge merely because of the availability of improved communications. What is important is for people in different parts of the world to recognise these interconnections with the rest of the world.
cards.quote: Globalisation, however, does not emerge merely because of the availability of improved communications. What is important is for people in different parts of the world to recognise these interconnections with the rest of the world.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: At the most simple level, globalisation results in an erosion of ____, that is, the ability of government to do what they do.
cards.back: At the most simple level, globalisation results in an erosion of state capacity, that is, the ability of government to do what they do.
cards.quote: At the most simple level, globalisation results in an erosion of state capacity, that is, the ability of government to do what they do.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: All over the world, the old `welfare state' is now giving way to a more ____.
cards.back: All over the world, the old `welfare state' is now giving way to a more minimalist state.
cards.quote: All over the world, the old `welfare state' is now giving way to a more minimalist state.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In place of the welfare state, it is the ____ that becomes the prime determinant of economic and social priorities.
cards.back: In place of the welfare state, it is the market that becomes the prime determinant of economic and social priorities.
cards.quote: In place of the welfare state, it is the market that becomes the prime determinant of economic and social priorities.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The entry and the increased role of ____ all over the world leads to a reduction in the capacity of governments
cards.back: The entry and the increased role of multinational companies all over the world leads to a reduction in the capacity of governments
cards.quote: The entry and the increased role of multinational companies all over the world leads to a reduction in the capacity of governments

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which essential functions does the state continue to discharge despite globalisation?
cards.back: The state continues to discharge its essential functions (law and order, national security) and consciously withdraws from certain domains from which it wishes to.
cards.quote: The state continues to discharge its essential functions (law and order, national security) and consciously withdraws from certain domains from which it wishes to.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In what respect has state capacity received a boost from globalisation?
cards.back: Indeed, in some respects state capacity has received a boost as a consequence of globalisation, with enhanced technologies available at the disposal of the state to collect information about its citizens.
cards.quote: Indeed, in some respects state capacity has received a boost as a consequence of globalisation, with enhanced technologies available at the disposal of the state to collect information about its citizens.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The mention of economic globalisation draws our attention immediately to the role of international institutions like the ____ and the ____
cards.back: The mention of economic globalisation draws our attention immediately to the role of international institutions like the IMF and the WTO
cards.quote: The mention of economic globalisation draws our attention immediately to the role of international institutions like the IMF and the WTO

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What does a broader understanding of economic globalisation require us to look at?
cards.back: A much broader way of understanding of economic globalisation requires us to look at the distribution of economic gains, i.e. who gets the most from globalisation and who gets less, indeed who loses from it.
cards.quote: A much broader way of understanding of economic globalisation requires us to look at the distribution of economic gains, i.e. who gets the most from globalisation and who gets less, indeed who loses from it.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the forms that economic flows or exchange can take.
cards.back:
commodities
capital
people
ideas
cards.quote: this flow or exchange can take various forms: commodities, capital, people and ideas.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Are the economic flows of globalisation all voluntary?
cards.back: Some of this is voluntary and some forced by international institutions and powerful countries.
cards.quote: Some of this is voluntary and some forced by international institutions and powerful countries.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What has happened to restrictions on imports under globalisation?
cards.back: Globalisation has involved greater trade in commodities across the globe; the restrictions imposed by different countries on allowing the imports of other countries have been reduced.
cards.quote: Globalisation has involved greater trade in commodities across the globe; the restrictions imposed by different countries on allowing the imports of other countries have been reduced.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What has happened to restrictions on movement of capital, and what does it mean for investors?
cards.back: Similarly, the restrictions on movement of capital across countries have also been reduced. In operational terms, it means that investors in the rich countries can invest their money in countries other than their own, including developing countries, where they might get better returns.
cards.quote: Similarly, the restrictions on movement of capital across countries have also been reduced. In operational terms, it means that investors in the rich countries can invest their money in countries other than their own, including developing countries, where they might get better returns.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Give NCERT's example of the flow of ideas across national boundaries.
cards.back: Globalisation has also led to the flow of ideas across national boundaries. The spread of internet and computer related services is an example of that.
cards.quote: Globalisation has also led to the flow of ideas across national boundaries. The spread of internet and computer related services is an example of that.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why has the movement of people not increased as much as that of capital and commodities?
cards.back: But globalisation has not led to the same degree of increase in the movement of people across the globe. Developed countries have carefully guarded their borders with visa policies to ensure that citizens of other countries cannot take away the jobs of their own citizens.
cards.quote: But globalisation has not led to the same degree of increase in the movement of people across the globe. Developed countries have carefully guarded their borders with visa policies to ensure that citizens of other countries cannot take away the jobs of their own citizens.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Do the same globalisation policies lead to the same results everywhere?
cards.back: In thinking about the consequences of globalisation, it is necessary to keep in mind that the same set of policies do not lead to the same results everywhere.
cards.quote: In thinking about the consequences of globalisation, it is necessary to keep in mind that the same set of policies do not lead to the same results everywhere.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What do those concerned about social justice say economic globalisation is likely to do?
cards.back: They point out that it is likely to benefit only a small section of the population while impoverishing those who were dependent on the government for jobs and welfare (education, health, sanitation, etc.).
cards.quote: They point out that it is likely to benefit only a small section of the population while impoverishing those who were dependent on the government for jobs and welfare (education, health, sanitation, etc.).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What do those worried about social justice want created to minimise the negative effects of globalisation on the weak?
cards.back: the need to ensure institutional safeguards or creating `social safety nets' to minimise the negative effects of globalisation on those who are economically weak.
cards.quote: They have emphasised the need to ensure institutional safeguards or creating `social safety nets' to minimise the negative effects of globalisation on those who are economically weak.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Some economists have described economic globalisation as ____ of the world.
cards.back: Some economists have described economic globalisation as recolonisation of the world.
cards.quote: Some economists have described economic globalisation as recolonisation of the world.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What do advocates of economic globalisation argue about growth and well-being?
cards.back: Advocates of economic globalisation argue that it generates greater economic growth and well-being for larger sections of the population when there is de-regulation.
cards.quote: Advocates of economic globalisation argue that it generates greater economic growth and well-being for larger sections of the population when there is de-regulation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What do advocates say about the inevitability of economic globalisation?
cards.back: They also argue that economic globalisation is inevitable and it is not wise to resist the march of history.
cards.quote: They also argue that economic globalisation is inevitable and it is not wise to resist the march of history.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What do more moderate supporters of globalisation say?
cards.back: More moderate supporters of globalisation say that globalisation provides a challenge that can be responded to intelligently without accepting it uncritically.
cards.quote: More moderate supporters of globalisation say that globalisation provides a challenge that can be responded to intelligently without accepting it uncritically.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What, however, cannot be denied is the increased momentum towards ____ and integration between governments
cards.back: What, however, cannot be denied is the increased momentum towards inter-dependence and integration between governments
cards.quote: What, however, cannot be denied is the increased momentum towards inter-dependence and integration between governments

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is cultural homogenisation?
cards.back: globalisation leads to the rise of a uniform culture or what is called cultural homogenisation.
cards.quote: globalisation leads to the rise of a uniform culture or what is called cultural homogenisation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the imposition of Western culture in the name of a global culture known as?
cards.back: name of a global culture is the imposition of Western culture on the rest of the world. This phenomenon is known as the soft power of US hegemony.
cards.quote: name of a global culture is the imposition of Western culture on the rest of the world. This phenomenon is known as the soft power of US hegemony.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What term do critics of US cultural dominance use for the world buying into the American dream?
cards.back: the `McDonaldisation' of the world
cards.quote: Those who make this argument often draw attention to the `McDonaldisation' of the world, with cultures seeking to buy into the dominant American dream.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why is cultural homogenisation called dangerous for the whole of humanity?
cards.back: This is dangerous not only for the poor countries but for the whole of humanity, for it leads to the shrinking of the rich cultural heritage of the entire globe.
cards.quote: This is dangerous not only for the poor countries but for the whole of humanity, for it leads to the shrinking of the rich cultural heritage of the entire globe.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How can external cultural influences affect our choices and our culture?
cards.back: Some external influences are negative because they reduce our choices. But sometimes external influences simply enlarge our choices, and sometimes they modify our culture without overwhelming the traditional.
cards.quote: Some external influences are negative because they reduce our choices. But sometimes external influences simply enlarge our choices, and sometimes they modify our culture without overwhelming the traditional.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is cultural heterogenisation?
cards.back: It leads to each culture becoming more different and distinctive. This phenomenon is called cultural heterogenisation.
cards.quote: While cultural homogenisation is an aspect of globalisation, the same process also generates precisely the opposite effect. It leads to each culture becoming more different and distinctive. This phenomenon is called cultural heterogenisation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: During the colonial period, as a consequence of Britain's imperial ambitions, India became an exporter of ____
cards.back: During the colonial period, as a consequence of Britain's imperial ambitions, India became an exporter of primary goods and raw materials
cards.quote: During the colonial period, as a consequence of Britain's imperial ambitions, India became an exporter of primary goods and raw materials

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: After independence, what did India decide about imports, and what was this policy called?
cards.back: We also decided not to allow others to export to us so that our own producers could learn to make things. This `protectionism' generated its own problems.
cards.quote: We also decided not to allow others to export to us so that our own producers could learn to make things. This `protectionism' generated its own problems.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What problems did protectionism generate in India?
cards.back: critical sectors such as health, housing and primary education did not receive the attention they deserved. India had a fairly sluggish rate of economic growth.
cards.quote: critical sectors such as health, housing and primary education did not receive the attention they deserved. India had a fairly sluggish rate of economic growth.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In which year did India embark on a programme of economic reforms, and why?
cards.back: In 1991, responding to a financial crisis and to the desire for higher rates of economic growth, India embarked on a programme of economic reforms
cards.quote: In 1991, responding to a financial crisis and to the desire for higher rates of economic growth, India embarked on a programme of economic reforms

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the ultimate test of India's economic reforms, according to NCERT?
cards.back: the ultimate test is not high growth rates as making sure that the benefits of growth are shared so that everyone is better off.
cards.quote: the ultimate test is not high growth rates as making sure that the benefits of growth are shared so that everyone is better off.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What do critics of globalisation on the left argue?
cards.back: Those on the left argue that contemporary globalisation represents a particular phase of global capitalism that makes the rich richer (and fewer) and the poor poorer.
cards.quote: Those on the left argue that contemporary globalisation represents a particular phase of global capitalism that makes the rich richer (and fewer) and the poor poorer.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What do critics of globalisation from the political right fear in political and economic terms?
cards.back: Critics of globalisation from the political right express anxiety over the political, economic and cultural effects. In political terms, they also fear the weakening of the state. Economically, they want a return to self-reliance and protectionism, at least in certain areas of the economy.
cards.quote: Critics of globalisation from the political right express anxiety over the political, economic and cultural effects. In political terms, they also fear the weakening of the state. Economically, they want a return to self-reliance and protectionism, at least in certain areas of the economy.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What are critics on the political right worried about culturally?
cards.back: Culturally, they are worried that traditional culture will be harmed and people will lose their age-old values and ways.
cards.quote: Culturally, they are worried that traditional culture will be harmed and people will lose their age-old values and ways.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Do anti-globalisation movements participate in global networks?
cards.back: It is important to note here that anti-globalisation movements too participate in global networks, allying with those who feel like them in other countries.
cards.quote: It is important to note here that anti-globalisation movements too participate in global networks, allying with those who feel like them in other countries.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What do many anti-globalisation movements actually oppose?
cards.back: Many anti-globalisation movements are not opposed to the idea of globalisation per se as much as they are opposed to a specific programme of globalisation, which they see as a form of imperialism.
cards.quote: Many anti-globalisation movements are not opposed to the idea of globalisation per se as much as they are opposed to a specific programme of globalisation, which they see as a form of imperialism.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What happened at the 1999 WTO Ministerial Meeting in Seattle?
cards.back: protests at Seattle alleging unfair trading practices by the economically powerful states. It was argued that the interests of the developing world were not given sufficient importance in the evolving global economic system.
cards.quote: protests at Seattle alleging unfair trading practices by the economically powerful states. It was argued that the interests of the developing world were not given sufficient importance in the evolving global economic system.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the World Social Forum (WSF)?
cards.back: The World Social Forum (WSF) is another global platform, which brings together a wide coalition composed of human rights activists, environmentalists, labour, youth and women activists opposed to neo-liberal globalisation.
cards.quote: The World Social Forum (WSF) is another global platform, which brings together a wide coalition composed of human rights activists, environmentalists, labour, youth and women activists opposed to neo-liberal globalisation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Where was the first WSF meeting organised, and where was the fourth held?
cards.back: The first WSF meeting was organised in Porto Alegre, Brazil in 2001. The fourth WSF meeting was held in Mumbai in 2004.
cards.quote: The first WSF meeting was organised in Porto Alegre, Brazil in 2001. The fourth WSF meeting was held in Mumbai in 2004.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Through what have left wing protests to economic liberalisation been voiced in India?
cards.back: There have been left wing protests to economic liberalisation voiced through political parties as well as through forums like the Indian Social Forum.
cards.quote: There have been left wing protests to economic liberalisation voiced through political parties as well as through forums like the Indian Social Forum.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who have organised protests against the entry of multinationals in India?
cards.back: Trade unions of industrial workforce as well as those representing farmer interests have organised protests against the entry of multinationals.
cards.quote: Trade unions of industrial workforce as well as those representing farmer interests have organised protests against the entry of multinationals.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The patenting of certain plants like ____ by American and European firms has also generated considerable opposition.
cards.back: The patenting of certain plants like Neem by American and European firms has also generated considerable opposition.
cards.quote: The patenting of certain plants like Neem by American and European firms has also generated considerable opposition.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What form has resistance to globalisation from the political right taken in India?
cards.back: Resistance to globalisation has also come from the political right. This has taken the form of objecting particularly to various cultural influences -- ranging from the availability of foreign T.V. channels provided by cable networks, celebration of Valentine's Day, and westernisation of the dress tastes of girl students in schools and colleges.
cards.quote: Resistance to globalisation has also come from the political right. This has taken the form of objecting particularly to various cultural influences -- ranging from the availability of foreign T.V. channels provided by cable networks, celebration of Valentine's Day, and westernisation of the dress tastes of girl students in schools and colleges.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Article 51 (Directive Principles): what shall the State endeavour to do? Name the four aims.
cards.back:
Promote international peace and security
Maintain just and honourable relations between nations
Foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised people with one another
Encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration
cards.quote: (a) Promote international peace and security (b) Maintain just and honourable relations between nations (c) Foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised people with one another; and (d) Encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the clearest manifestation of the linkages between India and overseas Indians during the freedom struggle?
cards.back: The creation of the Indian National Army (INA) by Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose during the Second World War was the clearest manifestation of the linkages established between India and overseas Indians during the freedom struggle.
cards.quote: The creation of the Indian National Army (INA) by Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose during the Second World War was the clearest manifestation of the linkages established between India and overseas Indians during the freedom struggle.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the Cold War era, with which India's independence coincided?
cards.back: India's attainment of independence coincided with the beginning of the Cold War era, a period which was marked by the political, economic, and military confrontation at the global level between the two blocs led by the superpowers, the US and the USSR.
cards.quote: India's attainment of independence coincided with the beginning of the Cold War era, a period which was marked by the political, economic, and military confrontation at the global level between the two blocs led by the superpowers, the US and the USSR.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who exercised profound influence on India's foreign policy from 1946 to 1964 as both PM and Foreign Minister?
cards.back: The first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru played a crucial role in setting the national agenda. He was his own foreign minister. Thus both as the Prime Minister and the Foreign Minister, he exercised profound influence in the formulation and implementation of India's foreign policy from 1946 to 1964.
cards.quote: The first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru played a crucial role in setting the national agenda. He was his own foreign minister. Thus both as the Prime Minister and the Foreign Minister, he exercised profound influence in the formulation and implementation of India's foreign policy from 1946 to 1964.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the three major objectives of Nehru's foreign policy.
cards.back:
preserve the hard-earned sovereignty
protect territorial integrity
promote rapid economic development
cards.quote: The three major objectives of Nehru's foreign policy were to preserve the hard-earned sovereignty, protect territorial integrity, and promote rapid economic development.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Through which strategy did Nehru wish to achieve the three objectives of his foreign policy?
cards.back: Nehru wished to achieve these objectives through the strategy of non-alignment.
cards.quote: Nehru wished to achieve these objectives through the strategy of non-alignment.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which parties opposed to communism wanted India to follow a pro-US foreign policy?
cards.back: Some political parties, which were opposed to communism, also wanted India to follow a pro-US foreign policy. These included the Bharatiya Jan Sangh and later the Swatantra Party.
cards.quote: Some political parties, which were opposed to communism, also wanted India to follow a pro-US foreign policy. These included the Bharatiya Jan Sangh and later the Swatantra Party.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In what three ways did independent India pursue the dream of a peaceful world?
cards.back:
advocating the policy of non-alignment
reducing Cold War tensions
contributing human resources to the UN peacekeeping operations
cards.quote: The foreign policy of independent India vigorously pursued the dream of a peaceful world by advocating the policy of non-alignment, by reducing Cold War tensions and by contributing human resources to the UN peacekeeping operations.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why did India not join either camp during the Cold War era?
cards.back: India wanted to keep away from the military alliances led by US and Soviet Union against each other.
cards.quote: India wanted to keep away from the military alliances led by US and Soviet Union against each other.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: During the Cold War, the US-led North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) and the Soviet-led ____ came into existence.
cards.back: During the Cold War, the US-led North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) and the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact came into existence.
cards.quote: During the Cold War, the US-led North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) and the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact came into existence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did India respond in 1956 to the Suez Canal attack on Egypt and to the Soviet invasion of Hungary?
cards.back: In 1956 when Britain attacked Egypt over the Suez Canal issue, India led the world protest against this neo-colonial invasion. But in the same year when the USSR invaded Hungary, India did not join its public condemnation.
cards.quote: In 1956 when Britain attacked Egypt over the Suez Canal issue, India led the world protest against this neo-colonial invasion. But in the same year when the USSR invaded Hungary, India did not join its public condemnation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which neighbour joined the US-led military alliances while India promoted non-alignment?
cards.back: While India was trying to convince the other developing countries about the policy of non-alignment, Pakistan joined the US-led military alliances.
cards.quote: While India was trying to convince the other developing countries about the policy of non-alignment, Pakistan joined the US-led military alliances.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was India's general policy towards power politics, as Nehru wrote to K. P. S. Menon in January 1947?
cards.back: Our general policy is to avoid entanglement in power politics and not to join any group of powers as against any other group.
cards.quote: Our general policy is to avoid entanglement in power politics and not to join any group of powers as against any other group.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which conference did India convene in March 1947, five months before independence?
cards.back: Under his leadership, India convened the Asian Relations Conference in March 1947, five months ahead of attaining its independence.
cards.quote: Under his leadership, India convened the Asian Relations Conference in March 1947, five months ahead of attaining its independence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did India support Indonesia's freedom struggle against the Dutch in 1949?
cards.back: India made earnest efforts for the early realisation of freedom of Indonesia from the Dutch colonial regime by convening an international conference in 1949 to support its freedom struggle.
cards.quote: India made earnest efforts for the early realisation of freedom of Indonesia from the Dutch colonial regime by convening an international conference in 1949 to support its freedom struggle.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did India firmly oppose, especially in South Africa, while supporting decolonisation?
cards.back: India was a staunch supporter of the decolonisation process and firmly opposed racism, especially apartheid in South Africa.
cards.quote: India was a staunch supporter of the decolonisation process and firmly opposed racism, especially apartheid in South Africa.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which conference marked the zenith of India's engagement with newly independent Asian and African nations?
cards.back: The Afro-Asian conference held in the Indonesian city of Bandung in 1955, commonly known as the Bandung Conference, marked the zenith of India's engagement with the newly independent Asian and African nations.
cards.quote: The Afro-Asian conference held in the Indonesian city of Bandung in 1955, commonly known as the Bandung Conference, marked the zenith of India's engagement with the newly independent Asian and African nations.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Bandung Conference later lead to?
cards.back: The Bandung Conference later led to the establishment of the NAM.
cards.quote: The Bandung Conference later led to the establishment of the NAM.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The First Summit of the NAM was held in ____ in September 1961.
cards.back: The First Summit of the NAM was held in Belgrade in September 1961.
cards.quote: The First Summit of the NAM was held in Belgrade in September 1961.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which five leaders formed the core leadership of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM)?
cards.back: Nehru with Nkrumah from Ghana, Nasser from Egypt, Sukarno from Indonesia and Tito from Yugoslavia at a meeting of nonaligned nations, New York, October 1960. These five comprised the core leadership of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM).
cards.quote: Nehru with Nkrumah from Ghana, Nasser from Egypt, Sukarno from Indonesia and Tito from Yugoslavia at a meeting of nonaligned nations, New York, October 1960. These five comprised the core leadership of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did India do after the Chinese revolution of 1949?
cards.back: After the Chinese revolution in 1949, India was one of the first countries to recognise the communist government.
cards.quote: After the Chinese revolution in 1949, India was one of the first countries to recognise the communist government.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who signed Panchsheel, the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, and when?
cards.back: The joint enunciation of Panchsheel, the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, by the Indian Prime Minister Nehru and the Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai on 29 April 1954 was a step in the direction of stronger relationship between the two countries.
cards.quote: The joint enunciation of Panchsheel, the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, by the Indian Prime Minister Nehru and the Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai on 29 April 1954 was a step in the direction of stronger relationship between the two countries.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did India concede through a clause of the 1954 Panchsheel agreement?
cards.back: through one of its clauses about respecting each other's territorial integrity and sovereignty, India conceded China's claim over Tibet.
cards.quote: through one of its clauses about respecting each other's territorial integrity and sovereignty, India conceded China's claim over Tibet.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Dalai Lama do in 1959?
cards.back: in 1959, the Dalai Lama crossed over into the Indian border and sought asylum which was granted.
cards.quote: in 1959, the Dalai Lama crossed over into the Indian border and sought asylum which was granted.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which place in Himachal Pradesh is perhaps the largest settlement of Tibetan refugees in India?
cards.back: Dharmashala in Himachal Pradesh is perhaps the largest refuge settlement of Tibetans in India. The Dalai Lama has also made Dharmashala his home in India.
cards.quote: Dharmashala in Himachal Pradesh is perhaps the largest refuge settlement of Tibetans in India. The Dalai Lama has also made Dharmashala his home in India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: China annexed Tibet in ____ and thus removed a historical buffer between the two countries.
cards.back: China annexed Tibet in 1950 and thus removed a historical buffer between the two countries.
cards.quote: China annexed Tibet in 1950 and thus removed a historical buffer between the two countries.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which two areas within Indian territory did China claim in the boundary dispute?
cards.back: China claimed two areas within the Indian territory: Aksai-chin area in the Ladakh region of Jammu and Kashmir and much of the state of Arunachal Pradesh in what was then called NEFA (North Eastern Frontier Agency).
cards.quote: China claimed two areas within the Indian territory: Aksai-chin area in the Ladakh region of Jammu and Kashmir and much of the state of Arunachal Pradesh in what was then called NEFA (North Eastern Frontier Agency).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Chinese do in the Aksai-chin area between 1957 and 1959?
cards.back: Between 1957 and 1959, the Chinese occupied the Aksai-chin area and built a strategic road there.
cards.quote: Between 1957 and 1959, the Chinese occupied the Aksai-chin area and built a strategic road there.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did China launch a massive invasion of India, while the world watched the Cuban Missile crisis?
cards.back: Around this time, while the entire world's attention was on the Cuban Missile crisis involving the two superpowers, China launched a swift and massive invasion in October 1962 on both the disputed regions.
cards.quote: Around this time, while the entire world's attention was on the Cuban Missile crisis involving the two superpowers, China launched a swift and massive invasion in October 1962 on both the disputed regions.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did the 1962 war with China end?
cards.back: Finally, China declared a unilateral ceasefire and its troops withdrew to where they were before the invasion began.
cards.quote: Finally, China declared a unilateral ceasefire and its troops withdrew to where they were before the invasion began.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which countries did India approach for military help in 1962, and what was the Soviet Union's stand?
cards.back: India had to approach the Americans and the British for military assistance to tide over the crisis. The Soviet Union remained neutral during the conflict.
cards.quote: India had to approach the Americans and the British for military assistance to tide over the crisis. The Soviet Union remained neutral during the conflict.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What sense did the 1962 China war induce, and what did it strengthen?
cards.back: It induced a sense of national humiliation and at the same time strengthened a spirit of nationalism.
cards.quote: It induced a sense of national humiliation and at the same time strengthened a spirit of nationalism.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Defence Minister, a close associate of Nehru, had to leave the cabinet after the 1962 war?
cards.back: Nehru's close associate and the then Defence Minister, V. Krishna Menon, had to leave the cabinet.
cards.quote: Nehru's close associate and the then Defence Minister, V. Krishna Menon, had to leave the cabinet.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What happened in the Lok Sabha for the first time after the 1962 war against Nehru's government?
cards.back: For the first time, a no-confidence motion against his government was moved and debated in the Lok Sabha.
cards.quote: For the first time, a no-confidence motion against his government was moved and debated in the Lok Sabha.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When were full diplomatic relations between India and China restored?
cards.back: It was in 1976 that full diplomatic relations were restored between the two countries.
cards.quote: It was in 1976 that full diplomatic relations were restored between the two countries.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who was the first top level leader to visit China in 1979, and which Prime Minister was the first after Nehru to visit?
cards.back: Atal Behari Vajpayee was the first top level leader (he was then External Affairs Minister) to visit China in 1979. Later, Rajiv Gandhi became the first Prime Minister after Nehru to visit China.
cards.quote: Atal Behari Vajpayee was the first top level leader (he was then External Affairs Minister) to visit China in 1979. Later, Rajiv Gandhi became the first Prime Minister after Nehru to visit China.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: After the Sino-Indian conflict, the CPI split in 1964. What did the pro-China faction go on to form?
cards.back: The pro-USSR faction remained within the CPI and moved towards closer ties with the Congress. The other faction was for sometime closer to China and was against any ties with the Congress. The party split in 1964 and the leaders of the latter faction formed the Communist Party of India (Marxist) (CPI-M).
cards.quote: The pro-USSR faction remained within the CPI and moved towards closer ties with the Congress. The other faction was for sometime closer to China and was against any ties with the Congress. The party split in 1964 and the leaders of the latter faction formed the Communist Party of India (Marxist) (CPI-M).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How was the Northeast reorganised after the 1962 China war?
cards.back: The process of its reorganisation began soon after the China war. Nagaland was granted statehood; Manipur and Tripura, though Union Territories, were given the right to elect their own legislative assemblies.
cards.quote: The process of its reorganisation began soon after the China war. Nagaland was granted statehood; Manipur and Tripura, though Union Territories, were given the right to elect their own legislative assemblies.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What happened between India and Pakistan in Jammu and Kashmir in 1947, and where was the issue referred?
cards.back: A proxy war broke out between the Indian and Pakistani armies in Jammu and Kashmir during 1947 itself. But this did not turn into a full war. The issue was then referred to the UN.
cards.quote: A proxy war broke out between the Indian and Pakistani armies in Jammu and Kashmir during 1947 itself. But this did not turn into a full war. The issue was then referred to the UN.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The India-Pakistan ____ was signed by Nehru and General Ayub Khan in 1960.
cards.back: The India-Pakistan Indus Waters Treaty was signed by Nehru and General Ayub Khan in 1960.
cards.quote: The India-Pakistan Indus Waters Treaty was signed by Nehru and General Ayub Khan in 1960.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who mediated the long-term dispute between India and Pakistan about the sharing of river waters?
cards.back: A long-term dispute about the sharing of river waters was resolved through mediation by the World Bank.
cards.quote: A long-term dispute about the sharing of river waters was resolved through mediation by the World Bank.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Where did Pakistan launch armed attacks in April 1965, and what followed in August-September?
cards.back: In April 1965 Pakistan launched armed attacks in the Rann of Kutch area of Gujarat. This was followed by a bigger offensive in Jammu and Kashmir in August-September.
cards.quote: In April 1965 Pakistan launched armed attacks in the Rann of Kutch area of Gujarat. This was followed by a bigger offensive in Jammu and Kashmir in August-September.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did Shastri order in 1965 to ease the pressure on the Kashmir front?
cards.back: In order to ease the pressure on the Kashmir front, Shastri ordered Indian troops to launch a counter-offensive on the Punjab border.
cards.quote: In order to ease the pressure on the Kashmir front, Shastri ordered Indian troops to launch a counter-offensive on the Punjab border.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which agreement did Shastri and Ayub Khan sign in January 1966, and who brokered it?
cards.back: Later, Indian Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri and Pakistan's General Ayub Khan signed the Tashkent Agreement, brokered by the Soviet Union, in January 1966.
cards.quote: Later, Indian Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri and Pakistan's General Ayub Khan signed the Tashkent Agreement, brokered by the Soviet Union, in January 1966.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which parties won in West and East Pakistan in Pakistan's first general election in 1970?
cards.back: Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's party emerged a winner in West Pakistan, while the Awami League led by Sheikh Mujib-ur Rahman swept through East Pakistan.
cards.quote: Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's party emerged a winner in West Pakistan, while the Awami League led by Sheikh Mujib-ur Rahman swept through East Pakistan.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How many refugees from East Pakistan did India have to bear in 1971?
cards.back: Throughout 1971, India had to bear the burden of about 80 lakh refugees who fled East Pakistan and took shelter in the neighbouring areas in India.
cards.quote: Throughout 1971, India had to bear the burden of about 80 lakh refugees who fled East Pakistan and took shelter in the neighbouring areas in India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who made a secret visit to China via Pakistan in July 1971?
cards.back: Henry Kissinger, the adviser to the US President Richard Nixon, made a secret visit to China via Pakistan in July 1971.
cards.quote: Henry Kissinger, the adviser to the US President Richard Nixon, made a secret visit to China via Pakistan in July 1971.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which treaty did India sign with the Soviet Union in August 1971, and why?
cards.back: In order to counter the US-Pakistan-China axis, India signed a 20-year Treaty of Peace and Friendship with the Soviet Union in August 1971. This treaty assured India of Soviet support if the country faced any attack.
cards.quote: In order to counter the US-Pakistan-China axis, India signed a 20-year Treaty of Peace and Friendship with the Soviet Union in August 1971. This treaty assured India of Soviet support if the country faced any attack.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did the full-scale India-Pakistan war over Bangladesh break out?
cards.back: After months of diplomatic tension and military build-up, a full-scale war between India and Pakistan broke out in December 1971.
cards.quote: After months of diplomatic tension and military build-up, a full-scale war between India and Pakistan broke out in December 1971.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Within ten days the Indian army had surrounded ____ from three sides and the Pakistani army of about 90,000 had to surrender.
cards.back: Within ten days the Indian army had surrounded Dhaka from three sides and the Pakistani army of about 90,000 had to surrender.
cards.quote: Within ten days the Indian army had surrounded Dhaka from three sides and the Pakistani army of about 90,000 had to surrender.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Later, the signing of the ____ between Indira Gandhi and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto on 3 July 1972 formalised the return of peace.
cards.back: Later, the signing of the Shimla Agreement between Indira Gandhi and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto on 3 July 1972 formalised the return of peace.
cards.quote: Later, the signing of the Shimla Agreement between Indira Gandhi and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto on 3 July 1972 formalised the return of peace.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which areas on the Indian side of the LoC were occupied in early 1999, leading to the Kargil conflict?
cards.back: In the early part of 1999 several points on the Indian side of the LoC in the Mashkoh, Dras, Kaksar and Batalik areas were occupied by forces claiming to be Mujahideens.
cards.quote: In the early part of 1999 several points on the Indian side of the LoC in the Mashkoh, Dras, Kaksar and Batalik areas were occupied by forces claiming to be Mujahideens.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How long did the Kargil conflict last, and when had India recovered many of the lost points?
cards.back: This conflict went on during May and June 1999. By 26 July 1999, India had recovered control of many of the lost points.
cards.quote: This conflict went on during May and June 1999. By 26 July 1999, India had recovered control of many of the lost points.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who led the Pakistan Army that took over the government of Pakistan soon after the Kargil conflict?
cards.back: Soon after the conflict, the government of Pakistan was taken over by the Pakistan Army led by the Army Chief, General Parvez Musharraf.
cards.quote: Soon after the conflict, the government of Pakistan was taken over by the Pakistan Army led by the Army Chief, General Parvez Musharraf.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which five-year plan was affected by the wars, and when could the Fourth Plan be initiated?
cards.back: The Third Plan (1961-66) was affected and it was followed by three Annual Plans and the Fourth Plan could be initiated only in 1969.
cards.quote: The Third Plan (1961-66) was affected and it was followed by three Annual Plans and the Fourth Plan could be initiated only in 1969.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did India undertake its first nuclear explosion?
cards.back: Another crucial development of this period was the first nuclear explosion undertaken by India in May 1974.
cards.quote: Another crucial development of this period was the first nuclear explosion undertaken by India in May 1974.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Under whose guidance was the nuclear programme initiated in the late 1940s?
cards.back: A significant component of his industrialisation plans was the nuclear programme initiated in the late 1940s under the guidance of Homi J. Bhabha.
cards.quote: A significant component of his industrialisation plans was the nuclear programme initiated in the late 1940s under the guidance of Homi J. Bhabha.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was Nehru's stand on nuclear weapons?
cards.back: Nehru was against nuclear weapons. So he pleaded with the superpowers for comprehensive nuclear disarmament.
cards.quote: Nehru was against nuclear weapons. So he pleaded with the superpowers for comprehensive nuclear disarmament.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the five nuclear weapon powers that tried to impose the NPT of 1968.
cards.back:
US
USSR
UK
France
China
cards.quote: the US, USSR, UK, France, and China (Taiwan then represented China)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did India view the Nuclear Non-proliferation Treaty (NPT) of 1968?
cards.back: India always considered the NPT as discriminatory and had refused to sign it.
cards.quote: India always considered the NPT as discriminatory and had refused to sign it.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How was India's first nuclear test of 1974 described?
cards.back: When India conducted its first nuclear test, it was termed as peaceful explosion.
cards.quote: When India conducted its first nuclear test, it was termed as peaceful explosion.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What caused the Oil Shock of 1973 that affected the world?
cards.back: Following the Arab-Israel War of 1973, the entire world was affected by the Oil Shock due to the massive hike in the oil prices by the Arab nations.
cards.quote: Following the Arab-Israel War of 1973, the entire world was affected by the Oil Shock due to the massive hike in the oil prices by the Arab nations.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: On which three matters is there a broad agreement among Indian political parties?
cards.back:
national integration
protection of international boundaries
questions of national interest
cards.quote: Indian politics is generally marked by a broad agreement among the parties on national integration, protection of international boundaries, and on questions of national interest.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which treaties did India oppose or refuse to sign in the 1990s?
cards.back: India opposed the indefinite extension of the NPT in 1995 and also refused to sign the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT).
cards.quote: India opposed the indefinite extension of the NPT in 1995 and also refused to sign the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: India conducted a series of nuclear tests in ____, demonstrating its capacity to use nuclear energy for military purposes.
cards.back: India conducted a series of nuclear tests in May 1998, demonstrating its capacity to use nuclear energy for military purposes.
cards.quote: India conducted a series of nuclear tests in May 1998, demonstrating its capacity to use nuclear energy for military purposes.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What happened after the nuclear tests in India and Pakistan in 1998?
cards.back: The international community was extremely critical of the nuclear tests in the subcontinent and sanctions were imposed on both India and Pakistan, which were subsequently waived.
cards.quote: The international community was extremely critical of the nuclear tests in the subcontinent and sanctions were imposed on both India and Pakistan, which were subsequently waived.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is India's nuclear doctrine?
cards.back: India's nuclear doctrine of credible minimum nuclear deterrence professes "no first use" and reiterates India's commitment to global, verifiable and non-discriminatory nuclear disarmament leading to a nuclear weapons free world.
cards.quote: India's nuclear doctrine of credible minimum nuclear deterrence professes "no first use" and reiterates India's commitment to global, verifiable and non-discriminatory nuclear disarmament leading to a nuclear weapons free world.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Janata Party government of 1977 announce about non-alignment?
cards.back: The Janata Party government that came to power in 1977 announced that it would follow genuine non-alignment. This implied that the pro-Soviet tilt in the foreign policy will be corrected.
cards.quote: The Janata Party government that came to power in 1977 announced that it would follow genuine non-alignment. This implied that the pro-Soviet tilt in the foreign policy will be corrected.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why did India's foreign policy shift to a more pro-US strategy after 1990?
cards.back: In the period after 1990, Russia, though it continues to be an important friend of India, has lost its global preeminence. Therefore, India's foreign policy has shifted to a more pro-US strategy.
cards.quote: In the period after 1990, Russia, though it continues to be an important friend of India, has lost its global preeminence. Therefore, India's foreign policy has shifted to a more pro-US strategy.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which issue continues to be the main issue between India and Pakistan?
cards.back: While Kashmir continues to be the main issue between the two countries, there have been many efforts to restore normal relations.
cards.quote: While Kashmir continues to be the main issue between the two countries, there have been many efforts to restore normal relations.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who said: 'The United Nations was not created to take humanity to heaven, but to save it from hell.'
cards.back: "The United Nations was not created to take humanity to heaven, but to save it from hell." - Dag Hammarskjold, the UN's second Secretary-General.
cards.quote: "The United Nations was not created to take humanity to heaven, but to save it from hell." - Dag Hammarskjold, the UN's second Secretary-General.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: An international organisation is not a ____ with authority over its members.
cards.back: An international organisation is not a super-state with authority over its members.
cards.quote: An international organisation is not a super-state with authority over its members.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When does an international organisation come into being?
cards.back: It comes into being when states agree to its creation.
cards.quote: It comes into being when states agree to its creation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the International Monetary Fund (IMF)?
cards.back: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is an international organisation that oversees those financial institutions and regulations that act at the international level.
cards.quote: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is an international organisation that oversees those financial institutions and regulations that act at the international level.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which organisation was the UN founded as a successor to?
cards.back: The UN was founded as a successor to the League of Nations.
cards.quote: The UN was founded as a successor to the League of Nations.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which war could the League of Nations not prevent, despite its initial success?
cards.back: However, despite its initial success, it could not prevent the Second World War (1939-45).
cards.quote: However, despite its initial success, it could not prevent the Second World War (1939-45).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who signed the Atlantic Charter in August 1941?
cards.back: 1941 August: Signing of the Atlantic Charter by the US President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British PM Winston S. Churchill
cards.quote: 1941 August: Signing of the Atlantic Charter by the US President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British PM Winston S. Churchill

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What happened in January 1942 when 26 Allied nations met in Washington, D.C.?
cards.back: 1942 January: 26 Allied nations fighting against the Axis Powers meet in Washington, D.C., to support the Atlantic Charter and sign the "Declaration by United Nations"
cards.quote: 1942 January: 26 Allied nations fighting against the Axis Powers meet in Washington, D.C., to support the Atlantic Charter and sign the "Declaration by United Nations"

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Yalta Conference of February 1945 decide about the UN?
cards.back: 1945 February: Yalta Conference of the "Big Three" (Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin) decides to organise a United Nations conference on the proposed world organisation
cards.quote: 1945 February: Yalta Conference of the "Big Three" (Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin) decides to organise a United Nations conference on the proposed world organisation

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Where was the 2-month long United Nations Conference on International Organisation held in 1945?
cards.back: April-May: The 2-month long United Nations Conference on International Organisation at San Francisco
cards.quote: April-May: The 2-month long United Nations Conference on International Organisation at San Francisco

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: On what date in 1945 was the UN Charter signed, and by how many nations?
cards.back: 1945 June 26: Signing of the UN Charter by 50 nations
cards.quote: 1945 June 26: Signing of the UN Charter by 50 nations

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How many original founding members did the UN have, and why 51 rather than 50?
cards.back: Poland signed on October 15; so the UN has 51 original founding members
cards.quote: Poland signed on October 15; so the UN has 51 original founding members

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When was the UN founded, and which day is celebrated as UN Day?
cards.back: 1945 October 24: the UN was founded (hence October 24 is celebrated as UN Day)
cards.quote: 1945 October 24: the UN was founded (hence October 24 is celebrated as UN Day)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did India join the UN?
cards.back: 1945 October 30: India joins the UN
cards.quote: 1945 October 30: India joins the UN

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the objective of the UN?
cards.back: The UN's objective is to prevent international conflict and to facilitate cooperation among states.
cards.quote: The UN's objective is to prevent international conflict and to facilitate cooperation among states.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why was the UN intended to bring countries together for social and economic development?
cards.back: Furthermore, since conflicts often arose from the lack of social and economic development, the UN was intended to bring countries together to improve the prospects of social and economic development all over the world.
cards.quote: Furthermore, since conflicts often arose from the lack of social and economic development, the UN was intended to bring countries together to improve the prospects of social and economic development all over the world.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How many votes does each member have in the UN General Assembly?
cards.back: In the UN General Assembly, all members have one vote each.
cards.quote: In the UN General Assembly, all members have one vote each.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the five permanent members of the UN Security Council.
cards.back:
the United States
Russia
the United Kingdom
France
China
cards.quote: In the UN Security Council, there are five permanent members. These are: the United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, France and China.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why were the five permanent members of the Security Council selected?
cards.back: These states were selected as permanent members as they were the most powerful immediately after the Second World War and because they constituted the victors in the War.
cards.quote: These states were selected as permanent members as they were the most powerful immediately after the Second World War and because they constituted the victors in the War.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who is the UN's most visible public figure and representative head?
cards.back: The UN's most visible public figure, and the representative head, is the Secretary-General.
cards.quote: The UN's most visible public figure, and the representative head, is the Secretary-General.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which two UN bodies discuss war and peace and differences between member states?
cards.back: War and peace and differences between member states are discussed in the General Assembly as well as the Security Council.
cards.quote: War and peace and differences between member states are discussed in the General Assembly as well as the Security Council.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What are the two basic kinds of reform facing the UN?
cards.back:
Reform of the organisation's structures and processes
A review of the issues that fall within the jurisdiction of the organisation
cards.quote: Two basic kinds of reforms face the UN: reform of the organisation's structures and processes; and a review of the issues that fall within the jurisdiction of the organisation.

source.section: Reform of the UN after the Cold War

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: On the reform of UN structures and processes, what has been the biggest discussion?
cards.back: On the reform of structures and processes, the biggest discussion has been on the functioning of the Security Council.
cards.quote: On the reform of structures and processes, the biggest discussion has been on the functioning of the Security Council.

source.section: Reform of the UN after the Cold War

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: From which continents are there proposals to increase UN Security Council membership?
cards.back: In particular, there are proposals to increase membership from Asia, Africa and South America.
cards.quote: In particular, there are proposals to increase membership from Asia, Africa and South America.

source.section: Reform of the UN after the Cold War

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What reforms do the US and other Western countries want in the UN?
cards.back: Beyond this, the US and other Western countries want improvements in the UN's budgetary procedures and its administration.
cards.quote: Beyond this, the US and other Western countries want improvements in the UN's budgetary procedures and its administration.

source.section: Reform of the UN after the Cold War

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What are the two views on which issues the UN should give priority to?
cards.back: some countries and experts want the organisation to play a greater or more effective role in peace and security missions, while others want its role to be confined to development and humanitarian work
cards.quote: some countries and experts want the organisation to play a greater or more effective role in peace and security missions, while others want its role to be confined to development and humanitarian work

source.section: Reform of the UN after the Cold War

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the three main complaints in the 1992 UN General Assembly resolution on the Security Council.
cards.back:
The Security Council no longer represents contemporary political realities.
Its decisions reflect only Western values and interests and are dominated by a few powers.
It lacks equitable representation.
cards.quote: The resolution reflected three main complaints: The Security Council no longer represents contemporary political realities. Its decisions reflect only Western values and interests and are dominated by a few powers. It lacks equitable representation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who, on 1 January 1997, initiated an inquiry into how the UN should be reformed?
cards.back: on 1 January 1997, the UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan initiated an inquiry
cards.quote: on 1 January 1997, the UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan initiated an inquiry

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the six criteria proposed for new permanent and non-permanent members of the Security Council.
cards.back:
A major economic power
A major military power
A substantial contributor to the UN budget
A big nation in terms of its population
A nation that respects democracy and human rights
A country that would make the Council more representative of the world's diversity in terms of geography, economic systems, and culture
cards.quote: A major economic power A major military power A substantial contributor to the UN budget A big nation in terms of its population A nation that respects democracy and human rights A country that would make the Council more representative of the world's diversity in terms of geography, economic systems, and culture

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The World Bank was created during the Second World War in ____.
cards.back: The World Bank was created during the Second World War in 1944.
cards.quote: The World Bank was created during the Second World War in 1944.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which countries are the activities of the World Bank focused on?
cards.back: Its activities are focused on the developing countries.
cards.quote: Its activities are focused on the developing countries.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the five areas the World Bank works on.
cards.back:
human development (education, health)
agriculture and rural development (irrigation, rural services)
environmental protection (pollution reduction, establishing and enforcing regulations)
infrastructure (roads, urban regeneration, electricity)
governance (anti-corruption, development of legal institutions)
cards.quote: human development (education, health), agriculture and rural development (irrigation, rural services), environmental protection (pollution reduction, establishing and enforcing regulations), infrastructure (roads, urban regeneration, electricity) and governance (anti-corruption, development of legal institutions)

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the World Bank often criticised for?
cards.back: It is often criticised for setting the economic agenda of the poorer nations, attaching stringent conditions to its loans and forcing free market reforms.
cards.quote: It is often criticised for setting the economic agenda of the poorer nations, attaching stringent conditions to its loans and forcing free market reforms.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In the Security Council, there are ____ permanent members and ____ non-permanent members.
cards.back: In the Security Council, there are five permanent members and ten non-permanent members.
cards.quote: In the Security Council, there are five permanent members and ten non-permanent members.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The main privileges of the five permanent members are permanency and the ____ power.
cards.back: The main privileges of the five permanent members are permanency and the veto power.
cards.quote: The main privileges of the five permanent members are permanency and the veto power.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: For how long do non-permanent members of the Security Council serve at a time?
cards.back: The non-permanent members serve for only two years at a time and give way after that period to newly elected members.
cards.quote: The non-permanent members serve for only two years at a time and give way after that period to newly elected members.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Can a country be re-elected immediately after completing a term of two years as a non-permanent member?
cards.back: A country cannot be re-elected immediately after completing a term of two years.
cards.quote: A country cannot be re-elected immediately after completing a term of two years.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why did many want the veto power of the permanent members abolished?
cards.back: Many perceived the veto to be in conflict with the concept of democracy and sovereign equality in the UN and thought that the veto was no longer right or relevant.
cards.quote: Many perceived the veto to be in conflict with the concept of democracy and sovereign equality in the UN and thought that the veto was no longer right or relevant.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the veto power in the UN Security Council?
cards.back: However, the permanent members can vote in a negative manner so that even if all other permanent and non-permanent members vote for a particular decision, any permanent member's negative vote can stall the decision. This negative vote is the veto.
cards.quote: However, the permanent members can vote in a negative manner so that even if all other permanent and non-permanent members vote for a particular decision, any permanent member's negative vote can stall the decision. This negative vote is the veto.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Do the non-permanent members of the Security Council have the veto power?
cards.back: Most importantly, the nonpermanent members do not have the veto power.
cards.quote: Most importantly, the nonpermanent members do not have the veto power.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What danger is there if the veto is removed?
cards.back: Without the veto, there is the danger as in 1945 that the great powers would lose interest in the world body, that they would do what they pleased outside it, and that without their support and involvement the body would be ineffective.
cards.quote: Without the veto, there is the danger as in 1945 that the great powers would lose interest in the world body, that they would do what they pleased outside it, and that without their support and involvement the body would be ineffective.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did the heads of all UN member-states meet to celebrate 60 years of the UN and review the situation?
cards.back: the heads of all the member-states met in September 2005 to celebrate the anniversary and review the situation
cards.quote: the heads of all the member-states met in September 2005 to celebrate the anniversary and review the situation

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the seven steps decided at the 2005 UN summit to make the UN more relevant.
cards.back:
Creation of a Peacebuilding Commission
Acceptance of the responsibility of the international community in case of failures of national governments to protect their own citizens from atrocities
Establishment of a Human Rights Council (operational since 19 June 2006)
Agreements to achieve the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs)
Condemnation of terrorism in all its forms and manifestations
Creation of a Democracy Fund
An agreement to wind up the Trusteeship Council
cards.quote: Creation of a Peacebuilding Commission Acceptance of the responsibility of the international community in case of failures of national governments to protect their own citizens from atrocities Establishment of a Human Rights Council (operational since 19 June 2006) Agreements to achieve the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) Condemnation of terrorism in all its forms and manifestations Creation of a Democracy Fund An agreement to wind up the Trusteeship Council

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which fund was created in 2005 to promote democracy through the UN?
cards.back: Creation of a Democracy Fund
cards.quote: Creation of a Democracy Fund

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which UN council was agreed in 2005 to be wound up?
cards.back: An agreement to wind up the Trusteeship Council
cards.quote: An agreement to wind up the Trusteeship Council

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What does India believe should be central to the UN's agenda?
cards.back: India believes that development should be central to the UN's agenda as it is a vital precondition for the maintenance of international peace and security.
cards.quote: India believes that development should be central to the UN's agenda as it is a vital precondition for the maintenance of international peace and security.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is one of India's major concerns about the Security Council?
cards.back: One of India's major concerns has been the composition of the Security Council, which has remained largely static while the UN General Assembly membership has expanded considerably.
cards.quote: One of India's major concerns has been the composition of the Security Council, which has remained largely static while the UN General Assembly membership has expanded considerably.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When was the Security Council expanded from 11 to 15 members?
cards.back: the membership of the UN Security Council was expanded from 11 to 15 in 1965.
cards.quote: the membership of the UN Security Council was expanded from 11 to 15 in 1965.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What change in membership does India support in the Security Council?
cards.back: India supports an increase in the number of both permanent and non-permanent members.
cards.quote: India supports an increase in the number of both permanent and non-permanent members.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: On what grounds of population and democracy does India seek a permanent Security Council seat?
cards.back: India is the most populous country in the world comprising almost one-fifth of the world population. Moreover, India is also the world's largest democracy.
cards.quote: India is the most populous country in the world comprising almost one-fifth of the world population. Moreover, India is also the world's largest democracy.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is India's record on financial contributions to the UN?
cards.back: India has also made regular financial contributions to the UN and never faltered on its payments.
cards.quote: India has also made regular financial contributions to the UN and never faltered on its payments.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What does permanent membership of the Security Council signify symbolically?
cards.back: India is aware that permanent membership of the Security Council also has symbolic importance. It signifies a country's growing importance in world affairs.
cards.quote: India is aware that permanent membership of the Security Council also has symbolic importance. It signifies a country's growing importance in world affairs.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Indian capability makes some countries reluctant to see India as a permanent Security Council member?
cards.back: Some countries, for instance, are concerned about India's nuclear weapons capabilities.
cards.quote: Some countries, for instance, are concerned about India's nuclear weapons capabilities.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which two continents are the only ones without representation in the permanent membership of the Security Council?
cards.back: There are those who feel that Africa and South America must be represented in any expansion of the permanent membership since those are the only continents not to have representation in the present structure.
cards.quote: There are those who feel that Africa and South America must be represented in any expansion of the permanent membership since those are the only continents not to have representation in the present structure.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the World Trade Organisation (WTO)?
cards.back: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) is an international organisation which sets the rules for global trade.
