cards.quote: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) is an international organisation which sets the rules for global trade.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When was the WTO set up and which organisation did it succeed?
cards.back: This organisation was set up in 1995 as the successor to the General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs (GATT) created after the Second World War.
cards.quote: This organisation was set up in 1995 as the successor to the General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs (GATT) created after the Second World War.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How are decisions taken in the WTO?
cards.back: All decisions are taken unanimously
cards.quote: All decisions are taken unanimously

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which major economic powers have used the WTO to frame trade rules to advance their own interests?
cards.back: the major economic powers such as the US, EU and Japan have managed to use the WTO to frame rules of trade to advance their own interests
cards.quote: the major economic powers such as the US, EU and Japan have managed to use the WTO to frame rules of trade to advance their own interests

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) was established in ____.
cards.back: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) was established in 1957.
cards.quote: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) was established in 1957.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Whose proposal did the IAEA come into being to implement?
cards.back: It came into being to implement US President Dwight Eisenhower's "Atoms for Peace" proposal.
cards.quote: It came into being to implement US President Dwight Eisenhower's "Atoms for Peace" proposal.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What does the IAEA seek to promote and prevent?
cards.back: It seeks to promote the peaceful use of nuclear energy and to prevent its use for military purposes.
cards.quote: It seeks to promote the peaceful use of nuclear energy and to prevent its use for military purposes.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What do IAEA teams regularly inspect nuclear facilities for?
cards.back: IAEA teams regularly inspect nuclear facilities all over the world to ensure that civilian reactors are not being used for military purposes.
cards.quote: IAEA teams regularly inspect nuclear facilities all over the world to ensure that civilian reactors are not being used for military purposes.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why can US power not be easily checked by the UN?
cards.back: US power cannot be easily checked. First of all, with the disappearance of the Soviet Union, the US stands as the only superpower.
cards.quote: US power cannot be easily checked. First of all, with the disappearance of the Soviet Union, the US stands as the only superpower.

source.section: The UN in a Unipolar World

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which financial position gives the US unmatched power within the UN?
cards.back: As the single largest contributor to the UN, the US has unmatched financial power.
cards.quote: As the single largest contributor to the UN, the US has unmatched financial power.

source.section: The UN in a Unipolar World

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How does the physical location of the UN give the US additional influence?
cards.back: The fact that the UN is physically located within the US territory gives Washington additional sources of influence.
cards.quote: The fact that the UN is physically located within the US territory gives Washington additional sources of influence.

source.section: The UN in a Unipolar World

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What does the UN provide the rest of the world in dealing with US attitudes and policies?
cards.back: As for the rest of the world, the UN provides an arena in which it is possible to modify US attitudes and policies.
cards.quote: As for the rest of the world, the UN provides an arena in which it is possible to modify US attitudes and policies.

source.section: The UN in a Unipolar World

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What does NCERT conclude about the UN as an imperfect body?
cards.back: The UN is an imperfect body, but without it the world would be worse off.
cards.quote: The UN is an imperfect body, but without it the world would be worse off.

source.section: The UN in a Unipolar World

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is Amnesty International?
cards.back: Amnesty International is an NGO that campaigns for the protection of human rights all over the world.
cards.quote: Amnesty International is an NGO that campaigns for the protection of human rights all over the world.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which declaration does Amnesty International promote respect for?
cards.back: It promotes respect for all the human rights in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
cards.quote: It promotes respect for all the human rights in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is Human Rights Watch?
cards.back: Human Rights Watch is another international NGO involved in research and advocacy on human rights.
cards.quote: Human Rights Watch is another international NGO involved in research and advocacy on human rights.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the three campaigns or coalitions that Human Rights Watch helped build.
cards.back:
the campaigns to ban landmines
to stop the use of child soldiers
to establish the International Criminal Court
cards.quote: It helped in building international coalitions like the campaigns to ban landmines, to stop the use of child soldiers and to establish the International Criminal Court.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Secretary-General (1946-1952) from Norway worked for a ceasefire between India and Pakistan on Kashmir?
cards.back: Trygve Lie (1946-1952) Norway; lawyer and foreign minister; worked for ceasefire between India and Pakistan on Kashmir
cards.quote: Trygve Lie (1946-1952) Norway; lawyer and foreign minister; worked for ceasefire between India and Pakistan on Kashmir

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Secretary-General was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize posthumously in 1961?
cards.back: Dag Hammarskjöld (1953-1961) Sweden; Economist and lawyer; worked for resolving the Suez Canal dispute and the decolonisation of Africa; awarded Nobel Peace Prize posthumously in 1961 for his efforts to settle the Congo crisis
cards.quote: Dag Hammarskjöld (1953-1961) Sweden; Economist and lawyer; worked for resolving the Suez Canal dispute and the decolonisation of Africa; awarded Nobel Peace Prize posthumously in 1961 for his efforts to settle the Congo crisis

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Secretary-General (1961-1971) worked to resolve the Cuban Missile Crisis and established the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus?
cards.back: U Thant (1961-1971) Burma (Myanmar); teacher and diplomat; worked for resolving the Cuban Missile Crisis and ending the Congo crisis; established the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus
cards.quote: U Thant (1961-1971) Burma (Myanmar); teacher and diplomat; worked for resolving the Cuban Missile Crisis and ending the Congo crisis; established the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Secretary-General (1972-1981) oversaw the relief operation in Bangladesh?
cards.back: Kurt Waldheim (1972-1981) Austria; diplomat and foreign minister; made efforts to resolve the problems of Namibia and Lebanon; oversaw the relief operation in Bangladesh
cards.quote: Kurt Waldheim (1972-1981) Austria; diplomat and foreign minister; made efforts to resolve the problems of Namibia and Lebanon; oversaw the relief operation in Bangladesh

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Secretary-General (1982-1991) mediated between Britain and Argentina after the Falklands War?
cards.back: Javier Perez de Cuellar (1982-1991) Peru; lawyer and diplomat; worked for peace in Cyprus, Afghanistan and El Salvador; mediated between Britain and Argentina after the Falklands War
cards.quote: Javier Perez de Cuellar (1982-1991) Peru; lawyer and diplomat; worked for peace in Cyprus, Afghanistan and El Salvador; mediated between Britain and Argentina after the Falklands War

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Secretary-General (1992-1996) issued the report An Agenda for Peace?
cards.back: Boutros Boutros-Ghali (1992-1996) Egypt; diplomat, jurist, foreign minister; issued a report, An Agenda for Peace
cards.quote: Boutros Boutros-Ghali (1992-1996) Egypt; diplomat, jurist, foreign minister; issued a report, An Agenda for Peace

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Secretary-General (1997-2006, Ghana) declared the US-led invasion of Iraq an illegal act?
cards.back: Kofi A. Annan (1997-2006) Ghana; UN official; created the Global Fund to fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria; declared the US-led invasion of Iraq as an illegal act
cards.quote: Kofi A. Annan (1997-2006) Ghana; UN official; created the Global Fund to fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria; declared the US-led invasion of Iraq as an illegal act

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Secretary-General established the Peacebuilding Commission and the Human Rights Council in 2005 and won the 2001 Nobel Peace Prize?
cards.back: Kofi A. Annan (1997-2006) Ghana; UN official; created the Global Fund to fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria; declared the US-led invasion of Iraq as an illegal act; established the Peacebuilding Commission and the Human Rights Council in 2005; awarded the 2001 Nobel Peace Prize.
cards.quote: Kofi A. Annan (1997-2006) Ghana; UN official; created the Global Fund to fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria; declared the US-led invasion of Iraq as an illegal act; established the Peacebuilding Commission and the Human Rights Council in 2005; awarded the 2001 Nobel Peace Prize.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Secretary-General (2007-2016), the second Asian to hold the post, highlighted climate change?
cards.back: Ban Ki-moon (2007-2016) Republic of Korea (South Korea); diplomat and foreign minister; the second Asian to hold the post; highlighted climate change
cards.quote: Ban Ki-moon (2007-2016) Republic of Korea (South Korea); diplomat and foreign minister; the second Asian to hold the post; highlighted climate change

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is meant by the Left in politics?
cards.back: Left often refers to those who are in favour of state control of the economy and prefers state regulation over free competition.
cards.quote: Left often refers to those who are in favour of state control of the economy and prefers state regulation over free competition.

source.section: What is Left and what is Right?

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is meant by the Right in politics?
cards.back: The Right refers to those who believe that free competition and market economy alone ensure progress and that the government should not unnecessarily intervene in the economy.
cards.quote: The Right refers to those who believe that free competition and market economy alone ensure progress and that the government should not unnecessarily intervene in the economy.

source.section: What is Left and what is Right?

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Types of models of modern development India had before it on the eve of Independence.
cards.back:
the liberal-capitalist model as in much of Europe and the US
the socialist model as in the USSR
cards.quote: On the eve of Independence, India had before it, two models of modern development: the liberal-capitalist model as in much of Europe and the US and the socialist model as in the USSR.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Besides Nehru within the Congress, whose leaders were impressed by the Soviet model of development?
cards.back: These included not just the leaders of the Communist Party of India, but also those of the Socialist Party and leaders like Nehru within the Congress.
cards.quote: These included not just the leaders of the Communist Party of India, but also those of the Socialist Party and leaders like Nehru within the Congress.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: According to NCERT, what did modernisation as in the West involve?
cards.back: the process of modernisation as in the West, which involved the breakdown of traditional social structures and the rise of capitalism and liberalism
cards.quote: It was believed that every country would go through the process of modernisation as in the West, which involved the breakdown of traditional social structures and the rise of capitalism and liberalism.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: On which one point was there a consensus in India about development, despite the differences?
cards.back: Despite the various differences, there was a consensus on one point: that development could not be left to private actors, that there was the need for the government to develop a design or plan for development.
cards.quote: Despite the various differences, there was a consensus on one point: that development could not be left to private actors, that there was the need for the government to develop a design or plan for development.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The Planning Commission was set up in ____ by a simple resolution of the Government of India.
cards.back: The Planning Commission was set up in March, 1950 by a simple resolution of the Government of India.
cards.quote: The Planning Commission was set up in March, 1950 by a simple resolution of the Government of India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Is the Planning Commission a body set up by the Constitution?
cards.back: the Planning Commission is not one of the many commissions and other bodies set up by the Constitution
cards.quote: the Planning Commission is not one of the many commissions and other bodies set up by the Constitution

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the role of the Planning Commission, and when did its recommendations become effective?
cards.back: It has an advisory role and its recommendations become effective only when the Union Cabinet approved these.
cards.quote: It has an advisory role and its recommendations become effective only when the Union Cabinet approved these.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who was the Chairperson of the Planning Commission?
cards.back: The Prime Minister was its Chairperson.
cards.quote: The Prime Minister was its Chairperson.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What role did the Planning Commission come to play in India?
cards.back: It became the most influential and central machinery for deciding what path and strategy India would adopt for its development.
cards.quote: It became the most influential and central machinery for deciding what path and strategy India would adopt for its development.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What replaced the Planning Commission, and when did it come into existence?
cards.back: The Government of India replaced the Planning Commission with a new institution named NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India). This came into existence on 1 January 2015.
cards.quote: The Government of India replaced the Planning Commission with a new institution named NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India). This came into existence on 1 January 2015.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the Bombay Plan?
cards.back: a section of the big industrialists got together in 1944 and drafted a joint proposal for setting up a planned economy in the country. It was called the Bombay Plan.
cards.quote: a section of the big industrialists got together in 1944 and drafted a joint proposal for setting up a planned economy in the country. It was called the Bombay Plan.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Bombay Plan want the state to do?
cards.back: The Bombay Plan wanted the state to take major initiatives in industrial and other economic investments.
cards.quote: The Bombay Plan wanted the state to take major initiatives in industrial and other economic investments.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the experiences that contributed to the worldwide consensus on planning in the 1940s and 1950s.
cards.back:
Great Depression in Europe
inter-war reconstruction of Japan and Germany
spectacular economic growth against heavy odds in the Soviet Union in the 1930s and 1940s
cards.quote: The experience of Great Depression in Europe, the inter-war reconstruction of Japan and Germany, and most of all the spectacular economic growth against heavy odds in the Soviet Union in the 1930s and 1940s contributed to this consensus.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: As in the ____, the Planning Commission of India opted for five year plans (FYP).
cards.back: As in the USSR, the Planning Commission of India opted for five year plans (FYP).
cards.quote: As in the USSR, the Planning Commission of India opted for five year plans (FYP).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is a five year plan?
cards.back: the Government of India prepares a document that has a plan for all its income and expenditure for the next five years.
cards.quote: the Government of India prepares a document that has a plan for all its income and expenditure for the next five years.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which budget is spent on routine items on a yearly basis?
cards.back: ‘non-plan’ budget that is spent on routine items on a yearly basis
cards.quote: ‘non-plan’ budget that is spent on routine items on a yearly basis

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What advantage does a five year plan give the government?
cards.back: A five year plan has the advantage of permitting the government to focus on the larger picture and make long-term intervention in the economy.
cards.quote: A five year plan has the advantage of permitting the government to focus on the larger picture and make long-term intervention in the economy.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In which month and year was the actual First Five Year Plan Document released?
cards.back: The draft of the First Five Year Plan and then the actual Plan Document, released in December 1951, generated a lot of excitement in the country.
cards.quote: The draft of the First Five Year Plan and then the actual Plan Document, released in December 1951, generated a lot of excitement in the country.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did the excitement with planning peak, and until which plan did it continue somewhat?
cards.back: The excitement with planning reached its peak with the launching of the Second Five Year Plan in 1956 and continued somewhat till the Third Five Year Plan in 1961.
cards.quote: The excitement with planning reached its peak with the launching of the Second Five Year Plan in 1956 and continued somewhat till the Third Five Year Plan in 1961.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the government decide when the Fourth Plan was due to start in 1966?
cards.back: The Fourth Plan was due to start in 1966. By this time, the novelty of planning had declined considerably, and moreover, India was facing acute economic crisis. The government decided to take a ‘plan holiday’.
cards.quote: The Fourth Plan was due to start in 1966. By this time, the novelty of planning had declined considerably, and moreover, India was facing acute economic crisis. The government decided to take a ‘plan holiday’.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which period did the First Five Year Plan cover, and what did it seek to do?
cards.back: The First Five Year Plan (1951–1956) sought to get the country’s economy out of the cycle of poverty.
cards.quote: The First Five Year Plan (1951–1956) sought to get the country’s economy out of the cycle of poverty.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which sector did the First Five Year Plan mainly address?
cards.back: The First Five Year Plan addressed, mainly, the agrarian sector including investment in dams and irrigation.
cards.quote: The First Five Year Plan addressed, mainly, the agrarian sector including investment in dams and irrigation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which large-scale dam project received huge allocations in the First Five Year Plan?
cards.back: Huge allocations were made for large-scale projects like the Bhakhra Nangal Dam.
cards.quote: Huge allocations were made for large-scale projects like the Bhakhra Nangal Dam.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the First Plan identify as the principal obstacle to agricultural growth?
cards.back: The Plan identified the pattern of land distribution in the country as the principal obstacle in the way of agricultural growth. It focused on land reforms as the key to the country's development.
cards.quote: The Plan identified the pattern of land distribution in the country as the principal obstacle in the way of agricultural growth. It focused on land reforms as the key to the country's development.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Second Five Year Plan stress, and who led the team that drafted it?
cards.back: The Second FYP stressed on heavy industries. It was drafted by a team of economists and planners under the leadership of P. C. Mahalanobis.
cards.quote: The Second FYP stressed on heavy industries. It was drafted by a team of economists and planners under the leadership of P. C. Mahalanobis.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who founded the Indian Statistical Institute (1931) and was the architect of the Second Plan?
cards.back: P.C. Mahalanobis (1893-1972): Scientist and statistician of international repute; founder of Indian Statistical Institute (1931); architect of the Second Plan
cards.quote: P.C. Mahalanobis (1893-1972): Scientist and statistician of international repute; founder of Indian Statistical Institute (1931); architect of the Second Plan

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Congress session declared a socialist pattern of society as its goal, and where was it held?
cards.back: the Congress party at its session held at Avadi near the then Madras city, passed an important resolution. It declared that ‘socialist pattern of society’ was its goal.
cards.quote: the Congress party at its session held at Avadi near the then Madras city, passed an important resolution. It declared that ‘socialist pattern of society’ was its goal.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the government impose to protect domestic industries during the Second Plan?
cards.back: The government imposed substantial tariffs on imports in order to protect domestic industries.
cards.quote: The government imposed substantial tariffs on imports in order to protect domestic industries.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which industries developed in the public sector during the Second Plan period?
cards.back: electricity, railways, steel, machineries and communication
cards.quote: As savings and investment were growing in this period, a bulk of these industries like electricity, railways, steel, machineries and communication could be developed in the public sector.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why did India have to spend precious foreign exchange during the Second Plan?
cards.back: India was technologically backward, so it had to spend precious foreign exchange to buy technology from the global market.
cards.quote: India was technologically backward, so it had to spend precious foreign exchange to buy technology from the global market.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What difficulty did Indian planners face in balancing industry and agriculture?
cards.back: as industry attracted more investment than agriculture, the possibility of food shortage loomed large. The Indian planners found balancing industry and agriculture really difficult.
cards.quote: as industry attracted more investment than agriculture, the possibility of food shortage loomed large. The Indian planners found balancing industry and agriculture really difficult.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What unmistakable bias did critics point out in the Third Plan's strategies?
cards.back: The Third Plan was not significantly different from the Second. Critics pointed out that the plan strategies from this time around displayed an unmistakable “urban bias”.
cards.quote: The Third Plan was not significantly different from the Second. Critics pointed out that the plan strategies from this time around displayed an unmistakable “urban bias”.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What happened to the proportion of savings from the early 1960s till the early 1970s?
cards.back: Later, from the early 1960s till the early 1970s, the proportion of savings in the country actually dropped consistently.
cards.quote: Later, from the early 1960s till the early 1970s, the proportion of savings in the country actually dropped consistently.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What decision of the National Front government in 1990 raised the 'Mandal issue'?
cards.back: This followed the decision by the new National Front government in 1990, to implement the recommendation of the Mandal Commission that jobs in central government should be reserved for the Other Backward Classes.
cards.quote: This followed the decision by the new National Front government in 1990, to implement the recommendation of the Mandal Commission that jobs in central government should be reserved for the Other Backward Classes.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the 'Mandal issue'?
cards.back: This dispute between the supporters and opponents of OBC reservations was known as the 'Mandal issue' and was to play an important role in shaping politics since 1989.
cards.quote: This dispute between the supporters and opponents of OBC reservations was known as the 'Mandal issue' and was to play an important role in shaping politics since 1989.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the structural adjustment programme (new economic reforms) of the 1990s?
cards.back: Third, the economic policy followed by the various governments took a radically different turn. This is known as the initiation of the structural adjustment programme or the new economic reforms.
cards.quote: Third, the economic policy followed by the various governments took a radically different turn. This is known as the initiation of the structural adjustment programme or the new economic reforms.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who started the new economic reforms, and when did they first become very visible?
cards.back: Started by Rajiv Gandhi, these changes first became very visible in 1991 and radically changed the direction that the Indian economy had pursued since Independence.
cards.quote: Started by Rajiv Gandhi, these changes first became very visible in 1991 and radically changed the direction that the Indian economy had pursued since Independence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who were the Finance Minister and Prime Minister in the initial phase of the New Economic Policy?
cards.back: Manmohan Singh, the then Finance Minister, with Prime Minister Narsimha Rao, in the initial phase of the 'New Economic Policy'.
cards.quote: Manmohan Singh, the then Finance Minister, with Prime Minister Narsimha Rao, in the initial phase of the 'New Economic Policy'.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Supreme Court decision led to the construction of the Ram Temple at Ayodhya?
cards.back: These changes culminated in the construction of the Ram Temple at Ayodhya following the decision of the constitutional bench of the Supreme Court (which was announced on November 9, 2019).
cards.quote: These changes culminated in the construction of the Ram Temple at Ayodhya following the decision of the constitutional bench of the Supreme Court (which was announced on November 9, 2019).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Ram Janmabhoomi Temple Movement transform in Indian politics?
cards.back: The Ram Janmabhoomi Temple Movement, becoming the central issue, transformed the direction of the discourse on secularism and democracy.
cards.quote: The Ram Janmabhoomi Temple Movement, becoming the central issue, transformed the direction of the discourse on secularism and democracy.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who are the Other Backward Classes (OBCs)?
cards.back: These are communities other than SC and ST who suffer from educational and social backwardness. These are also referred to as 'backward castes'.
cards.quote: These are communities other than SC and ST who suffer from educational and social backwardness. These are also referred to as 'backward castes'.

source.section: Political Rise of Other Backward Classes

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In what form did the rise of non-Congress parties with OBC support first find national expression?
cards.back: the rise of these parties first found political expression at the national level in the form of the Janata Party government in 1977.
cards.quote: the rise of these parties first found political expression at the national level in the form of the Janata Party government in 1977.

source.section: Political Rise of Other Backward Classes

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name two constituents of the Janata Party with a powerful rural base among the OBC.
cards.back: Many of the constituents of the Janata Party, like the Bharatiya Kranti Dal and the Samyukta Socialist Party, had a powerful rural base among some sections of the OBC.
cards.quote: Many of the constituents of the Janata Party, like the Bharatiya Kranti Dal and the Samyukta Socialist Party, had a powerful rural base among some sections of the OBC.

source.section: Political Rise of Other Backward Classes

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the OBC-based parties of this period seek?
cards.back: This period saw the emergence of many parties that sought better opportunities for OBCs in education and employment and also raised the question of the share of power enjoyed by the OBCs.
cards.quote: This period saw the emergence of many parties that sought better opportunities for OBCs in education and employment and also raised the question of the share of power enjoyed by the OBCs.

source.section: Political Rise of Other Backward Classes

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Since when did reservations for the OBC exist in southern States?
cards.back: Reservations for the OBC were in existence in southern States since the 1960s, if not earlier.
cards.quote: Reservations for the OBC were in existence in southern States since the 1960s, if not earlier.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Chief Minister of Bihar pioneered reservations for OBCs in north India?
cards.back: Karpoori Thakur, the then Chief Minister of Bihar, was a pioneer in this direction.
cards.quote: Karpoori Thakur, the then Chief Minister of Bihar, was a pioneer in this direction.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did the central government appoint the commission on backward classes?
cards.back: Following this, the central government appointed a Commission in 1978 to look into and recommend ways to improve the conditions of the backward classes.
cards.quote: Following this, the central government appointed a Commission in 1978 to look into and recommend ways to improve the conditions of the backward classes.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the official name of the Mandal Commission, and who chaired it?
cards.back: Therefore, this commission was officially known as the Second Backward Classes Commission. Popularly, the commission is known as the Mandal Commission, after the name of its Chairperson, Bindeshwari Prasad Mandal.
cards.quote: Therefore, this commission was officially known as the Second Backward Classes Commission. Popularly, the commission is known as the Mandal Commission, after the name of its Chairperson, Bindeshwari Prasad Mandal.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: For what purpose was the Mandal Commission set up?
cards.back: The Mandal Commission was set up to investigate the extent of educational and social backwardness among various sections of Indian society and recommend ways of identifying these 'backward classes'.
cards.quote: The Mandal Commission was set up to investigate the extent of educational and social backwardness among various sections of Indian society and recommend ways of identifying these 'backward classes'.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In which year did the Mandal Commission give its recommendations?
cards.back: The Commission gave its recommendations in 1980.
cards.quote: The Commission gave its recommendations in 1980.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What share of seats and jobs did the Mandal Commission recommend reserving for backward classes?
cards.back: It therefore recommended reserving 27 per cent of seats in educational institutions and government jobs for these groups.
cards.quote: It therefore recommended reserving 27 per cent of seats in educational institutions and government jobs for these groups.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Besides reservation, what other recommendation did the Mandal Commission make for OBCs?
cards.back: The Mandal Commission also made many other recommendations, like, land reform, to improve the conditions of the OBCs.
cards.quote: The Mandal Commission also made many other recommendations, like, land reform, to improve the conditions of the OBCs.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did the National Front government decide to implement the Mandal Commission's job reservation?
cards.back: In August 1990, the National Front government decided to implement one of the recommendations of Mandal Commission pertaining to reservations for OBCs in jobs in the central government and its
cards.quote: In August 1990, the National Front government decided to implement one of the recommendations of Mandal Commission pertaining to reservations for OBCs in jobs in the central government and its

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The decision was also challenged in the Supreme Court and came to be known as the '____ case', after the name of one of the petitioners.
cards.back: The decision was also challenged in the Supreme Court and came to be known as the 'Indira Sawhney case', after the name of one of the petitioners.
cards.quote: The decision was also challenged in the Supreme Court and came to be known as the 'Indira Sawhney case', after the name of one of the petitioners.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Supreme Court rule in November 1992 on the OBC reservation decision?
cards.back: In November 1992, the Supreme Court gave a ruling upholding the decision of the government.
cards.quote: In November 1992, the Supreme Court gave a ruling upholding the decision of the government.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In ____ the Backward and Minority Communities Employees Federation (BAMCEF) was formed.
cards.back: In 1978 the Backward and Minority Communities Employees Federation (BAMCEF) was formed.
cards.quote: In 1978 the Backward and Minority Communities Employees Federation (BAMCEF) was formed.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: BAMCEF took a strong position for political power to which groups, called the 'bahujan'?
cards.back: It took a strong position in favour of political power to the 'bahujan' – the SC, ST, OBC and minorities.
cards.quote: It took a strong position in favour of political power to the 'bahujan' – the SC, ST, OBC and minorities.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which party emerged under Kanshi Ram after BAMCEF and the Dalit Shoshit Samaj Sangharsh Samiti?
cards.back: It was out of this that the subsequent Dalit Shoshit Samaj Sangharsh Samiti and later the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) emerged under the leadership of Kanshi Ram.
cards.quote: It was out of this that the subsequent Dalit Shoshit Samaj Sangharsh Samiti and later the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) emerged under the leadership of Kanshi Ram.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why was the BSP's breakthrough in Uttar Pradesh in 1989 and 1991 significant?
cards.back: But in 1989 and the 1991 elections, it achieved a breakthrough in Uttar Pradesh. This was the first time in independent India that a political party supported mainly by Dalit voters had achieved this kind of political success.
cards.quote: But in 1989 and the 1991 elections, it achieved a breakthrough in Uttar Pradesh. This was the first time in independent India that a political party supported mainly by Dalit voters had achieved this kind of political success.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In which States did the BSP begin with support largely from Dalit voters?
cards.back: The BSP began as a small party supported largely by Dalit voters in Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh.
cards.quote: The BSP began as a small party supported largely by Dalit voters in Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: On what kind of politics was the BSP under Kanshi Ram envisaged?
cards.back: In fact, the BSP, under Kanshi Ram's leadership was envisaged as an organisation based on pragmatic politics.
cards.quote: In fact, the BSP, under Kanshi Ram's leadership was envisaged as an organisation based on pragmatic politics.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How have Dalit politics and OBC politics developed in many parts of India?
cards.back: In many parts of India, Dalit politics and OBC politics have developed independently and often in competition with each other.
cards.quote: In many parts of India, Dalit politics and OBC politics have developed independently and often in competition with each other.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which organisations did Kanshi Ram found, and when did he found the BSP?
cards.back: founder of BAMCEF, DS-4 and finally the BSP in 1984
cards.quote: founder of BAMCEF, DS-4 and finally the BSP in 1984

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Besides the rise of OBCs, what other long-term development marked this period?
cards.back: The other long-term development during this period was the visible rise of politics based on religious identity leading to a debate about secularism and democracy.
cards.quote: The other long-term development during this period was the visible rise of politics based on religious identity leading to a debate about secularism and democracy.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Hindutva was popularised by ____, as the basis of Indian nationhood.
cards.back: Hindutva was popularised by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, as the basis of Indian nationhood.
cards.quote: Hindutva was popularised by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, as the basis of Indian nationhood.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did 'Hindutva' basically mean?
cards.back: It basically meant that to be an Indian, one must accept India as their 'fatherland' (pitrubhu) as well as their holy land (punyabhu).
cards.quote: It basically meant that to be an Indian, one must accept India as their 'fatherland' (pitrubhu) as well as their holy land (punyabhu).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What do believers of 'Hindutva' argue about building a strong nation?
cards.back: Believers of 'Hindutva' argue that a strong nation can be built on the basis of a united national culture.
cards.quote: Believers of 'Hindutva' argue that a strong nation can be built on the basis of a united national culture.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the Shah Bano case of 1985?
cards.back: In this case a 62-year old divorced Muslim woman, had filed a case for maintenance from her former husband. The Supreme Court ruled in favour of Shah Bano.
cards.quote: In this case a 62-year old divorced Muslim woman, had filed a case for maintenance from her former husband. The Supreme Court ruled in favour of Shah Bano.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which 1986 Act nullified the Supreme Court's judgement in the Shah Bano case?
cards.back: On the demand of some Muslim leaders, the government passed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 that nullified the Supreme Court's judgement.
cards.quote: On the demand of some Muslim leaders, the government passed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 that nullified the Supreme Court's judgement.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did the BJP criticise the Congress government's action after the Shah Bano judgement?
cards.back: The BJP criticised this action of the Congress government as an unnecessary concession and 'appeasement' of the minority community.
cards.quote: The BJP criticised this action of the Congress government as an unnecessary concession and 'appeasement' of the minority community.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In which year was the three-dome structure built at the Ayodhya site?
cards.back: A three-dome structure was built at the site of Shri Ram's birth place in 1528
cards.quote: A three-dome structure was built at the site of Shri Ram's birth place in 1528

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In which year was the Ayodhya structure sealed due to the onset of court proceedings?
cards.back: Over the years, this issue evolved into a prolonged legal battle, leading to the structure being sealed in 1949 due to the onset of court proceedings.
cards.quote: Over the years, this issue evolved into a prolonged legal battle, leading to the structure being sealed in 1949 due to the onset of court proceedings.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Faizabad district court rule in 1986 about the Ayodhya structure?
cards.back: In 1986, the situation regarding the three-dome structure took a significant turn when the Faizabad (now Ayodhya) district court ruled to unlock the structure, allowing people to worship there.
cards.quote: In 1986, the situation regarding the three-dome structure took a significant turn when the Faizabad (now Ayodhya) district court ruled to unlock the structure, allowing people to worship there.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: After the 1986 unlocking, what remained prohibited at the Ayodhya site although Shilaanyas was done?
cards.back: although Shilaanyas for the temple was done, further construction remained prohibited.
cards.quote: although Shilaanyas for the temple was done, further construction remained prohibited.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How and when was the Ayodhya issue finally resolved?
cards.back: Through a number of democratic and legal procedures including court hearings, mediation attempts, popular movements, and finally with a 5-0 verdict of a constitutional bench of the Supreme Court on November 9, 2019, the Ayodhya issue was resolved.
cards.quote: Through a number of democratic and legal procedures including court hearings, mediation attempts, popular movements, and finally with a 5-0 verdict of a constitutional bench of the Supreme Court on November 9, 2019, the Ayodhya issue was resolved.

source.section: From Legal Proceedings to Amicable Acceptance

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Supreme Court's 9 November 2019 verdict allot, and to whom?
cards.back: The verdict allotted the disputed site to the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teertha Kshetra Trust for the construction of Ram temple and directed the concerned government to allot appropriate site for the construction of a Mosque to the Sunni Central Waqf Board.
cards.quote: The verdict allotted the disputed site to the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teertha Kshetra Trust for the construction of Ram temple and directed the concerned government to allot appropriate site for the construction of a Mosque to the Sunni Central Waqf Board.

source.section: From Legal Proceedings to Amicable Acceptance

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: On what evidence was the Ayodhya issue resolved following due process of law?
cards.back: This issue was resolved following the due process of law based on evidences such as archaeological excavations and historical records.
cards.quote: This issue was resolved following the due process of law based on evidences such as archaeological excavations and historical records.

source.section: From Legal Proceedings to Amicable Acceptance

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the first element of the consensus that emerged among most parties after 1989?
cards.back: First, agreement on new economic policies – while many groups are opposed to the new economic policies, most political parties are in support of the new economic policies.
cards.quote: First, agreement on new economic policies – while many groups are opposed to the new economic policies, most political parties are in support of the new economic policies.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the second element of the consensus that emerged among most parties after 1989?
cards.back: Second, acceptance of the political and social claims of the backward castes – political parties have recognised that the social and political claims of the backward castes need to be accepted.
cards.quote: Second, acceptance of the political and social claims of the backward castes – political parties have recognised that the social and political claims of the backward castes need to be accepted.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Indian nationalism sought to balance the principles of ____.
cards.back: Indian nationalism sought to balance the principles of unity and diversity.
cards.quote: Indian nationalism sought to balance the principles of unity and diversity.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How does the Indian democratic approach treat political expressions of regional aspirations?
cards.back: Democracy allows the political expressions of regional aspirations and does not look upon them as anti-national.
cards.quote: Democracy allows the political expressions of regional aspirations and does not look upon them as anti-national.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How may the 1980s be seen in terms of regional aspirations?
cards.back: 1980s may be seen as a period of rising regional aspirations for autonomy, often outside the framework of the Indian Union.
cards.quote: 1980s may be seen as a period of rising regional aspirations for autonomy, often outside the framework of the Indian Union.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did most regional struggles of the 1980s conclude?
cards.back: It is also not surprising that most of these struggles were long drawn and concluded in negotiated settlements or accords between the central government and the groups leading the movement for autonomy.
cards.quote: It is also not surprising that most of these struggles were long drawn and concluded in negotiated settlements or accords between the central government and the groups leading the movement for autonomy.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When were the States of Punjab and Haryana created?
cards.back: This demand was finally accepted and the States of Punjab and Haryana were created in 1966.
cards.quote: This demand was finally accepted and the States of Punjab and Haryana were created in 1966.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which two north-eastern regions witnessed strong movements demanding separation from India soon after Independence?
cards.back: First Nagaland and then Mizoram witnessed strong movements demanding separation from India.
cards.quote: First Nagaland and then Mizoram witnessed strong movements demanding separation from India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which States were created later, after Punjab and Haryana, to meet the challenge of diversity?
cards.back: Later, the States of Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand were created.
cards.quote: Later, the States of Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand were created.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Under which Article did Jammu and Kashmir have a special status before 2019?
cards.back: Jammu and Kashmir had a special status under Article 370 of the Indian Constitution.
cards.quote: Jammu and Kashmir had a special status under Article 370 of the Indian Constitution.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which community was displaced on a large scale from the Kashmir valley?
cards.back: there was also a large scale displacement of Kashmiri Pandits from the Kashmir valley.
cards.quote: there was also a large scale displacement of Kashmiri Pandits from the Kashmir valley.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which region of Jammu and Kashmir is a mix of foothills and plains and predominantly Hindu?
cards.back: The Jammu region is a mix of foothills and plains. It is predominantly inhabited by the Hindus.
cards.quote: The Jammu region is a mix of foothills and plains. It is predominantly inhabited by the Hindus.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who mostly inhabit the Kashmir region of Jammu and Kashmir?
cards.back: The Kashmir region mainly comprises of the Kashmir valley. It is inhabited mostly by Kashmiri Muslims with the remaining being Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists and others.
cards.quote: The Kashmir region mainly comprises of the Kashmir valley. It is inhabited mostly by Kashmiri Muslims with the remaining being Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists and others.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Describe the Ladakh region of Jammu and Kashmir.
cards.back: The Ladakh region is mainly mountainous. It has very little population which is almost equally divided between Buddhists and Muslims.
cards.quote: The Ladakh region is mainly mountainous. It has very little population which is almost equally divided between Buddhists and Muslims.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who was the ruler of J&K before 1947 and what did he want?
cards.back: Its ruler, Maharaja Hari Singh did not want to merge either with India or Pakistan but to have an independent status for his state.
cards.quote: Its ruler, Maharaja Hari Singh did not want to merge either with India or Pakistan but to have an independent status for his state.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the regional aspiration of the people of J&K who thought of themselves as Kashmiris above all called?
cards.back: Kashmiriyat
cards.quote: they thought of themselves as Kashmiris above all. This issue of regional aspiration is known as Kashmiriyat.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who led the popular movement in J&K that wanted to get rid of the Maharaja but was against joining Pakistan?
cards.back: The popular movement in the State, led by Sheikh Abdullah of the National Conference, wanted to get rid of the Maharaja, but was against joining Pakistan.
cards.quote: The popular movement in the State, led by Sheikh Abdullah of the National Conference, wanted to get rid of the Maharaja, but was against joining Pakistan.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The ____ was a secular organisation and had a long association with the Congress.
cards.back: The National Conference was a secular organisation and had a long association with the Congress.
cards.quote: The National Conference was a secular organisation and had a long association with the Congress.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Maharaja sign before India drove back the infiltrators from the Kashmir valley in 1947?
cards.back: India extended the military support and drove back the infiltrators from Kashmir valley, but only after the Maharaja had signed an ‘Instrument of Accession’ with the Government of India.
cards.quote: India extended the military support and drove back the infiltrators from Kashmir valley, but only after the Maharaja had signed an ‘Instrument of Accession’ with the Government of India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did the UN resolution recommend a three step process to resolve the Kashmir issue?
cards.back: the issue was taken to the United Nations Organisation, which in its resolution dated 21 April 1948 recommended a three step process to resolve the issue.
cards.quote: the issue was taken to the United Nations Organisation, which in its resolution dated 21 April 1948 recommended a three step process to resolve the issue.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The three step process recommended by the UN resolution of 21 April 1948, in order.
cards.back:
Firstly, Pakistan had to withdraw its entire nationalities, who entered into Kashmir.
Secondly, India needed to progressively reduce its forces so as to maintain law and order.
Thirdly, a plebiscite was to be conducted in a free and impartial manner.
cards.quote: Firstly, Pakistan had to withdraw its entire nationalities, who entered into Kashmir. Secondly, India needed to progressively reduce its forces so as to maintain law and order. Thirdly, a plebiscite was to be conducted in a free and impartial manner.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who became PM of J&K in March 1948, and under which Article was provisional autonomy granted?
cards.back: Sheikh Abdullah took over as the Prime Minister of the State of J&K in March 1948 while India agreed to grant it provisional autonomy under the Article 370.
cards.quote: Sheikh Abdullah took over as the Prime Minister of the State of J&K in March 1948 while India agreed to grant it provisional autonomy under the Article 370.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the Indian territory under illegal occupation of Pakistan called?
cards.back: it is the Indian territory which is under illegal occupation of Pakistan called as Pakistan occupied Jammu and Kashmir (POJK).
cards.quote: it is the Indian territory which is under illegal occupation of Pakistan called as Pakistan occupied Jammu and Kashmir (POJK).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the section of people outside J&K believe about Article 370?
cards.back: There is a section of people outside of J&K that believed that the special status of the State conferred by Article 370 did not allow full integration of the State with India.
cards.quote: There is a section of people outside of J&K that believed that the special status of the State conferred by Article 370 did not allow full integration of the State with India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the three major grievances of Kashmiris about Article 370 autonomy.
cards.back:
First, the promise that Accession would be referred to the people of the State after the situation created by tribal invasion was normalised, has not been fulfilled.
Secondly, there was a feeling that the special federal status guaranteed by Article 370, had been eroded in practice.
Thirdly, it was felt that democracy which is practiced in the rest of India has not been similarly institutionalised in the State of Jammu and Kashmir.
cards.quote: First, the promise that Accession would be referred to the people of the State after the situation created by tribal invasion was normalised, has not been fulfilled. This generated the demand for a plebiscite. Secondly, there was a feeling that the special federal status guaranteed by Article 370, had been eroded in practice. This had led to the demand for restoration of autonomy or ‘Greater State Autonomy’. Thirdly, it was felt that democracy which is practiced in the rest of India has not been similarly institutionalised in the State of Jammu and Kashmir.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When was Sheikh Abdullah dismissed as Prime Minister of J&K?
cards.back: He was dismissed in 1953 and kept in detention for a number of years.
cards.quote: He was dismissed in 1953 and kept in detention for a number of years.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What change in 1965 altered the designation of the head of government of J&K?
cards.back: A change in the provision of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir was made in 1965 by which the Prime Minister of the state was designated as Chief Minister of the state.
cards.quote: A change in the provision of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir was made in 1965 by which the Prime Minister of the state was designated as Chief Minister of the state.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who became the first Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir?
cards.back: Accordingly, Ghulam Mohammed Sadiq of the Indian National Congress became the first Chief Minister of the state.
cards.quote: Accordingly, Ghulam Mohammed Sadiq of the Indian National Congress became the first Chief Minister of the state.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What happened in 1974 between Indira Gandhi and Sheikh Abdullah?
cards.back: In 1974 Indira Gandhi reached an agreement with Sheikh Abdullah and he became the Chief Minister of the State.
cards.quote: In 1974 Indira Gandhi reached an agreement with Sheikh Abdullah and he became the Chief Minister of the State.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who led the National Conference and became Chief Minister after Sheikh Abdullah died in 1982?
cards.back: Sheikh Abdullah died in 1982 and the leadership of the National Conference went to his son, Farooq Abdullah, who became the Chief Minister.
cards.quote: Sheikh Abdullah died in 1982 and the leadership of the National Conference went to his son, Farooq Abdullah, who became the Chief Minister.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What happened to Farooq Abdullah soon after he became Chief Minister in 1982?
cards.back: But he soon was dismissed by the Governor and a breakaway faction of the National Conference came to power for a brief period.
cards.quote: But he soon was dismissed by the Governor and a breakaway faction of the National Conference came to power for a brief period.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: With which party did the National Conference agree to an electoral alliance in 1986?
cards.back: the National Conference in 1986 agreed to have an electoral alliance with the Congress, the ruling party in the Centre.
cards.quote: the National Conference in 1986 agreed to have an electoral alliance with the Congress, the ruling party in the Centre.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was widely believed about the 1987 Assembly election in Jammu and Kashmir?
cards.back: But it was widely believed that the results did not reflect popular choice, and that the entire election process was rigged.
cards.quote: But it was widely believed that the results did not reflect popular choice, and that the entire election process was rigged.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What had gripped Jammu and Kashmir by 1989?
cards.back: By 1989, the State had come in the grip of a militant movement mobilised around the cause of a separate Kashmiri nation.
cards.quote: By 1989, the State had come in the grip of a militant movement mobilised around the cause of a separate Kashmiri nation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which country gave moral, material and military support to the Kashmir insurgents?
cards.back: The insurgents got moral, material and military support from Pakistan.
cards.quote: The insurgents got moral, material and military support from Pakistan.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which party came to power in the 1996 Jammu and Kashmir Assembly elections, and with what demand?
cards.back: Assembly elections in the State were held only in 1996 in which the National Conference led by Farooq Abdullah came to power with a demand for regional autonomy for Jammu and Kashmir.
cards.quote: Assembly elections in the State were held only in 1996 in which the National Conference led by Farooq Abdullah came to power with a demand for regional autonomy for Jammu and Kashmir.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which coalition government replaced the National Conference after the 2002 elections in J&K?
cards.back: At the end of its term, elections were held in the State in 2002. The National Conference failed to win a majority and was replaced by a coalition government of People’s Democratic Party (PDP) and Congress.
cards.quote: At the end of its term, elections were held in the State in 2002. The National Conference failed to win a majority and was replaced by a coalition government of People’s Democratic Party (PDP) and Congress.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Under the 2002 PDP-Congress coalition agreement, who headed the government first, and who succeeded him?
cards.back: As per the coalition agreement, Mufti Mohammed headed the government for the first three years succeeded by Ghulam Nabi Azad
cards.quote: As per the coalition agreement, Mufti Mohammed headed the government for the first three years succeeded by Ghulam Nabi Azad

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who headed the NC and INC coalition government that came to power in J&K in 2009?
cards.back: Another coalition government (composed of NC and INC) came into power headed by Omar Abdullah in 2009.
cards.quote: Another coalition government (composed of NC and INC) came into power headed by Omar Abdullah in 2009.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which coalition government came to power in J&K after the 2014 election?
cards.back: Consequently a coalition government led by Mufti Mohammed Sayeed of the PDP came into power with the BJP as its partner.
cards.quote: Consequently a coalition government led by Mufti Mohammed Sayeed of the PDP came into power with the BJP as its partner.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who became the first woman Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir in April 2016?
cards.back: his daughter Mahbooba Mufti became the first woman Chief Minister of the state in April 2016.
cards.quote: his daughter Mahbooba Mufti became the first woman Chief Minister of the state in April 2016.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why was President’s rule imposed in J&K in June 2018?
cards.back: The President’s rule was imposed in June 2018 after BJP withdrew its support to the Mufti government.
cards.quote: The President’s rule was imposed in June 2018 after BJP withdrew its support to the Mufti government.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What happened on 5 August 2019 to Article 370 and to the State of Jammu and Kashmir?
cards.back: On 5 August 2019, Article 370 was abolished by the Jammu & Kashmir Reorganisation Act 2019 and the state was constituted into two Union Territories, viz., Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.
cards.quote: On 5 August 2019, Article 370 was abolished by the Jammu & Kashmir Reorganisation Act 2019 and the state was constituted into two Union Territories, viz., Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which organisation did the Dravidian movement form under E.V. Ramasami ‘Periyar’?
cards.back: The Dravidian movement led to the formation of Dravidar Kazhagam [DK] under the leadership of Tamil social reformer E.V. Ramasami “Periyar”.
cards.quote: The Dravidian movement led to the formation of Dravidar Kazhagam [DK] under the leadership of Tamil social reformer E.V. Ramasami “Periyar”.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Dravidar Kazhagam oppose and affirm?
cards.back: The organisation strongly opposed the Brahmins’ dominance and affirmed regional pride against the political, economic and cultural domination of the North.
cards.quote: The organisation strongly opposed the Brahmins’ dominance and affirmed regional pride against the political, economic and cultural domination of the North.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why was the Dravidian movement limited to Tamil Nadu?
cards.back: Initially, the Dravidian movement spoke in terms of the whole of south India; however lack of support from other States limited the movement to Tamil Nadu.
cards.quote: Initially, the Dravidian movement spoke in terms of the whole of south India; however lack of support from other States limited the movement to Tamil Nadu.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: To which party was the political legacy of the Dravidian movement transferred after the DK split?
cards.back: The DK split and the political legacy of the movement was transferred to Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK).
cards.quote: The DK split and the political legacy of the movement was transferred to Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How did the DMK make its entry into politics, and when?
cards.back: The DMK made its entry into politics with a three pronged agitation in 1953-54.
cards.quote: The DMK made its entry into politics with a three pronged agitation in 1953-54.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which 1965 agitation added to the DMK’s popularity?
cards.back: The success of the anti-Hindi agitation of 1965 added to the DMK’s popularity.
cards.quote: The success of the anti-Hindi agitation of 1965 added to the DMK’s popularity.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In which Assembly elections did sustained agitations bring the DMK to power in Tamil Nadu?
cards.back: Sustained political agitations brought the DMK to power in the Assembly elections of 1967.
cards.quote: Sustained political agitations brought the DMK to power in the Assembly elections of 1967.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: After the death of which DMK leader did the party split?
cards.back: Though the DMK split after the death of its leader, C. Annadurai, the influence of Dravidian parties in Tamil politics actually increased.
cards.quote: Though the DMK split after the death of its leader, C. Annadurai, the influence of Dravidian parties in Tamil politics actually increased.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which two parties claimed the Dravidian legacy after the DMK split?
cards.back: After the split there were two parties – the DMK and the All India Anna DMK (AIADMK) – that claimed Dravidian legacy.
cards.quote: After the split there were two parties – the DMK and the All India Anna DMK (AIADMK) – that claimed Dravidian legacy.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is regional politics in Tamil Nadu a good example of?
cards.back: Initially seen as a threat to Indian nationalism, regional politics in Tamil Nadu is a good example of the compatibility of regionalism and nationalism.
cards.quote: Initially seen as a threat to Indian nationalism, regional politics in Tamil Nadu is a good example of the compatibility of regionalism and nationalism.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which party, formed in 1920 as the political wing of the Sikhs, led the movement for a ‘Punjabi suba’?
cards.back: The Akali Dal, which was formed in 1920 as the political wing of the Sikhs, had led the movement for the formation of a ‘Punjabi suba’.
cards.quote: The Akali Dal, which was formed in 1920 as the political wing of the Sikhs, had led the movement for the formation of a ‘Punjabi suba’.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In which years did the Akalis come to power after Punjab’s reorganisation?
cards.back: After the reorganisation, the Akalis came to power in 1967 and then in 1977.
cards.quote: After the reorganisation, the Akalis came to power in 1967 and then in 1977.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the three reasons why the Akalis’ political position remained precarious.
cards.back:
Firstly, their government was dismissed by the Centre mid-way through its term.
Secondly, they did not enjoy strong support among the Hindus.
Thirdly, the Sikh community, like all other religious communities, was internally differentiated on caste and class lines.
cards.quote: The Akalis discovered that despite the redrawing of the boundaries, their political position remained precarious. Firstly, their government was dismissed by the Centre mid-way through its term. Secondly, they did not enjoy strong support among the Hindus. Thirdly, the Sikh community, like all other religious communities, was internally differentiated on caste and class lines.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which resolution of 1973 reflected the Akali demand for political autonomy for Punjab?
cards.back: a section of Akalis began to demand political autonomy for the region. This was reflected in a resolution passed at their conference at Anandpur Sahib in 1973.
cards.quote: a section of Akalis began to demand political autonomy for the region. This was reflected in a resolution passed at their conference at Anandpur Sahib in 1973.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Anandpur Sahib Resolution assert and want?
cards.back: The Anandpur Sahib Resolution asserted regional autonomy and wanted to redefine centre-state relationship in the country.
cards.quote: The Anandpur Sahib Resolution asserted regional autonomy and wanted to redefine centre-state relationship in the country.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What goal did the Anandpur Sahib Resolution declare for the Sikh qaum?
cards.back: The resolution also spoke of the aspirations of the Sikh qaum (community or nation) and declared its goal as attaining the bolbala (dominance or hegemony) of the Sikhs.
cards.quote: The resolution also spoke of the aspirations of the Sikh qaum (community or nation) and declared its goal as attaining the bolbala (dominance or hegemony) of the Sikhs.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was the Anandpur Sahib Resolution a plea for?
cards.back: The Resolution was a plea for strengthening federalism in India.
cards.quote: The Resolution was a plea for strengthening federalism in India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: After the Akali government was dismissed in 1980, what question did the Akali Dal launch a movement on?
cards.back: after the Akali government had been dismissed in 1980, the Akali Dal launched a movement on the question of the distribution of water between Punjab and its neighbouring States.
cards.quote: after the Akali government had been dismissed in 1980, the Akali Dal launched a movement on the question of the distribution of water between Punjab and its neighbouring States.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was ‘Operation Blue Star’ of June 1984?
cards.back: In June 1984, the Government of India carried out ‘Operation Blue Star’, code name for army action in the Golden Temple.
cards.quote: In June 1984, the Government of India carried out ‘Operation Blue Star’, code name for army action in the Golden Temple.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When and by whom was Prime Minister Indira Gandhi assassinated?
cards.back: Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated on 31 October 1984 outside her residence by her bodyguards.
cards.quote: Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated on 31 October 1984 outside her residence by her bodyguards.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why did Indira Gandhi’s two Sikh bodyguards assassinate her?
cards.back: Both the assassins were Sikhs and wanted to take revenge for Operation Blue Star.
cards.quote: Both the assassins were Sikhs and wanted to take revenge for Operation Blue Star.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which area was worst affected by the anti-Sikh violence after Indira Gandhi’s assassination?
cards.back: More than two thousand Sikhs were killed in the national capital, the area worst affected by this violence.
cards.quote: More than two thousand Sikhs were killed in the national capital, the area worst affected by this violence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Whose report said the 1984 attacks on Sikhs were made in a systematic manner without much fear of the police?
cards.back: Justice Nanavati Commission of Inquiry, Report, Vol. I, 2005
cards.quote: The attacks were made in a systematic manner and without much fear of the police, almost suggesting that they were assured that they would not be harmed while committing those acts or even after. Justice Nanavati Commission of Inquiry, Report, Vol. I, 2005

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which Prime Minister apologised in Parliament in 2005 for the anti-Sikh violence of 1984?
cards.back: Twenty years later, speaking in the Parliament in 2005, Prime Minister Manmohan Singh expressed regret over these killings and apologised to the nation for the anti-Sikh violence.
cards.quote: Twenty years later, speaking in the Parliament in 2005, Prime Minister Manmohan Singh expressed regret over these killings and apologised to the nation for the anti-Sikh violence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: With whom did Rajiv Gandhi reach an agreement in July 1985?
cards.back: In July 1985, he reached an agreement with Harchand Singh Longowal, then the President of the Akali Dal.
cards.quote: In July 1985, he reached an agreement with Harchand Singh Longowal, then the President of the Akali Dal.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the agreement of July 1985 between Rajiv Gandhi and Longowal known as?
cards.back: This agreement, known as the Rajiv Gandhi - Longowal Accord or the Punjab Accord, was a step towards bringing normalcy to Punjab.
cards.quote: This agreement, known as the Rajiv Gandhi - Longowal Accord or the Punjab Accord, was a step towards bringing normalcy to Punjab.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Punjab Accord agree about Chandigarh and the Punjab-Haryana border dispute?
cards.back: It was agreed that Chandigarh would be transferred to Punjab, a separate commission would be appointed to resolve the border dispute between Punjab and Haryana,
cards.quote: It was agreed that Chandigarh would be transferred to Punjab, a separate commission would be appointed to resolve the border dispute between Punjab and Haryana,

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Under the Punjab Accord (1985), the tribunal was to decide the sharing of which river water, among which States?
cards.back: a tribunal would be set up to decide the sharing of Ravi-Beas river water among Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan.
cards.quote: a tribunal would be set up to decide the sharing of Ravi-Beas river water among Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Punjab Accord provide for the victims of militancy and about AFSPA?
cards.back: agreement also provided for compensation to and better treatment of those affected by the militancy in Punjab and the withdrawal of the application of Armed Forces Special Powers Act in Punjab.
cards.quote: agreement also provided for compensation to and better treatment of those affected by the militancy in Punjab and the withdrawal of the application of Armed Forces Special Powers Act in Punjab.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which alliance won the first normal elections in Punjab in the post-militancy era in 1997?
cards.back: The alliance of Akali Dal (Badal) and the BJP scored a major victory in1997, in the first normal elections in the State in the post-militancy era.
cards.quote: The alliance of Akali Dal (Badal) and the BJP scored a major victory in1997, in the first normal elections in the State in the post-militancy era.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the States of the North-East often called “the seven sisters”.
cards.back:
Arunachal Pradesh
Assam
Nagaland
Manipur
Tripura
Mizoram
Meghalaya
cards.quote: Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Nagaland, Manipur, Tripura, Mizoram and Meghalaya, which earlier constituted the North-East region, are often called “the seven sisters”.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which State added to the North-East is referred to as the ‘Brother’ to the seven sisters?
cards.back: Sikkim, which has been added to the list is – referred to as the ‘Brother’ to those seven states.
cards.quote: Sikkim, which has been added to the list is – referred to as the ‘Brother’ to those seven states.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How wide is the corridor connecting the North-East to the rest of India?
cards.back: A small corridor of about 22 kilometers connects the region to the rest of the country.
cards.quote: A small corridor of about 22 kilometers connects the region to the rest of the country.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: With which countries does the North-East share boundaries?
cards.back: Otherwise the region shares boundaries with China, Myanmar and Bangladesh and serves as India’s gateway to South East Asia.
cards.quote: Otherwise the region shares boundaries with China, Myanmar and Bangladesh and serves as India’s gateway to South East Asia.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which parts of the North-East were erstwhile Princely States?
cards.back: Tripura, Manipur and Khasi Hills of Meghalaya were erstwhile Princely States which merged with India after Independence.
cards.quote: Tripura, Manipur and Khasi Hills of Meghalaya were erstwhile Princely States which merged with India after Independence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When were Nagaland, Manipur, Tripura, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh created as States?
cards.back: Nagaland State was created in 1963; Manipur, Tripura and Meghalaya in 1972 while Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh became separate States only in 1987.
cards.quote: Nagaland State was created in 1963; Manipur, Tripura and Meghalaya in 1972 while Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh became separate States only in 1987.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the three issues that dominate the politics of the North-East.
cards.back:
demands for autonomy
movements for secession
opposition to ‘outsiders’
cards.quote: Three issues dominate the politics of North-East: demands for autonomy, movements for secession, and opposition to ‘outsiders’.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did demands for political autonomy arise in the North-East?
cards.back: Demands for political autonomy arose when the non-Assamese felt that the Assam government was imposing Assamese language on them.
cards.quote: Demands for political autonomy arose when the non-Assamese felt that the Assam government was imposing Assamese language on them.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Into which body did the Eastern India Tribal Union transform in 1960?
cards.back: They formed the Eastern India Tribal Union which later transformed into a more comprehensive All Party Hill Leaders Conference in 1960.
cards.quote: They formed the Eastern India Tribal Union which later transformed into a more comprehensive All Party Hill Leaders Conference in 1960.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which States did the Central Government create out of Assam?
cards.back: At different points of time the Central Government had to create Meghalaya, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh out of Assam.
cards.quote: At different points of time the Central Government had to create Meghalaya, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh out of Assam.

cards.subject: political_science
