cards.front: By which year was the reorganisation of the North-East completed?
cards.back: The reorganisation of the North-East was completed by 1972.
cards.quote: The reorganisation of the North-East was completed by 1972.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which communities of Assam got autonomy under District Councils, and which got an Autonomous Council?
cards.back: Karbis and Dimasas have been granted autonomy under District Councils while Bodos were recently granted Autonomous Council.
cards.quote: Karbis and Dimasas have been granted autonomy under District Councils while Bodos were recently granted Autonomous Council.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What gave popular support to the Mizo secession movement?
cards.back: But the movement for secession gained popular support after the Assam government failed to respond adequately to the great famine of 1959 in Mizo hills.
cards.quote: But the movement for secession gained popular support after the Assam government failed to respond adequately to the great famine of 1959 in Mizo hills.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which organisation was formed under Laldenga after the Mizos’ anger?
cards.back: The Mizos’ anger led to the formation of the Mizo National Front (MNF) under the leadership of Laldenga.
cards.quote: The Mizos’ anger led to the formation of the Mizo National Front (MNF) under the leadership of Laldenga.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When did the MNF start an armed campaign for independence?
cards.back: In 1966 the MNF started an armed campaign for independence.
cards.quote: In 1966 the MNF started an armed campaign for independence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Between whom was the peace agreement of 1986 signed in Mizoram?
cards.back: In 1986 a peace agreement was signed between Rajiv Gandhi and Laldenga.
cards.quote: In 1986 a peace agreement was signed between Rajiv Gandhi and Laldenga.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did Mizoram get and what did the MNF give up under the 1986 accord?
cards.back: As per this accord Mizoram was granted full-fledged statehood with special powers and the MNF agreed to give up secessionist struggle.
cards.quote: As per this accord Mizoram was granted full-fledged statehood with special powers and the MNF agreed to give up secessionist struggle.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who took over as Chief Minister of Mizoram after the 1986 accord?
cards.back: Laldenga took over as the Chief Minister.
cards.quote: Laldenga took over as the Chief Minister.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who led the section of Nagas that declared independence from India in 1951?
cards.back: Led by Angami Zapu Phizo, a section of the Nagas declared independence from India way back in 1951.
cards.quote: Led by Angami Zapu Phizo, a section of the Nagas declared independence from India way back in 1951.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which movement is the best example of movements against ‘outsiders’ in the North-East?
cards.back: The Assam Movement from 1979 to 1985 is the best example of such movements against ‘outsiders’.
cards.quote: The Assam Movement from 1979 to 1985 is the best example of such movements against ‘outsiders’.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which students’ group led the anti-foreigner Assam Movement in 1979?
cards.back: In 1979 the All Assam Students’ Union (AASU), a students’ group not affiliated to any party, led an anti-foreigner movement.
cards.quote: In 1979 the All Assam Students’ Union (AASU), a students’ group not affiliated to any party, led an anti-foreigner movement.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: After which year did the Assam Movement demand outsiders be sent back?
cards.back: The movement demanded that all outsiders who had entered the State after 1951 should be sent back.
cards.quote: The movement demanded that all outsiders who had entered the State after 1951 should be sent back.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Rajiv Gandhi-led government entered into negotiations with the AASU leaders, leading to the signing of an accord in ____.
cards.back: Rajiv Gandhi-led government entered into negotiations with the AASU leaders, leading to the signing of an accord in 1985.
cards.quote: Rajiv Gandhi-led government entered into negotiations with the AASU leaders, leading to the signing of an accord in 1985.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the 1985 Assam accord provide about foreigners who migrated into Assam?
cards.back: According to this agreement those foreigners who migrated into Assam during and after Bangladesh war and since, were to be identified and deported.
cards.quote: According to this agreement those foreigners who migrated into Assam during and after Bangladesh war and since, were to be identified and deported.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which regional party did the AASU and Asom Gana Sangram Parishad form after the Assam Movement?
cards.back: With the successful completion of the movement, the AASU and the Asom Gana Sangram Parishad organised themselves as a regional political party called Asom Gana Parishad (AGP).
cards.quote: With the successful completion of the movement, the AASU and the Asom Gana Sangram Parishad organised themselves as a regional political party called Asom Gana Parishad (AGP).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Assam accord not solve?
cards.back: Assam accord brought peace and changed the face of politics in Assam, but it did not solve the problem of immigration.
cards.quote: Assam accord brought peace and changed the face of politics in Assam, but it did not solve the problem of immigration.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What was Sikkim’s status at the time of independence?
cards.back: At the time of independence, Sikkim was a ‘protectorate’ of India.
cards.quote: At the time of independence, Sikkim was a ‘protectorate’ of India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which party swept the first democratic elections to the Sikkim assembly in 1974?
cards.back: The first democratic elections to Sikkim assembly in 1974 were swept by Sikkim Congress which stood for greater integration with India.
cards.quote: The first democratic elections to Sikkim assembly in 1974 were swept by Sikkim Congress which stood for greater integration with India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Sikkim assembly ask for in April 1975?
cards.back: The assembly first sought the status of ‘associate state’ and then in April 1975 passed a resolution asking for full integration with India.
cards.quote: The assembly first sought the status of ‘associate state’ and then in April 1975 passed a resolution asking for full integration with India.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which number State of the Indian union did Sikkim become?
cards.back: The Indian Parliament accepted this request immediately and Sikkim became the 22nd State of the Indian union.
cards.quote: The Indian Parliament accepted this request immediately and Sikkim became the 22nd State of the Indian union.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the first and most elementary lesson from the cases of regional aspirations?
cards.back: First and the most elementary lesson is that regional aspirations are very much a part of democratic politics.
cards.quote: First and the most elementary lesson is that regional aspirations are very much a part of democratic politics.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the second lesson about responding to regional aspirations?
cards.back: The second lesson is that the best way to respond to regional aspirations is through democratic negotiations rather than through suppression.
cards.quote: The second lesson is that the best way to respond to regional aspirations is through democratic negotiations rather than through suppression.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The ____ of the Constitution allows different tribes complete autonomy of preserving their practices and customary laws.
cards.back: The Sixth Schedule of the Constitution allows different tribes complete autonomy of preserving their practices and customary laws.
cards.quote: The Sixth Schedule of the Constitution allows different tribes complete autonomy of preserving their practices and customary laws.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What does security imply at its most basic?
cards.back: At its most basic, security implies freedom from threats.
cards.quote: At its most basic, security implies freedom from threats.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: According to NCERT, to which threats does security relate?
cards.back: security relates only to extremely dangerous threats-- threats that could so endanger core values that those values would be damaged beyond repair if we did not do something to deal with the situation.
cards.quote: security relates only to extremely dangerous threats-- threats that could so endanger core values that those values would be damaged beyond repair if we did not do something to deal with the situation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the two groups of notions of security.
cards.back:
traditional
non-traditional
cards.quote: Let us begin by putting the various notions of security under two groups: traditional and non-traditional conceptions of security.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In the traditional conception of security, the greatest danger to a country is from ____ threats.
cards.back: military. In the traditional conception of security, the greatest danger to a country is from military threats.
cards.quote: In the traditional conception of security, the greatest danger to a country is from military threats.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which core values does a military threat from another country endanger, in the traditional conception?
cards.back: The source of this danger is another country which by threatening military action endangers the core values of sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity.
cards.quote: The source of this danger is another country which by threatening military action endangers the core values of sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What three basic choices does a government have in responding to the threat of war?
cards.back:
to surrender
to prevent the other side from attacking by promising to raise the costs of war to an unacceptable level
to defend itself
cards.quote: to surrender; to prevent the other side from attacking by promising to raise the costs of war to an unacceptable level; and to defend itself when war actually

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In traditional security policy, what are deterrence and defence?
cards.back: security policy is concerned with preventing war, which is called deterrence, and with limiting or ending war, which is called defence.
cards.quote: security policy is concerned with preventing war, which is called deterrence, and with limiting or ending war, which is called defence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the third component of traditional security policy?
cards.back: Traditional security policy has a third component called balance of power.
cards.quote: Traditional security policy has a third component called balance of power.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How is a balance of power maintained, according to NCERT?
cards.back: A good part of maintaining a balance of power is to build up one's military power, although economic and technological power are also important since they are the basis for military power.
cards.quote: A good part of maintaining a balance of power is to build up one's military power, although economic and technological power are also important since they are the basis for military power.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the fourth component of traditional security policy?
cards.back: A fourth and related component of traditional security policy is alliance building.
cards.quote: A fourth and related component of traditional security policy is alliance building.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is an alliance?
cards.back: An alliance is a coalition of states that coordinate their actions to deter or defend against military attack.
cards.quote: An alliance is a coalition of states that coordinate their actions to deter or defend against military attack.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How are most alliances formalised?
cards.back: Most alliances are formalised in written treaties
cards.quote: Most alliances are formalised in written treaties

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When can alliances change, according to NCERT?
cards.back: Alliances are based on national interests and can change when national interests change.
cards.quote: Alliances are based on national interests and can change when national interests change.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In the traditional view, where do most threats to a country come from?
cards.back: In the traditional view of security, then, most threats to a country's security come from outside its borders.
cards.quote: In the traditional view of security, then, most threats to a country's security come from outside its borders.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why do most threats come from outside borders in the traditional view of security?
cards.back: That is because the international system is a rather brutal arena in which there is no central authority capable of controlling behaviour.
cards.quote: That is because the international system is a rather brutal arena in which there is no central authority capable of controlling behaviour.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How does NCERT describe the authority of the UN in world politics?
cards.back: as presently constituted, the UN is a creature of its members and has authority only to the extent that the membership allows it to have authority and obeys it.
cards.quote: as presently constituted, the UN is a creature of its members and has authority only to the extent that the membership allows it to have authority and obeys it.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In world politics, who is responsible for each country's security?
cards.back: So, in world politics, each country has to be responsible for its own security.
cards.quote: So, in world politics, each country has to be responsible for its own security.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What must traditional security also concern itself with, besides external threats?
cards.back: Traditional security must also, therefore, concern itself with internal security.
cards.quote: Traditional security must also, therefore, concern itself with internal security.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why was internal security given less importance after the Second World War?
cards.back: The reason it is not given so much importance is that after the Second World War it seemed that, for the most powerful countries on earth, internal security was more or less assured.
cards.quote: The reason it is not given so much importance is that after the Second World War it seemed that, for the most powerful countries on earth, internal security was more or less assured.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The Cold War between the two superpowers was responsible for approximately ____ of all wars in the post-Second World War period.
cards.back: The Cold War between the two superpowers was responsible for approximately one-third of all wars in the post-Second World War period.
cards.quote: The Cold War between the two superpowers was responsible for approximately one-third of all wars in the post-Second World War period.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In what two ways were the security challenges of new Asian and African countries different from Europe's?
cards.back:
the new countries faced the prospect of military conflict with neighbouring countries
they had to worry about internal military conflict
cards.quote: For one thing, the new countries faced the prospect of military conflict with neighbouring countries. For another, they had to worry about internal military conflict.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Internally, the new states worried about threats from ____ which wanted to form independent countries.
cards.back: Internally, the new states worried about threats from separatist movements which wanted to form independent countries.
cards.quote: Internally, the new states worried about threats from separatist movements which wanted to form independent countries.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: For what reasons should countries go to war, according to traditional security?
cards.back: It is now an almost universally-accepted view that countries should only go to war for the right reasons, primarily self-defence or to protect other people from genocide.
cards.quote: It is now an almost universally-accepted view that countries should only go to war for the right reasons, primarily self-defence or to protect other people from genocide.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When must force be used, according to traditional security?
cards.back: Force must in any case be used only after all the alternatives have failed.
cards.quote: Force must in any case be used only after all the alternatives have failed.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the most important forms of cooperation in traditional security.
cards.back:
disarmament
arms control
confidence building
cards.quote: Traditional views of security do not rule out other forms of cooperation as well. The most important of these are disarmament, arms control, and confidence building.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is disarmament?
cards.back: Disarmament requires all states to give up certain kinds of weapons.
cards.quote: Disarmament requires all states to give up certain kinds of weapons.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which conventions banned biological and chemical weapons?
cards.back: For example, the 1972 Biological Weapons Convention (BWC) and the 1997 Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) banned the production and possession of these weapons.
cards.quote: For example, the 1972 Biological Weapons Convention (BWC) and the 1997 Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) banned the production and possession of these weapons.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which type of weapons of mass destruction did the superpowers not give up?
cards.back: But the superpowers -- the US and Soviet Union -- did not want to give up the third type of weapons of mass destruction, namely, nuclear weapons, so they pursued arms control.
cards.quote: But the superpowers -- the US and Soviet Union -- did not want to give up the third type of weapons of mass destruction, namely, nuclear weapons, so they pursued arms control.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is arms control?
cards.back: Arms control regulates the acquisition or development of weapons.
cards.quote: Arms control regulates the acquisition or development of weapons.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the 1972 Anti-ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty try to stop?
cards.back: The Anti-ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty in 1972 tried to stop the United States and Soviet Union from using ballistic missiles as a defensive shield to launch a nuclear attack.
cards.quote: The Anti-ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty in 1972 tried to stop the United States and Soviet Union from using ballistic missiles as a defensive shield to launch a nuclear attack.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What did the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) of 1968 regulate?
cards.back: The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) of 1968 was an arms control treaty in the sense that it regulated the acquisition of nuclear weapons: those countries that had tested and manufactured nuclear weapons before 1967 were allowed to keep their weapons; and those that had not done so were to give up the right to acquire them.
cards.quote: The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) of 1968 was an arms control treaty in the sense that it regulated the acquisition of nuclear weapons: those countries that had tested and manufactured nuclear weapons before 1967 were allowed to keep their weapons; and those that had not done so were to give up the right to acquire them.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is confidence building?
cards.back: Confidence building is a process in which countries share ideas and information with their rivals.
cards.quote: Confidence building is a process in which countries share ideas and information with their rivals.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is the purpose of confidence building?
cards.back: In short, confidence building is a process designed to ensure that rivals do not go to war through misunderstanding or misperception.
cards.quote: In short, confidence building is a process designed to ensure that rivals do not go to war through misunderstanding or misperception.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is force in traditional security?
cards.back: In traditional security, force is both the principal threat to security and the principal means of achieving security.
cards.quote: In traditional security, force is both the principal threat to security and the principal means of achieving security.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What are non-traditional notions of security?
cards.back: Non-traditional notions of security go beyond military threats to include a wide range of threats and dangers affecting the conditions of human existence.
cards.quote: Non-traditional notions of security go beyond military threats to include a wide range of threats and dangers affecting the conditions of human existence.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: In the traditional conception of security, what is the referent?
cards.back: the referent is the state with its territory and governing institutions.
cards.quote: the referent is the state with its territory and governing institutions.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who is the referent in non-traditional security ("Security for who?")?
cards.back: In the non-traditional conceptions, the referent is expanded. When we ask `Security for who?' proponents of non-traditional security reply `Not just the state but also individuals or communities or indeed all of humankind'.
cards.quote: In the non-traditional conceptions, the referent is expanded. When we ask `Security for who?' proponents of non-traditional security reply `Not just the state but also individuals or communities or indeed all of humankind'.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What are non-traditional views of security also called?
cards.back:
human security
global security
cards.quote: Nontraditional views of security have been called `human security' or `global security'.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is human security?
cards.back: Human security is about the protection of people more than the protection of states.
cards.quote: Human security is about the protection of people more than the protection of states.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Do secure states automatically mean secure peoples?
cards.back: But secure states do not automatically mean secure peoples.
cards.quote: But secure states do not automatically mean secure peoples.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who has killed more people during the last 100 years, own governments or foreign armies?
cards.back: Indeed, during the last 100 years, more people have been killed by their own governments than by foreign armies.
cards.quote: Indeed, during the last 100 years, more people have been killed by their own governments than by foreign armies.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Narrow vs broad human security: the threats covered.
cards.back:
Proponents of the `narrow' concept of human security focus on violent threats to individuals
Proponents of the `broad' concept of human security argue that the threat agenda should include hunger, disease and natural disasters
cards.quote: Proponents of the `narrow' concept of human security focus on violent threats to individuals or, as former UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan puts it, "the protection of communities and individuals from internal violence". Proponents of the `broad' concept of human security argue that the threat agenda should include hunger, disease and natural disasters because these kill far more people than war, genocide and terrorism combined.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What two freedoms does the broadest formulation of human security stress?
cards.back: the broadest formulation stresses what has been called `freedom from want' and `freedom from fear', respectively.
cards.quote: the broadest formulation stresses what has been called `freedom from want' and `freedom from fear', respectively.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: The idea of global security emerged in the ____ in response to the global nature of threats
cards.back: The idea of global security emerged in the 1990s in response to the global nature of threats
cards.quote: The idea of global security emerged in the 1990s in response to the global nature of threats

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Why is international cooperation vital for global threats?
cards.back: Since these problems are global in nature, international cooperation is vital, even though it is difficult to achieve.
cards.quote: Since these problems are global in nature, international cooperation is vital, even though it is difficult to achieve.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is terrorism?
cards.back: Terrorism refers to political violence that targets civilians deliberately and indiscriminately.
cards.quote: Terrorism refers to political violence that targets civilians deliberately and indiscriminately.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What is international terrorism?
cards.back: International terrorism involves the citizens or territory of more than one country.
cards.quote: International terrorism involves the citizens or territory of more than one country.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What do terrorist groups seek to do by force or threat of force?
cards.back: Terrorist groups seek to change a political context or condition that they do not like by force or threat of force.
cards.quote: Terrorist groups seek to change a political context or condition that they do not like by force or threat of force.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Since ____ when terrorists attacked the World Trade Centre in America
cards.back: Since 11 September 2001 when terrorists attacked the World Trade Centre in America
cards.quote: Since 11 September 2001 when terrorists attacked the World Trade Centre in America

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Types of human rights, as classified in NCERT.
cards.back:
political rights such as freedom of speech and assembly
economic and social rights
the rights of colonised people or ethnic and indigenous minorities
cards.quote: Human rights have come to be classified into three types. The first type is political rights such as freedom of speech and assembly. The second type is economic and social rights. The third type is the rights of colonised people or ethnic and indigenous minorities.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which developments since the 1990s led to the debate on UN intervention to stop human rights abuses?
cards.back: Since the 1990s, developments such as Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, the genocide in Rwanda, and the Indonesian military's killing of people in East Timor have led to a debate on whether or not the UN should intervene to stop human rights abuses.
cards.quote: Since the 1990s, developments such as Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, the genocide in Rwanda, and the Indonesian military's killing of people in East Timor have led to a debate on whether or not the UN should intervene to stop human rights abuses.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What are the two views on the UN acting against human rights violations?
cards.back: There are those who argue that the UN Charter empowers the international community to take up arms in defence of human rights. Others argue that the national interests of the powerful states will determine which instances of human rights violations the UN will act upon.
cards.quote: There are those who argue that the UN Charter empowers the international community to take up arms in defence of human rights. Others argue that the national interests of the powerful states will determine which instances of human rights violations the UN will act upon.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How do income and population growth affect rich and poor states?
cards.back: High per capita income and low population growth make rich states or rich social groups get richer, whereas low incomes and high population growth reinforce each other to make poor states and poor groups get poorer.
cards.quote: High per capita income and low population growth make rich states or rich social groups get richer, whereas low incomes and high population growth reinforce each other to make poor states and poor groups get poorer.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What gap between countries does NCERT say disparity in income and population growth contributes to?
cards.back: Globally, this disparity contributes to the gap between the Northern and Southern countries of the world.
cards.quote: Globally, this disparity contributes to the gap between the Northern and Southern countries of the world.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which region has most of the world's armed conflicts and is also the poorest region of the world?
cards.back: most of the world's armed conflicts now take place in sub-Saharan Africa, which is also the poorest region of the world.
cards.quote: most of the world's armed conflicts now take place in sub-Saharan Africa, which is also the poorest region of the world.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What has poverty in the South led to?
cards.back: Poverty in the South has also led to large-scale migration to seek a better life, especially better economic opportunities, in the North.
cards.quote: Poverty in the South has also led to large-scale migration to seek a better life, especially better economic opportunities, in the North.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Migrants vs refugees: who they are.
cards.back:
migrants (those who voluntarily leave their home countries)
refugees (those who flee from war, natural disaster or political persecution)
cards.quote: International law and norms make a distinction between migrants (those who voluntarily leave their home countries) and refugees (those who flee from war, natural disaster or political persecution).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Must states accept refugees and migrants?
cards.back: States are generally supposed to accept refugees, but they do not have to accept migrants.
cards.quote: States are generally supposed to accept refugees, but they do not have to accept migrants.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Who are internally displaced people?
cards.back: people who have fled their homes but remain within national borders are called `internally displaced people'.
cards.quote: people who have fled their homes but remain within national borders are called `internally displaced people'.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which community is NCERT's example of an internally displaced community?
cards.back: Kashmiri Pandits that fled the violence in the Kashmir Valley in the early 1990s are an example of an internally displaced community.
cards.quote: Kashmiri Pandits that fled the violence in the Kashmir Valley in the early 1990s are an example of an internally displaced community.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the health epidemics NCERT lists as spreading rapidly across countries.
cards.back: Health epidemics such as HIV-AIDS, bird flu, and severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) have rapidly spread across countries through migration, business, tourism and military operations.
cards.quote: Health epidemics such as HIV-AIDS, bird flu, and severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) have rapidly spread across countries through migration, business, tourism and military operations.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What do epidemics demonstrate about states?
cards.back: Such epidemics demonstrate the growing interdependence of states making their borders less meaningful than in the past and emphasise the need for international cooperation.
cards.quote: Such epidemics demonstrate the growing interdependence of states making their borders less meaningful than in the past and emphasise the need for international cooperation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What minimum criterion must an issue meet to qualify as a security problem?
cards.back: To qualify as a security problem, therefore, an issue must share a minimum common criterion, say, of threatening the very existence of the referent (a state or group of people) though the precise nature of this threat may be different.
cards.quote: To qualify as a security problem, therefore, an issue must share a minimum common criterion, say, of threatening the very existence of the referent (a state or group of people) though the precise nature of this threat may be different.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: How do the Maldives and Southern Africa face different security threats?
cards.back: the Maldives may feel threatened by global warming because a big part of its territory may be submerged with the rising sea level, whereas for countries in Southern Africa, HIV-AIDS poses a serious threat
cards.quote: the Maldives may feel threatened by global warming because a big part of its territory may be submerged with the rising sea level, whereas for countries in Southern Africa, HIV-AIDS poses a serious threat

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Which tribe in Rwanda faced a threat to its existence in 1994?
cards.back: In 1994, the Tutsi tribe in Rwanda faced a threat to its existence as nearly five lakh of its people were killed by the rival Hutu tribe in a matter of weeks.
cards.quote: In 1994, the Tutsi tribe in Rwanda faced a threat to its existence as nearly five lakh of its people were killed by the rival Hutu tribe in a matter of weeks.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: What do non-traditional threats require, cooperation or military confrontation?
cards.back: We can see that dealing with many of these nontraditional threats to security require cooperation rather than military confrontation.
cards.quote: We can see that dealing with many of these nontraditional threats to security require cooperation rather than military confrontation.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: At what levels may cooperation in cooperative security take place?
cards.back: Cooperation may be bilateral (i.e. between any two countries), regional, continental, or global.
cards.quote: Cooperation may be bilateral (i.e. between any two countries), regional, continental, or global.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: Name the players that cooperative security may involve.
cards.back:
international organisations (the UN, the World Health Organisation, the World Bank, the IMF etc.)
nongovernmental organisations (Amnesty International, the Red Cross, private foundations and charities, religious organisations, trade unions, associations, social and development organisations)
businesses and corporations
great personalities (e.g. Mother Teresa, Nelson Mandela)
cards.quote: Cooperative security may also involve a variety of other players, both international and national--international organisations (the UN, the World Health Organisation, the World Bank, the IMF etc.), nongovernmental organisations (Amnesty International, the Red Cross, private foundations and charities, religious organisations, trade unions, associations, social and development organisations), businesses and corporations, and great personalities (e.g. Mother Teresa, Nelson Mandela).

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When may cooperative security involve the use of force?
cards.back: Cooperative security may involve the use of force as a last resort.
cards.quote: Cooperative security may involve the use of force as a last resort.

cards.subject: political_science
cards.front: When is non-traditional security much better served, regarding the use of force?
cards.back: Non-traditional security is much better when the use of force is sanctioned and applied collectively by the international community rather than when an individual country decides to use force on its own.
cards.quote: Non-traditional security is much better when the use of force is sanctioned and applied collectively by the international community rather than when an individual country decides to use force on its own.
